intro:
**The Narrative of the Oppressed and the Mirage of Tyranny**

Al-Qaṣaṣ, "The Stories," is the twenty-eighth chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 88 verses of late Makkan revelation. It is the final and most detailed of the three *Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm* chapters, taking its title from verse 25, where Moses arrives exhausted at the wells of Midian and recounts *al-qaṣaṣ* (the narrative of his life) to the venerable elder (traditionally identified with Shuʿayb or a righteous Midianite patriarch), who consoles him with the words: *“Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people.”* Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ is particularly renowned in Islamic history for verse 85, traditionally revealed at the station of Juḥfah during the Prophet's dangerous, sorrowful emigration (*Hijrah*) from Makkah to Madinah: *“Indeed, He who has mandated upon you the Qur'an will surely return you to an appointment / place of return (*maʿād*)”*—a divine guarantee that he would return victorious to the city from which he was being driven. The sūrah provides the most emotionally intimate, biographical account of the infancy, youth, exile, and prophetic commissioning of Moses found in the entire sacred text, framed as an explicit, living mirror for the persecuted Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and his companions.

**The Epic Biography of Moses and the Fall of Qārūn**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Qaṣaṣ is built around two monumental historical portraits: the political tyranny of Pharaoh versus the divine empowerment of Moses, and the financial hubris of Korah (*Qārūn*) versus the spiritual wealth of the righteous. The first movement (1–43) delivers the gripping, cinematic narrative of Moses: Pharaoh's murderous decree, the desperate mother of Moses inspired to cast her infant into the Nile, the baby fetched by the family of Pharaoh, the intervention of Moses' sister watching from afar, Moses refusing all wet-nurses until his own mother's breast is restored to him *“so that her eye might be comforted and she might not grieve and that she might know that the promise of Allah is true”* (28:13). It traces his youth: the accidental manslaughter of the Egyptian while defending an Israelite, the secret warning from a man running from the furthest end of the city that the council was plotting his execution, Moses fleeing in terror across the desert to Midian, watering the flocks for the two modest daughters of the elderly sage, being hired for eight or ten years of service, traveling with his family in the cold, seeing the divine fire at the side of Mount Ṭūr, receiving the staff and radiant hand, returning to confront Pharaoh. Pharaoh's minister Hāmān ordered to build a lofty brick tower to view the God of Moses, culminating in the drowning of the tyrant and his armies cast into the sea like refuse. The second movement (44–75) turns to the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, confirming that he was not present on the western slope of Sinai when the decree was given, nor among the people of Midian, but this revelation is a direct mercy from his Lord. It rebukes the pagan excuses that following guidance would cause them to be snatched from their land, and presents the tragic narrative of Qārūn (76–84): an Israelite had of such vast treasures that the mere keys to his vaults weighed down a band of strong men, who boasted that his riches were acquired through his own scientific intellect (*“I was only given it because of knowledge I have,”* 28:78). The sūrah describes the catastrophic climax: the earth splitting open and swallowing Qārūn, his palatial estate, and his gold into the subterranean void, leaving the materialistic onlookers who had earlier envied him to reflect with horror on their folly. The epilogue (85–88) delivers the promise of return to Makkah, commands the Prophet never to be an assistant to the disbelievers, and concludes with the immortal metaphysical declaration of verse 88: *“Everything will perish except His Face. To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.”*

verses.1:
> Ṭâ-Sĩn-Mĩm

**Three Letters That Halt the Reading**

The chapter opens with three letters pronounced one by one: Ṭā, Sīn, Mīm. Twenty-nine sūrahs of the Qur'an begin with such letter combinations — the ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿāt, the "disjointed" or separated letters, so called because each letter is recited in isolation, name by name, rather than blended into a word. The reciter who reaches this verse does not read a word; he spells. The pause built into that spelling is part of the text's rhetoric, because every human book a seventh-century Arab knew began by introducing its author or its subject, and this Book begins by asking to be sounded letter by letter before it says anything at all. Whatever the letters mean, their effect is immediate: the listener is told at the threshold that what follows is not arranged the way human speech is arranged, and that its authority will not rest on the conventions of oratory. Fourteen letters of the Arabic alphabet appear across these openings. The commentators observed that a Book revealed in plain Arabic (26:195 — *“in a clear Arabic tongue”*) should begin with bare letters of that same Arabic — a sign, several of them argued, that the challenge of the Qur'an was issued from inside the language, not from outside it.

**The Same Three Letters Open Two Moses Chapters**

Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm opens this sūrah and also Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:1 — *“Ṭâ-Sĩn-Mĩm”*), and the pairing deserves attention because the two chapters are a matched pair by theme. Chapter 26 carries the longest sustained account of Moses' confrontation with Pharaoh before the assembled court, complete with the contest with the sorcerers and the exodus. Chapter 28 carries the arc that chapter 26 leaves off — the birth in a genocidal Egypt, the killing in the street, the flight to Madyan, and the commission at the burning bush. The shared letters function like a series title. Sūrah al-Naml, which falls between them, opens with Ṭā-Sīn alone and the words “Ṭâ-Sĩn. These are the verses of the Quran; the clear Book.” (27:1). The letters therefore do not float free of context: they recur where the Qur'an is about to unfold its grandest continuous narratives, and the earliest listeners could have learned to hear them as a signal that a prophetic story was about to begin.

**How the Sūrah Was Learned and Passed On**

Ibn Kathīr opens his commentary on this sūrah with a report recorded by Imām Aḥmad from Maʿdīkarib. A group came to ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and asked him to recite *Ṭā Sīn Mīm* to them. He answered that he did not have it, and sent them to a man who had taken it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself: Khabbāb ibn al-Aratt. They went to Khabbāb, and he recited it to them. The report is small, but it shows how a sūrah moved through the first generation. Ibn Masʿūd was among the earliest and most learned reciters of the Companions, and he still would not recite from anything but a chain he could vouch for; he sent the askers to the one man in reach who had heard these letters from the Prophet's ﷺ own mouth. The Book that opens by spelling itself out was carried, from the first, by people who knew exactly whom they had learned each sūrah from.
verses.2:
> These are the verses of the clear Book

**Verses That Are Also Signs**

The word translated "verses" is āyāt, and the Qur'an deliberately stretches that word across two registers. An āyah is a sign — the alternation of night and day is called a āyah, so is the creation of the heavens, so is a miracle worked through a prophet — and the recited units of the Book itself carry the same name. By calling its own verses āyāt, the Qur'an puts the words a believer recites in the same category as the cosmos: both are evidence, both demand a verdict, and neither can be treated as decoration. A reader who accepts the rising of the sun as meaningful but the recited verse as literature has already failed the category. This chapter will go on to use āyah in the narrow sense as well, for the proofs Moses will carry into Egypt; the word's range is the argument. Revelation and creation issue from one Author, so their tokens bear one name.

**A Formula That Opens the Narrative Chapters**

The sentence is a formula, and its placements are the point. Sūrah Yūsuf opens: “Alif-Lãm-Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book.” (12:1). Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ opens its second verse with the same words (26:2 — *“These are the verses of the clear Book”*). Both chapters are narrative giants — the first tells Joseph from the well to the throne of Egypt, the second unfurls prophet after prophet before ending in the longest account of Moses before Pharaoh. The formula does for these chapters what a seal does for a decree: it authenticates the narrator before the narration starts. Stories are exactly the genre where a community expects embellishment, where the listener assumes the teller is shaping events for effect. The Qur'an plants its credential at the gate — this telling is not folklore polished by retelling but revelation accountable to truth — and then permits itself a storyteller's art with a clear conscience.

Ibn Kathīr's gloss on the adjective is worth keeping beside the formula. The clear Book, he writes, is the Book that is plain in itself and makes the reality of things plain: it tells what has happened and what will happen. Both senses are needed for the chapter that follows. The story of Moses is a report of what happened; the promise to the oppressed, sounded in verse 5, is a statement of what will happen. One adjective covers both, and the opening verse claims clarity for the future as confidently as for the past.
verses.3:
> We narrate to you ˹O Prophet˺ part of the story of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for people who believe

**A Part Deliberately Told**

"Part of the story" is the second claim, and it is the more striking one. The verse concedes selection openly: not the whole account, but a portion chosen for this audience at this moment. The Qur'an returns to Moses in more than twenty chapters, and the episodes shift — his infancy in this sūrah, his mission speeches in chapter 26, the wonders in chapter 20, his prayer for expansion of his chest in chapter 20 as well. Selection of this kind is a form of argument. The portion chosen here runs from a mother's despair to a fugitive's flight, and that arc is precisely the shape of the Makkan believers' own circumstances: hemmed in by a power that kills their sons, awaiting a deliverance they cannot see. A comprehensive chronicle would have buried the application; a selected episode aims it. The concession of partiality in the verse is what guards its truthfulness — no one claims the part is the whole, and the part is true as told.

Ibn Kathīr sets this verse beside the opening of the Joseph story, where the same voice makes the same claim (12:3 — *“We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the best of stories through Our revelation of this Quran, though before this you were totally unaware ˹of them˺”*). He reads the phrase *in truth* as a promise about the quality of the telling: the events are related as they really were, as though the listener were present and watching them himself. That is a strong claim for a "part" of a story. It means the selection is honest at the level of detail as well as at the level of choice. Nothing in the portion told has been shaped away from what happened, and the reader who was not there is being given the view of one who was.

**What Belief Reads in the Same Text**

Two readers can hold the same chapter and leave with different possessions. One leaves with an episode of ancient politics — an infant adrift, a palace intrigue, an extradition flight. The believer leaves with the machinery laid bare: that God's will ran beneath every scene, choosing the oppressed, turning the river into a corridor, feeding His enemy's household with the child who would end it. The Qur'an itself marks the difference later in this very sūrah, in the confession that most people do not know (28:13 — *“But most people do not know”*) — knowledge of the pattern is granted, not automatic. This verse therefore functions as a set of instructions appended to the story: read as a believer, which means read for the handling of God inside events, and the "part" told will turn out to be the part that matters.
verses.4:
> Indeed, Pharaoh ˹arrogantly˺ elevated himself in the land and divided its people into ˹subservient˺ groups, one of which he persecuted, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women. He was truly one of the corruptors

**Tyranny Organized Like a Census**

The verse sketches a system, not a mood. Pharaoh "elevated himself in the land" — the classical commentators read this as rule exercised through tyranny and oppression within his own kingdom, and some connect it to his claim, recorded elsewhere in the Qur'an, to be the highest lord of his people. Then comes the machinery: the population is divided into factions, one faction is marked down for persecution, and the persecution has a scheduled procedure — sons slain, women kept alive. Elevation, classification, and culling form one sequence, and the sequence is the essence of the verse. Tyranny in the Qur'an's portrait of Egypt is not the caprice of a hot-tempered king; it is administration.

Ibn Kathīr's gloss on the verse keeps the same order. *Elevated himself* means that Pharaoh was an arrogant oppressor and tyrant. The *groups* were classes he made of his subjects, each one assigned to whatever work of state he wanted from it. The group he weakened was the Children of Israel, who in Ibn Kathīr's words were at that time the best of people, and who were nonetheless put to the most menial labour and worked night and day for him and his people. He adds the point the verse's last clause invites: Pharaoh took his precautions against the boy he feared, and the precautions did nothing against the decree, because when God's term comes it is not delayed. The killing of the sons was a policy; its failure was written before it began.

**Why the Sons and Not the Daughters**

The text gives no reason for the asymmetry, and one classical commentator drew the right conclusion from that silence: the Qur'an records the practice without explaining it because the practice requires no defense to be recognizable — it is simply what domination does. The commentators did preserve explanations from the wider tradition, the commonest being that soothsayers or a dream warned Pharaoh of an Israelite boy who would end his kingdom. Two observations weigh against that as the driving motive. First, the same decree is reissued long after Moses stands before Pharaoh: his chiefs protest the threat Moses poses and Pharaoh answers, “We will kill their sons and keep their women. We will completely dominate them.” (7:127), and again later, “Kill the sons of those who believe with him and keep their women.” (40:25). Second, the Qur'an earlier summarized the whole Egyptian period as torment that included “slaughtering your sons and keeping your women” (2:49). The repetition across decades points to collective punishment as standing policy — a tool for keeping a subject people weak — rather than a single prophecy-panic. The Bible's own account of Pharaoh's order to the midwives (Exodus 1) records the same policy shape.
verses.5:
> But it was Our Will to favour those who were oppressed in the land, making them models ˹of faith˺ as well as successors

**Leadership Conferred on the Enslaved**

Two offices are bestowed, and both are startling in context. They are to be made "models ˹of faith˺" — leaders, in the classical understanding: people set foremost in faith and in commanding what is right — and they are to be made successors, heirs who inherit standing in the land. The Qur'an applies this leadership language elsewhere to prophets and to the righteous: it speaks of making guides who call to God by His permission, and of Abraham being raised to leadership for mankind. The pattern underneath the applications is consistent. Leadership in this Book is conferred on the lowly as a trust, never seized by the mighty as a prize, and the men and women who emerge from servitude carrying it testify by their origin to where authority comes from. Egypt's Israelites had spent a generation being told their lives were negotiable; the verse opens by handing them the one title Pharaoh's court could neither grant nor revoke.

**Heirs of a Land They Never Owned**

"Successors" names the inheritance, and the sūrah will not here specify its terms — but the Qur'an settles the question elsewhere, at the sea's far shore: “And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands, which We had showered with blessings.” (7:137). The inheritance was Egypt itself, its cultivated abundance and its standing — not seized as plunder by conquest's own logic, but transferred as a heir's portion after the previous holder forfeited it. The legal imagination of the verse is worth marking: a heir succeeds because the predecessor has died, and the verse has already confined Pharaoh's regime to corruption. What follows in the sūrah is the reading of a will.

Ibn Kathīr closes the promise with the two verses that record its payment. The first is the one quoted above, from the far shore of the sea (7:137, quoted above). The second is the summary at the end of the exodus account in Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:59 — *“So it was. And We awarded it ˹all˺ to the Children of Israel”*). He reads the two together as the receipt for this verse: what was announced here as intention was later recorded there as done, and the gap between the two is the whole story the sūrah is about to tell.
verses.6:
> and to establish them in the land; and through them show Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers ˹the fulfilment of˺ what they feared

**Established Where They Had Been Property**

The decree now names its second term: establishment in the land. The verb behind "establish" carries the sense of being given firm footing, empowerment, and settled authority — the very things the Israelites had been denied under a system that kept them landless and expendable. The geography sharpens the point: the land in question is Egypt itself, and the Qur'an elsewhere states the outcome without disguise, that the oppressed were made successors in its eastern and western parts (7:137 — *“And ˹so˺ We made the oppressed people successors of the eastern and western lands, which We had showered with blessings.”*). A people who could not lawfully keep their own sons are promised secure standing in the capital of the man destroying them. The verse therefore completes what the previous verse began: favor decided, leadership conferred, and now permanence granted. Nothing in the sequence depends on Israelite power, because at this stage of the story they have none — which is exactly the point, since the promise is issued as pure decree while the knives are still working.

The last clause of the verse is the one Ibn Kathīr lingers on. Pharaoh hoped that his strength and power would save him from Moses, and none of it helped him in the slightest. For all his standing as a king he could not oppose the decree of God, which is never overcome; what had been written from eternity, that Pharaoh would meet his end at Moses' hands, was carried out. The phrasing keeps the verse's own irony. Pharaoh, Hāmān and their soldiers *feared* one thing, and the fear was well informed. What they were shown was not a surprise but the arrival of exactly what they had organised the killing of the sons to prevent.

**Hāmān Beside the Throne**

The verse names Pharaoh's chief officer, and the naming is worth pausing over because Hāmān appears six times across the Qur'an — here and in verses 8 and 38 of this chapter, then in chapter 29, and twice in chapter 40, where his most famous commission is issued: “O Hamân! Build me a high tower so I may reach the pathways” (40:36) — the tower by which Pharaoh proposed to climb toward the God of Moses. The figure who can be ordered to mobilize the state's builders and materials for such a project is plainly the second man in the kingdom. That functional picture — deputy in authority, director of great public works — is what Muslim scholars who examined the identification question closely concluded the name should carry, treating Hāmān as a title of office on the pattern of "Pharaoh" itself, associated with the high priesthood of Amun and the supervision of construction. The office explains the texts; the texts are what the officeholder would have controlled.

**Six Mentions, One Assistant**

Trace Hāmān through the Qur'an and a single portrait emerges. He is named here at the politics of persecution (28:6 — *“and to establish them in the land; and through them show Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers ˹the fulfilment of˺ what they feared”*), again when the basket reaches the palace (28:8 — *“And ˹it so happened that˺ Pharaoh’s people picked him up, only to become their enemy and source of grief. Surely Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers were sinful”*), and at the tower project, where Pharaoh orders him to mobilize the builders (28:38 — *“Pharaoh declared, “O chiefs! I know of no other god for you but myself. So bake bricks out of clay for me, O Hamân, and build a high tower so I may look at the God of Moses, although I am sure he is a liar.”*).

Chapter 29 lists him among the punished councils of the past, and chapter 40 names him twice in the last act — at the court's vote to kill Moses (40:24 — *“to Pharaoh, Hamân, and Korah. But they responded: “Magician! Total liar!”*) and at the tower's commission (40:36 — *“Pharaoh ordered, “O Hamân! Build me a high tower so I may reach the pathways”*). Six mentions, and in every one he stands at Pharaoh's shoulder. The pattern is the office: the Qur'an never shows him acting alone, because his function in the story is to be the machinery of another man's will — the executor without whom the tyrant's decrees would remain rhetoric. That is why his presence at the persecution in this verse matters as much as his presence at the tower. Persecution on the Egyptian scale required administration, and administration required a Hāmān; the verse includes "their soldiers" in the same clause for the same reason. Guilt in this Book is not confined to the man on the throne, and the sūrah's later scenes of judgment will name the assistant among the ruined precisely because the record kept him beside his principal at every stage of the crime.
verses.7:
> We inspired the mother of Moses: “Nurse him, but when you fear for him, put him then into the river, and do not fear or grieve. We will certainly return him to you, and make him one of the messengers.”

**A Mother Told to Do the Unthinkable**

The command sequence is ruthless on its face: nurse him, and at the moment fear arrives, place him in the river. Every maternal instinct runs the other way, and the verse asks its first reader to feel the contradiction before resolving it. A mother's arms are the one place Egypt's decree cannot reach, and the instruction schedules their surrender for the very hour the danger peaks. Obedience here precedes explanation — she is not told how the river will help, only that she must not fear and must not grieve, and that the outcome is guaranteed twice over: he will be returned, and he will be made one of the messengers.

Ibn Kathīr relates, without naming a chain for it, the background that made the mother's fear so precise. When the killing of the Israelite boys had gone on for some time, the Copts complained to Pharaoh that at this rate the Children of Israel would die out and the Copts themselves would be left to do the heavy labour. So the order was changed: the boys were killed one year and spared the next. Aaron, on this account, was born in a year of sparing, and Moses in a year of killing. Pharaoh had midwives who went round the women, wrote down the names of those who were pregnant, and attended the births; a girl was left alone, and a boy was taken by the killers. Moses' mother, the report says, showed none of the usual signs of pregnancy and escaped the register, but when she gave birth to a boy she was left with the child and no plan. That is the point at which the verse opens, and it explains why the inspiration begins with a command to nurse him: he was already hidden, and the danger was the next visit.

**Inspiration Without Prophethood**

The verb is the Qur'an's revelation verb — We inspired — yet the recipient is a woman the tradition insists was not a prophet. The word's range in the Qur'an makes room for her: the same verb describes what God cast into the hearts of Jesus' disciples, and what He communicated to the bee, teaching it where to build its home (16:68 — *“And your Lord inspired the bees: “Make ˹your˺ homes in the mountains, the trees, and in what people construct”*) and how to draw its provision (5:111 — *“And how I inspired the disciples, “Believe in Me and My messenger!” They declared, “We believe and bear witness that we fully submit ˹to Allah˺.”*). Classical theology sorted such matters into prophetic revelation on one side and inspiration — a casting into the heart without office — on the other. One commentator argued pointedly that even had Gabriel conveyed this message, its arrival would not have made her a prophet, since the tradition holds by consensus that she was not one. The sorting matters for the verse's tenderness. God spoke to this mother directly enough that she could act on it, without conferring rank on her, because the situation required guidance and she was the one who needed it. Revelation's economy in the Qur'an is never wasteful of rank and never stingy with help.

**Two Prohibitions, One Peace**

"Do not fear or grieve" names two different wounds, and the commentators drew the line between them: fear suffers over what may come, grief over what has gone. She is forbidden both halves of maternal agony — the anticipated loss of the child she is about to release and the mourning for him once he is gone. The pairing belongs to a refrain the Qur'an reserves for the people of the Garden, who are told of themselves that “There will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.” (3:170). Placing that grammar in a mother's ear, on the riverbank, at the hour of surrender, amounts to handing her the peace of the saved in advance of the world to come.

**The River as a Road**

The river that carries death decrees for her people becomes, by command, the corridor of rescue. Chapter 20 tells the same moment with one more piece of equipment — “Put him into a chest, then put it into the river.” (20:39) — and the commentaries treat the two accounts as one narrative told at different resolutions, the chest named there and the river here.

Ibn Kathīr's telling of the chest fills in the routine that the two accounts compress. The mother's house stood on the bank of the Nile. She made a box into a cradle and nursed the child at home; whenever someone she feared came to the house, she put him in the box, set it in the river and tied it with a rope. One day, as the report he relates has it, a feared visitor came, she put the child in the box, and she forgot the rope. The water carried him past Pharaoh's house. The detail matters for the verse's tenderness. The command was not to throw the child away but to keep him within reach, and the day the reach broke was the day the promise took over: he came back to her not by the rope but by the return the verse had guaranteed (20:39, quoted above).
verses.8:
> And ˹it so happened that˺ Pharaoh’s people picked him up, only to become their enemy and source of grief. Surely Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers were sinful

**The Rescue Delivered to the Enemy's Door**

Of all the houses on the river, the basket drifts to the one under whose seal the killing decree went out. The verse does not flinch from the fact that the rescue was carried out by the enemy's own household — the people who pulled him up were the people whose policy had condemned him. Providence in this sūrah works by capture: the hunters are made the couriers, the wolf den is made the nursery, and the closer the child is brought to the center of Egyptian power, the more completely that power is penetrated. Any other deliverance — a fisherman's family, a village upstream — would have saved the boy and accomplished nothing more. This deliverance saves the boy and installs him, at state expense, at the exact point where Egypt's decisions are made. The verse's opening phrase, rendered "˹it so happened that˺", concedes the human view: from the riverbank it looked like chance, a floating box, a palace servant's idle curiosity. The verse then states the other view in the grammar of purpose.

**Lovability as Strategy**

How does a condemned Israelite infant survive intake into the household that kills his kind? Chapter 20 supplies the mechanism, spoken by God to Moses long afterward: “And I blessed you with lovability from Me ˹O Moses˺ so that you would be brought up under My ˹watchful˺ Eye.” (20:39). The charm that disarmed the palace was not the baby's luck; it was a deployed attribute, a sweetness assigned for the purpose. The detail repays attention because it shows the plan operating at the level of feelings. Pharaoh's household was not overpowered into mercy — no plague had yet fallen, no sign had been shown. They were moved, and the moving was managed.

Ibn Kathīr's account follows the box past the palace wall. Some of the servant women picked it up and carried it to Pharaoh's wife, not knowing what was inside and afraid to open it without her. When it was opened they saw a child with the most beautiful features, and God filled her heart with love for him as soon as she saw him. Ibn Kathīr gives two reasons for that love in one sentence: because she was blessed, and because God intended to honour her through the child and to bring about her husband's ruin through him. The verse's *only to become their enemy* is therefore not a twist added later. On this reading the love and the enmity were planted together, in the same moment, by the same hand that had sent the box (20:39, quoted above).
verses.9:
> Pharaoh’s wife said ˹to him˺, “˹This baby is˺ a source of joy for me and you. Do not kill him. Perhaps he may be useful to us or we may adopt him as a son.” They were unaware ˹of what was to come˺

**One Speech Against a Royal Mood**

The verse catches the moment of decision, and it is a woman who turns it. The household's default procedure for an Israelite boy was the knife; into that procedure the wife inserts a sentence that reframes the entire object: “˹This baby is˺ a source of joy for me and you” (28:9). Her grammar does the work — the pronouns fold Pharaoh into the blessing, making the child's survival a shared interest rather than her private sentiment, and the closing plea is a command to the king himself: do not kill him. One classical report imagines his reply — a comfort for you, but for me, no — and whether or not he said it, the scene it imagines is exactly the one the verse shows: the family's men see a threat, the wife sees a son.The political fact underneath the dialogue is that extermination policies run on unanimity. One voice inside the palace, placed to speak at the moment of intake, was enough to break it.

Ibn Kathīr names her Āsiyah bint Muzāḥim, and the reply mentioned above — a comfort for you, but not for me — is the one he records. When Pharaoh saw the child he wanted to kill him, fearing that he was one of the Children of Israel; she came to the child's defence and said the words the verse preserves. Ibn Kathīr's comment on Pharaoh's answer is the whole verse in miniature: it was true in both halves, for God guided her through the boy and destroyed Pharaoh at his hands. He reads *perhaps he may be useful to us* the same way, as a hope fulfilled beyond her measure, since through this child she was guided and brought to Paradise. The wish to adopt him he explains simply: she had no children from Pharaoh. And the closing clause, *they were unaware*, he glosses as their ignorance of what God had planned for them when they picked him up.

**Āsiyah in the Company of Four**

The Qur'an does not name Pharaoh's wife, but the tradition does, and it ranks her without embarrassment. The Prophet himself named her among the four women who stand at the head of the women of the worlds — Maryam, Khadījah, Fāṭimah, and Āsiyah — in a narration carried by Muslim (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2430). The Qur'an elsewhere records her own prayer, made under torture in her husband's house: “My Lord! Build me a house in Paradise near You, deliver me from Pharaoh and his ˹evil˺ doing, and save me from the wrongdoing people.” (66:11). Read together, the two texts give her a biography in outline: a believer living inside the tyranny, dissenting at the decisive moment in this verse, and finally asking for delivery from her own household. Her sainthood was not a withdrawal from that household into safety; it was exercised precisely at the point of intake, when her word was the last wall between one Israelite child and the state's blade.
verses.10:
> And the heart of Moses’ mother ached so much that she almost gave away his identity, had We not reassured her heart in order for her to have faith ˹in Allah’s promise˺

**A Heart Emptied to Its Walls**

The Arabic says the mother's heart became empty, and the translators reach for "ached" to carry the weight of a word that pictures a vessel scraped bare. The classical commentators read the emptiness precisely: a heart emptied of everything except the remembrance of her son and the grief of separation — no room left for patience, strategy, or self-command. Some noted that the verb can carry a morning sense, so that the verse would say morning found her heart already emptied, the sleepless night compressed into two words. The state described is the far edge of maternal endurance, and the verse does not treat it as failure. A mother who felt nothing at the river would have been the failure; the text's honesty about the emptying is what makes the next clause — the almost-disclosure — comprehensible. She was not weak. She was a woman holding the two heaviest things a heart can hold, the command of God and the body of her child, and the verse reports what that weighed.

Ibn Kathīr lists who read the word this way. That her heart became empty of everything in this world except Moses was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū ʿUbaydah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah, and he records no dissent from it. The near-disclosure he explains from the same emptiness: in the force of her grief she came close to telling people that she had lost a son, and she would have given herself away had God not given her strength and patience. The verse's last clause is therefore not a change of subject. The strengthening of her heart and her remaining among the believers are one gift, because the belief being tested was belief in a promise she had been given only hours before.

**The Emptiness Filled in the Verses That Follow**

The emptiness of the mother's heart is filled in the next verses: God restores him to her so that her eye may be comforted and she not grieve, which is stated as the purpose of the whole arrangement (28:13 — *“This is how We returned him to his mother so that her heart would be put at ease, and not grieve, and that she would know that Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true.”*). The Book gives the same account in the sūrah of Ṭā Hā, where the child is returned and the sister follows him (20:39–40 — *“˹Remember˺ when your sister came along and proposed, ‘Shall I direct you to someone who will nurse him?’ So We reunited you with your mother so that her heart would be put at ease, and she would not grieve.”*), and the mother's state before the restoration is described in the same language of a heart that has become empty. The verse's mention of her near-disclosure is what makes the secrecy of the whole plan visible: she was held back by the strengthening, not by her own resolve.
verses.11:
> And she said to his sister, “Keep track of him!” So she watched him from a distance, while they were unaware

**The Sūrah of the Tracking**

This chapter bears the name al-Qaṣaṣ — the twenty-eighth sūrah, Makkan, eighty-eight verses, titled in English "The Story." The Arabic root behind the name carries a double sense that this verse happens to stage: qaṣṣ is to follow a thing closely, to trace it. It is also to narrate what one has traced. The sūrah is both a following and a telling, and its eleventh verse hands the following to a little girl. The mother who cannot walk to the river herself sends the next best thing, a daughter unremarkable enough to move through a slave society's streets unexamined, and the girl's assignment — keep track of him — is the first act of narration's raw material in the chapter. Before the story can be told, someone must be able to see it. The Qur'an's title so points back to a child on a surveillance errand, which is as good a statement as any of the book's habit of loading its greatest weights onto the figures the world's stories use for scenery.

Ibn Kathīr notes that the sister was the elder child, old enough to understand what she was being sent to do, and he glosses the command as an instruction to follow the child's traces and gather news of him around the city. The three glosses he preserves on *from a distance* describe one craft from three angles. Ibn ʿAbbās said she watched *off to the side*. Mujāhid said she looked from afar. Qatādah said she began to look at him as though she were not really interested. The last is the most exact, because it names the skill the errand required: not distance alone, but an appearance of indifference in a street where interest in an Israelite baby could be fatal. The verse's *while they were unaware* is the report of her success.

**The Root That Names the Chapter and Runs Through Its Story**

The verb on the girl's assignment belongs to the root that gives this sūrah its name. Qaṣṣ in Arabic is to follow a thing closely, to pursue its trail — and, from that, to relate what the pursuit found. The chapter is called al-Qaṣaṣ, "the following, the stories," and this verse is where the root's two senses meet in one command: the sister is told to keep track of him, and what she tracks becomes the story. The root returns at the other end of the episode, when the fugitive stands at a well in Madyan and "told him his whole story" (28:25) — the trail followed in Egypt becomes the account given in a stranger's house, and the chapter's title brackets the whole arc.
verses.12:
> And We had caused him to refuse all wet-nurses at first, so his sister suggested, “Shall I direct you to a family who will bring him up for you and take good care of him?”

**A Problem Manufactured for a Purpose**

The design inside the difficulty is the verse's theology. The refusal does not merely save Moses from an unknown nurse; it manufactures the one vacancy in Egypt that only his mother can fill, and it manufactures it inside Pharaoh's own household, on Pharaoh's own initiative. Had the baby nursed contentedly from the first woman offered, he would have been raised to weaning by strangers, and the promise made to his mother — We will certainly return him to you (28:7 — *“We will certainly return him to you, and make him one of the messengers.”*) — would have needed another path. The refusal is that path. The pattern deserves naming because the sūrah will repeat it: providence in this chapter usually advances by arranging a problem, not by removing one. The mother's emptied heart, the sister's watching, and now the baby's hunger are all weights, and each weight is a hinge. The Qur'an's God does not wait for convenient openings; He schedules the inconvenience and then stands in it.

**The Sister's Proposal**

Into the manufactured vacancy walks the only person who knows the solution: a girl the court has never seen, suggesting a family — hers — in words that promise competence and discretion. Her brother's own account in chapter 20 compresses the moment: “when your sister came along and proposed” (20:40) is how the Qur'an later describes her entrance to Moses himself.

Ibn Kathīr fills in the scene between the refusal and the proposal. Once the wife of Pharaoh had come to love the child and had asked that he not be killed, the wet-nurses of the household were brought to him, and he would take milk from none of them. So the household carried him out to the marketplace, hoping to find a woman he would accept, and it was there that his sister saw him in their arms and recognised him without giving any sign. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report Ibn Kathīr carries, adds the danger her words created. When she offered to direct them to a family, they grew suspicious, seized her and asked how she knew these people would be sincere and would care for him. She answered that they would be sincere because they wanted the king to be pleased and hoped for his reward, and they let her go. The answer was true, and it gave nothing away.

**The First Sign Was a Refusal**

Moses' life will fill with signs — a staff that becomes a serpent, a hand that shines, a sea that opens — but the first of his signs is recorded here, and it is completely negative: a baby who will not eat. God's power is displayed as an inability, placed in the smallest body in the story, and the palace feels it as frustration without ever learning its name. The pattern is one the sūrah will keep: the instrument Egypt despises carries the blow Egypt cannot answer. A slave nation's son will judge its king; a stammering tongue (20:27 — *“and remove the impediment from my tongue”*) will out-argue its priesthood; a shepherd's staff will swallow its sorcery. Strength and significance run on different tracks in this Book, and the verse marks the crossing point early, in a hunger that no wealth could relieve. The wet-nurses of Pharaoh's capital — the finest milk Egypt could buy — were defeated by an infant's turned face, and the defeat was total: not one succeeded, not once. What the court read as illness was obedience, and what the mother read as God's doing (28:13 — *“This is how We returned him to his mother so that her heart would be put at ease, and not grieve, and that she would know that Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true. But most people do not know”*) was already, in the plan's own order, the opening sign of a prophetic career. The refusal also protected the secret at both ends. Had any nurse succeeded, the palace would have raised a child with no tie to Israel; because none succeeded, the one woman who could feed him was sent for, and the search for a nurse became the search that ended in his mother's arms.
verses.13:
> This is how We returned him to his mother so that her heart would be put at ease, and not grieve, and that she would know that Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true. But most people do not know

**The Promise Kept in a Feeding**

"so We returned him" — the verse announces its own key: the return promised at the riverbank (28:7 — *“We will certainly return him to you, and make him one of the messengers.”*) has been carried out, and the verse's opening word, so, invites the reader to study the mechanism. The promise was kept not by an angel striding into the palace with a verdict, but by a nursing arrangement that every participant understood as ordinary commerce. The mother is reunited with her son lawfully, publicly, and at Pharaoh's expense; the tyrant who could not tolerate one Israelite child now cannot function without him. The classical commentators identify God's Promise here as precisely this return, foretold when she was told to release him. The shape of the fulfillment is the lesson: no part of the promise was scaled down to fit the method. She received the child whole, alive, and restored — but the delivery route ran through the enemy's kitchen, which is where heaven's postal service apparently keeps its doors.

Ibn Kathīr's narrative gives the return its domestic shape. They brought the child to his mother, she gave him her breast, and he took it; they rejoiced and sent the good news to Pharaoh's wife, who called for the woman, treated her kindly and rewarded her well, never realising that she was the child's mother. Āsiyah asked her to stay in the palace and nurse him there. She declined: she had a husband and children and could not stay, but she would nurse him in her own home if that was wanted. Pharaoh's wife agreed, paid her a regular wage, and added gifts and clothing. Ibn Kathīr's own reflection follows the account: between the loss and the relief there was only a short time, a day and a night or thereabouts, *and Allah knows best*; and the One in whose hand all things lie gives those who fear Him a way out of every distress. He also notes the change the return worked in the mother. Having been promised that the child would be a messenger, she now knew it, and she raised him as a mother raises a son and as a believer treats a messenger.

**Comfort as a Stated Purpose**

The verse does something unusual with its grammar: it lists the mother's healing as an outcome in its own terms. Later in the Qur'an, the mother of Jesus receives the same solicitude under the palm tree, told to eat, drink, and be comforted when her labor is upon her (19:23–26 — *“So eat and drink, and put your heart at ease.”*).

**The Line of Knowledge Between Two Houses**

The verse splits its own cast into two kinds of knowers. On one side stands the mother, whose knowledge was purchased — a promise believed in terror, kept in silence, and then confirmed in her arms until she knew it was true. On the other side stands the palace, which handled the same events and remained exactly where it started: unaware (28:9 — *“Pharaoh’s wife said ˹to him˺, “˹This baby is˺ a source of joy for me and you. Do not kill him. Perhaps he may be useful to us or we may adopt him as a son.” They were unaware ˹of what was to come˺”*), unseeing, certain that its household had acquired a foundling. Nothing about the events themselves distinguished the two houses; the basket, the hunger, and the nursing contract were visible to both. What differed was the capacity to read them — the mother read because she had been given the promise, and the palace could not read because its whole way of seeing had no category for God's action in the world. The closing verdict — most people do not know — therefore draws a line through the story that no observer standing inside it could see. The sūrah itself is the instrument that moves its reader across that line: by telling what the palace could not see, it trains the believing audience in the reading skill the verse says most people lack.

The closing verdict Ibn Kathīr reads as a statement about consequences. Most people do not know the wisdom in what God does or the good ends He brings out of it, and so they judge an event by how it feels at the time. He sets beside it the rule the Qur'an states in another context altogether (2:216 — *“Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you and like something which is bad for you. Allah knows and you do not know”*). The mother's morning at the river is the rule's clearest case: the thing she dreaded most was the road by which her son came home, with a wage attached.
verses.14:
> And when he reached full strength and maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. This is how We reward the good-doers

**Forty, the Prophets' Hour**

The tradition fixed the numbers anyway. The commentators report thirty-three years for the first term and forty for the second, and forty is the age the Qur'an itself ties elsewhere to spiritual adulthood, in the verse commanding gratitude to parents: “when the child reaches their prime at the age of forty” (46:15). Forty is also, in Muslim tradition, the age at which Muhammad received the first revelation, and the pattern was read backward into the prophets generally — the age at which a man's judgment can carry a message. The precision should be held honestly: the commentators themselves disagreed on the split between the two terms, and the verse does not state a number. What the number-40 tradition preserves is the pattern — a long, unremarkable maturation before commission, prophethood arriving not to teenagers but to settled men. Moses at the burning bush will be a grown man with decades of formation behind him, and this verse is where the Qur'an notes the formation's completion.

Ibn Kathīr gives one early gloss for the gift and then a reading of the verse's place in the chapter. Mujāhid said that what was given here means prophethood; the *knowledge* Ibn Kathīr takes as knowledge of religion. And the sentence that follows the gift, he observes, opens the account of how Moses actually reached the station decreed for him. He reached it by way of the killing of the Egyptian, since that was what drove him out of Egypt to Midian, and Midian was where the road to the mountain began. The verse therefore does not close the youth of Moses with a reward and then start a new story. On this reading the reward and the next verse's disaster are one movement, and the man who is given wisdom in verse 14 is about to need all of it.

**The Same Payment Joseph Received**

The closing formula — This is how We reward the good-doers — is one of the Qur'an's refrain-verbs, sounded at the close of several prophetic stories, and its most striking repetition is in the previous sūrah's account of Joseph: “And when he reached maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. This is how We reward the good-doers.” (12:22). The near-identity is deliberate. Joseph — sold, enslaved, imprisoned — and Moses — hunted at birth, exiled by a killing — arrive at the same station by the same road: trials borne without corruption, followed by wisdom and knowledge as the recompense. The refrain also folds the mother back into the reward, since the commentators heard in the good-doers her endurance by the river; her son's formation is the verse's payment to her. The template the two verses share is the Qur'an's standing answer to the question of what virtue gets: not immunity from the trial, but a self equal to what comes after it.
verses.15:
> ˹One day˺ he entered the city unnoticed by its people. There he found two men fighting: one of his own people, and the other of his enemies. The man from his people called to him for help against his foe. So Moses punched him, causing his death. Moses cried, “This is from Satan’s handiwork. He is certainly a sworn, misleading enemy.”

**The Hour the Streets Emptied**

The verse times its scene with care: he entered the city at a moment of heedlessness, which the commentators most often read as midday, when the streets sleep in hot countries. The hour mattered because of who Moses was by then — a man raised inside Pharaoh's own house, identified with the court that owned the city, yet walking into its heart unrecognized. The commentators divided over how the non-recognition worked: some held that he was still understood to belong to Pharaoh's retinue, even called the son of Pharaoh. The heedlessness lay in the city's stupor at that hour; others held that he had already broken with the court and the people no longer remembered him.

Ibn Kathīr records the two timings with their chains, and he lets them stand side by side. Ibn Jurayj related from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the hour was between sunset and the night prayer. Ibn al-Munkadir related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that it was the middle of the day, and this second reading was also held by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Suddī and Qatādah. The two men in the fight he identifies from the same authorities: the one of Moses' own people was an Israelite and the other a Copt, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq all said. Mujāhid explained the blow as a punch of the fist, which is what the Arabic verb means, and the verse records that the man died of it. Ibn Kathīr adds that Moses took advantage of the fact that no one was paying attention; the hour was part of the act, not only its setting.

**"This Is from Satan's Handiwork"**

His verdict on the event names a third combatant: “This is from Satan's handiwork. He is certainly a sworn, misleading enemy.” (28:15). Moses does not blame the Egyptian's oppression, his own anger, or Israel's misery — he locates the fight's true author, the one who had engineered a quarrel so that the palace's favorite would become a killer in an ungoverned hour. The diagnosis carries the lesson the scene was built to teach. Partisanship — the raw summons of my man against their man — is the door Satan uses, because it recruits good people into escalated violence without ever presenting them a principle. Moses, the most powerful young man in Egypt, was managed in one afternoon into blood on his hands by his own side's emergency. He saw it instantly, and named it instantly, and the accuracy of his self-indictment is the first evidence in the sūrah of the wisdom verse 14 had just reported given to him.

**What the Verse Sets Up**

The verse takes Moses into the city at the hour when its people were unaware, and it puts him in the middle of a fight between one man of his own people and one of his enemies. Moses struck the Egyptian and killed him, and the verse records what he said afterwards: this is the work of Satan, who is an enemy that leads clearly astray. Then he prayed for forgiveness and promised never again to be a help to the wrongdoers, and the next day he found the same man in another quarrel and understood what he had taken on (28:18-19 — *“Then when Moses was about to lay his hands on their foe, the enemy said, “O Moses!”*). The Book tells the story with the man's own words in it, and it does not present him as a person who had his career planned.

**What the Commentators Explain**

The reports say Moses was grown and known in the palace at that point, and the quarrel he intervened in was between a man of the children of Israel and an Egyptian overseer. The Book describes the moment as the hour of heedlessness, and the commentators took it as midday, when the streets of the city emptied. The narrative matters for the sūrah's argument because everything Moses received later — the call, the signs, the mission to the king — was given to a man with this on his record, and the Book says so before it says anything else about him.

**Where the Account Goes**

From this killing the story moves to the flight to Midian, the years of work for the old man, and the return up the valley to the fire (28:22-30 — *“When Moses came to him and told him his whole story, the old man said, “Have no fear!”*). The sūrah draws the lesson at the end of the account, where the Prophet is told that he was not on the mountain when the call came and that the story is told as a reminder. The Book's method with its greatest messenger is the same as with everyone else: it shows the mistake, the prayer and the long road afterwards, and it tells the reader to take the whole of it.
verses.16:
> He pleaded, “My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me.” So He forgave him, ˹for˺ He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Answered Before the Plea Cooled**

The verse's hinge is its smallest clause: So He forgave him. No interval is recorded, no second request, no penance scheduled — the answer is carried in the same breath as the plea, and the closing names carry the reason: He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The Qur'an states the principle behind the scene as a standing rule: “Whoever commits evil or wrongs themselves then seeks Allah's forgiveness will certainly find Allah All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.” (4:110). The Prophet's own words carry the same rule into the details of a life: the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin (Sunan Ibn Mājah 4250, graded ḥasan by al-Albānī). What the verse adds to the principle is the speed. Forgiveness, in this scene, is not a bureaucratic outcome that follows processed remorse; it is the immediate posture of the One whose name the plea invoked. The future prophet learned at the scene of his worst act that his Lord's mercy did not need to be persuaded.

**The Same Confession Decades Later**

The Qur'an has Moses retell this event once, face to face with Pharaoh, and the retelling is faithful to the confession. Asked about the killing, the older Moses answers: “I did it then, lacking guidance.” (26:20) — an admission that names the same event, claims the act without excuse, and locates the failing where the original confession located it. He adds in the next breath that he fled from them in fear and that his Lord then gave him wisdom and made him a messenger (26:21 — *“So I fled from you when I feared you. Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers”*), which is this sūrah's sequence told in the first person. The consistency across the two tellings is itself evidence for the unity of the account: a fabricated tradition would have tidied the hero's worst hour. Instead, the Qur'an lets the man who will carry God's message to the greatest court on earth stand forever on the record as a man who killed, confessed in one sentence, and was forgiven in half of one.
verses.17:
> Moses pledged, “My Lord! For all Your favours upon me, I will never side with the wicked.”

**The Vow's Echo at the Summit**

Gratitude returns at the highest point of Moses' story, and God Himself raises it. At the commissioning, when Moses is elevated above all others by messages and direct speech, the command that seals the honor is: “So hold firmly to what I have given you and be grateful.” (7:144). The circle closes on the same duty this verse records him volunteering before he was ever commissioned. The beginning of his prophetic career and its exalted middle are bracketed by one instruction — be grateful — first self-imposed, then divinely commanded. The arrangement teaches what the Qur'an consistently holds about the relationship of the two: the gratitude God commands at the summit is not a new demand but the ratification of what the grateful do unprompted at the bottom. Moses' pledge in this verse, made by a fugitive with blood on his conscience, is the same act God will later command as a honor — which is as plain a statement as the Qur'an gives of where obedience and thankfulness meet.

**Allegiance Declared Before Any Office**

The pledge is remarkable for its timing: Moses declares his side before he holds any commission, before a single miracle, before God has addressed him even once. Identity in this Book precedes office — the two parties, the people of God and the party of the wicked, are joined by choice long before the choice carries authority or rank. Moses enlists in the first while holding the second's citizenship, and the enlistment costs him everything the palace offered. The vow also prefigures, with almost schematic precision, the role he will grow into: the man who promises never to support the wrongdoers will spend his prophetic career as the wrongdoers' named opponent, confronting the most complete wrongdoer his age produced. And the next morning shows the vow's fragility in his own hands — summoned again into the same quarrel, he moves to strike, and stops only because the enemy's tongue stops him (28:19 — *“Then when Moses was about to lay his hands on their foe, the enemy said, “O Moses!”*).

Ibn Kathīr's gloss on the two halves of the pledge is short and useful. The favours Moses names are the standing, power and blessings he had been given, which in his case meant a prince's upbringing inside the house that hunted his people. The *wicked* he vows never to side with are those who disbelieve in God and go against His commands. Put together, the pledge is a refusal to lend a palace-bred strength to the palace's purposes. It is spoken the morning after that strength has killed a man, and it names the only use of power the verse allows: not for the criminals, whoever they turn out to be.
verses.18:
> And so Moses became fearful, watching out in the city, when suddenly the one who sought his help the day before cried out to him again for help. Moses rebuked him, “Indeed, you are clearly a trouble-maker.”

**Morning After a Killing**

The verse opens on the state the killing left behind: fear, and vigilance — he watched out in the city. The commentators read the vigilance precisely: he was looking to see what consequences the death would produce, whether it had been seen, what the state would do. The pairing of the two words is the psychology of a man with a secret: fear supplies the dread, vigilance the scanning. Nothing in the verse suggests his fear was cowardice; a man afraid of nothing after killing someone in Pharaoh's capital would be a fool, since the state's response to an Egyptian's death at an Israelite's hands would fall on Israel's whole quarter. The verse also lets a day pass without narration — a day in which the death must have been discovered — and the silence prices the interval: Moses spent it inside the city he could no longer trust, at the center of the power he had now injured, waiting for the knock that had not yet come.

Ibn Kathīr's reading of the second day adds one detail that the verse implies and a reader can miss. The Israelite was not still in yesterday's quarrel; he was fighting a different Copt, and when Moses passed by he called for help against this new opponent. That is the ground of the rebuke. The word Moses uses, Ibn Kathīr explains, means one who plainly leads others astray and is manifestly given to evil, and it is applied to a man whose quarrels had already cost one life and were now inviting a second. The watching that opens the verse he glosses as turning around and looking out, waiting for the consequence of the killing to arrive. It arrives in the next verse, from the mouth of the man Moses had helped.

**A Rebuke Aimed at the Wrong Target**

Moses' answer is a sentence of blame: “Indeed, you are clearly a trouble-maker.” (28:18). The accuracy of the rebuke deserves to be tested, because the verse quietly complicates it. The man was a trouble in the sense that his quarrels kept summoning Moses into the open; but the death that made yesterday dangerous was delivered by Moses' own fist, and the verse has already — in Moses' own mouth — assigned that act to Satan's handiwork (28:15 — *“Moses cried, “This is from Satan’s handiwork.”*). The rebuke therefore tells only half the truth, and the half it omits is the one about the speaker. The Bible's parallel scene puts a gentler question in the same encounter — why would you strike your fellow? — aimed at the fighter, with Moses as bystander; the Qur'an makes Moses the accused rescuer and lets his irritation land on the client instead. The commentators were careful to note what the verse does not say: that the rebuke settles the guilt. Its function in the story is to show the friendship between the two men fraying under pressure, and pressure, in this sūrah, is the appointed instrument of revelation.
verses.19:
> Then when Moses was about to lay his hands on their foe, the enemy said, “O Moses! Do you intend to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land. You do not intend to make peace!”

**Yesterday Spoken Aloud**

The sentence that breaks Moses' cover is a question: “Do you intend to kill me as you killed a man yesterday?” (28:19). Its power lies in its tense. The killing had been private, unwitnessed as far as Moses knew, buried in a hour of urban sleep — and here it stands in the open street, packaged as an accusation, knowledge moving faster than any report Moses could imagine. The commentators traced the leak to the quarrel itself: the argument in verse 18 was loud enough to be heard, and suspicion did the rest. The scene teaches the physics of secrets: a deed done in heedlessness does not stay in the hour of heedlessness; it ripens in daylight until it speaks. The man's phrasing also does something crueler than exposure — it frames the killing as Moses' established character, "as you killed," a precedent rather than an incident. An accidental death, once spoken of this way, becomes a biography, and in a state like Pharaoh's Egypt, biography is enough to sentence.

Ibn Kathīr's account of the leak is more exact than the general one, and it turns on the Israelite's fear. When Moses moved to strike the Copt, the Israelite, out of his own cowardice and weakness, thought that Moses meant to hit him because of the rebuke, and he said in self-defence the words the verse records: do you mean to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? Until that moment no one knew of the killing except the two of them. The Copt heard it, carried the news to Pharaoh's gate, and Pharaoh, in a rage, resolved to kill Moses and sent men to bring him in. The secret was therefore not overheard; it was confessed, by the man Moses had saved, in front of the man Moses was about to save him from. The charge of tyranny came from the same frightened mouth, which is why the chapter never dignifies it with an answer.

**From Exposure to Exile**

The sentence names what Moses believed to be buried: the killing of the Egyptian the day before, which the sūrah has described as done in a moment of anger and followed by his own plea for forgiveness (28:15–16 — *“˹One day˺ he entered the city unnoticed by its people. There he found two men fighting: one of his own people, and the other of his enemies. The man from his people called to him for help against his foe. So Moses punched him, causing his death. Moses cried, “This is from Satan’s handiwork. He is certainly a sworn, misleading enemy.”*). The report reaching the town is the reason for the flight that follows: the man who warned him came running from the far end of the city with the news that the chiefs were deliberating on his execution (28:20 — *“And there came a man, rushing from the farthest end of the city.”*). The Book's account keeps the consequence attached to the act — the first killing did not go unnoticed, and the second was prevented by it — which is why Moses leaves Egypt as a man on the run.
verses.20:
> And there came a man, rushing from the farthest end of the city. He said, “O Moses! The chiefs are actually conspiring against you to put you to death, so leave ˹the city˺. I really advise you ˹to do so˺.”

**A Runner Outpaces the Council**

The verse opens with motion: a man comes rushing from the city's farthest end. The distance is the point — the warning travels faster than the process it warns about, because councils move at the speed of procedure while urgency moves at the speed of legs. The men the runner names are the malaʾ, the notables — the word the Qur'an uses for the leadership class that convenes against its prophets with grim regularity: the council around the Queen of Sheba, the chiefs of Moses' own later opponents, the assembly around Hūd and Ṣāliḥ, the notables of Shuʿayb's people, the courtiers plotting around Joseph's king. The class is consistent across the Book: not the mob, which can be moved, but the committee, which decides — landholders, priests, courtiers whose position depends on the arrangement a prophet has come to disturb.

Ibn Kathīr explains why the verse calls him simply *a man*. He earned the word by courage: he took a different and shorter route than the men Pharaoh had sent after Moses, and so he reached Moses before they did. The race is the verse's hidden picture. On one road the officers of the state are moving with the authority of a council's decision; on another a single man is running with nothing but his knowledge of the streets, and the single man wins. Ibn Kathīr glosses the conspiring as consultation among themselves about what to do with Moses, and the command to *leave* as an instruction to leave the land altogether, not merely the quarter.

**Who Was the Running Man**

The verse leaves him unnamed, and the commentators filled the silence in two directions: some said a believer from Pharaoh's own people, others an Israelite. The first suggestion recalls a later figure — the believing man of Pharaoh's household who, when the court votes to kill Moses at the height of his mission, stands up to argue the case (40:28 — *“A believing man from Pharaoh’s people, who was hiding his faith, argued, “Will you kill a man ˹only˺ for saying: ‘My Lord is Allah,’ while he has in fact come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?”*), introduced there as “A believing man from Pharaoh's people, who was hiding his faith” (40:28). Most commentators kept the two apart, and rightly: the believer of chapter 40 speaks openly in council at the crisis of the plagues, years after this scene, while this runner's act is covert and urgent. What the two figures share is the lesson of the verse: God's protection of His servants travels through people whose names history never asked for. The man is defined completely by function — he runs, he warns, he advises — and the sūrah grants him four clauses of direct speech and no identity, which is its own commentary on how deliverance is staffed.
verses.21:
> So Moses left the city in a state of fear and caution, praying, “My Lord! Deliver me from the wrongdoing people.”

**Exile From the City That Raised Him**

The man who owned no city leaves the only city he has ever known. Moses had been Egypt's adopted prince — housed, schooled, and identified with the court — and the verse records him walking out of it in fear, watching over his shoulder, a fugitive from the administration that considered him one of its own. The classical commentators connected the two descriptions — fearful here and fearful in the street scene before — as the same condition carried to its conclusion: he is concerned that Pharaoh's forces will catch and kill him. The completeness of the loss is easy to pass over. In one week Moses lost his standing, his cover, his client, and his country, and the sūrah spends no words mourning any of it.

Ibn Kathīr draws out what the flight cost the man making it. He left Egypt on his own, and he was not used to being alone; until that day he had lived in ease and luxury and in a position of leadership. The caution he glosses as turning to watch behind him, and the prayer as a plea to be saved from Pharaoh and his chiefs. He also records, with his usual care about what he cannot verify, that it was said an angel on horseback was sent to show him the way, and he leaves the report with the words *and Allah knows best*. The verse itself keeps to what is certain: a man who had never travelled alone walked out into the desert with a prayer for his only guide.

**The Crime Behind the Flight**

The Book explains the crime that caused the flight: Moses struck an Egyptian and killed him while defending a man of his own people, and the next day the same man asked him for help again, and the plot against Moses formed when it became known (28:15–20 — *“The man from his people called to him for help against his foe.”*). The sūrah's account is careful about Moses' responsibility, describing his own words of regret and his plea for forgiveness in the same passage (28:16 — *“He pleaded, “My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me.” So He forgave him, ˹for˺ He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*), so that the exile that begins here is a consequence of an act he had already repented. The Book records his departure at the same time in Sūrah al-Shuʿarāʾ, where he leaves fearing that they will call him a liar (26:21 — *“So I fled from you when I feared you. Then my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers”*).
verses.22:
> And as he made his way towards Midian, he said, “I trust my Lord will guide me to the right way.”

**The Right Way Running Through Strange Country**

The prayer's last phrase — the right way — will be answered within verses by a well, two women, an old man, and a marriage contract, which is the verse's own commentary: God's answer to prayers for guidance is usually a scene, not a syllable. Moses asked to be guided, and guidance arrived as a sequence of ordinary events that happened to be perfectly aimed — each one visible only as it occurred, none of them announced. The pattern is the sūrah's standing doctrine of providence, already displayed at the river and the palace, now operating in open desert.

Ibn Kathīr reads the prayer in two registers, and he says God answered it in both. Moses had taken a smooth and easy route and was glad of it, and the *right way* he asks for is first of all the straightest road to Midian. But the phrase is also the Qur'an's phrase for the straight path itself, and Ibn Kathīr writes that God did indeed guide him to it in this world and the next, making him one who was guided and who guided others. A prayer made about a road on a particular afternoon was heard as a prayer about a life, and both were granted.

**What the Journey Produced**

The Book reports what the journey produced: he arrives at the well of Midian and defends two women with their flock (28:23–24 — *“When he arrived at the well of Midian, he found a group of people watering ˹their herds˺.”*), and he is taken into the household of their father, who is identified by the commentators as the prophet Shuʿayb. The prayer of this verse is answered in a way the reader can trace, but the answer is not announced as a miracle: it comes as a well, a crowd, two women, and a man who offers a daughter in marriage and a term of years of work (28:25–28 — *“Then one of the two women came to him, walking bashfully.”*). The sūrah's providence is expressed in the ordinary sequence of events, and the verse records the prophet's trust before any of them had happened.
verses.23:
> When he arrived at the well of Midian, he found a group of people watering ˹their herds˺. Apart from them, he noticed two women holding back ˹their herd˺. He asked ˹them˺, “What is the problem?” They replied, “We cannot water ˹our animals˺ until the ˹other˺ shepherds are done, for our father is a very old man.”

**The Well as a Crossroads of Society**

The scene at the well is drawn from life as every desert society knew it: a water point, a queue of shepherds, animals pressing forward, and the day's whole economy arranged around the hours when the water is drawn. Wells in this world were more than infrastructure — they were meeting places, marketplaces, and the setting where strangers became guests, which is exactly what this one is about to become. The Qur'an stages the moment with documentary economy: a community of people watering, and apart from them, two women standing back with their flock. The camera angle is the fugitive's own — a man entering a strange country registers the water first, the crowd second, and the anomaly third. The anomaly is the two women waiting, and the verse's whole drama will grow out of that single observed exception. Providence, in this sūrah's method, rarely interrupts a scene; it hides inside one until the right question is asked.

Ibn Kathīr's glosses keep the scene physical. The two women were *holding back* their sheep from drinking alongside the shepherds' flocks, lest some harm come to the animals or to themselves in the crush. When Moses saw them he felt for them and took pity on them, and his question means: why do you not water your flock with these people? Their answer has two parts, and Ibn Kathīr reads the second as the explanation of the first. They cannot water until the men have drawn off, and their father is very old — that is, this is what has driven us to the position you see. The well of Midian had a queue and a custom, and the verse shows a stranger noticing whom the custom left standing at the back.

**The Turning Point of the Exile**

The meeting at the well is the turning point of Moses' exile, and the sūrah gives the whole sequence in the verses that follow: the watering of the flocks for the two women, the invitation to their father's house, the offer of marriage, and the contract of service (28:24–28 — *“Then one of the two women came to him, walking bashfully.”*). The place is the country of Midian, where the same sūrah will later place the well of the messengers in the story of Shuʿayb's people, and the Book elsewhere tells of Moses' marriage to the daughter of the man of Midian and the years he served (20:40 and the tradition's accounts — *“Then you stayed for a number of years among the people of Midian.”*). The scene is built on ordinary labour before it becomes the beginning of prophethood.

**What the Scene Shows**

The verse brings Moses to the well of Midian and puts two women waiting at the edge of it while the shepherds water their flocks, and the Book records his question and their answer: they cannot water until the men have gone, and their father is an old man. The picture is drawn from the life of every water point in Arabia and the Levant, and it gives the reader the social situation in three sentences. The verse then has Moses water the animals for them, and the verses that follow describe the prayer he made afterwards and the invitation from the father (28:24-25 — *“She said, “My father is inviting you so he may reward you for watering ˹our animals˺ for us.”*).

**What the Commentators Discussed**

The older commentators discussed the details the verse leaves out: the number of the women, the name of the town, and the reason the father had no sons to send with them. The reports name him as Shuʿayb, though some said the man was a different prophet or a righteous man, and the sūrah itself does not name him. The details the Book does give are the ones that carry the lesson: the two women keeping their distance from the men, the old father at home, and a stranger from Egypt who asked before he acted.

**What the Community Drew From It**

The passage became one of the Book's examples of modesty, of speech with a stranger, of helping without asking a return, and of the opportunity that follows a good deed. The jurists cited it in the chapters on water rights and on the distribution of a shared resource, and the commentators read Moses's prayer — my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me — as the model of a person asking with nothing in his hand. The sūrah tells the story to the Prophet in Makkah, where a stranger with no support was doing the same work, and the arrangement of the passage is the sūrah's own answer.
verses.24:
> So he watered ˹their herd˺ for them, then withdrew to the shade and prayed, “My Lord! I am truly in ˹desperate˺ need of whatever provision You may have in store for me.”

**FaQīr: The Grammar of Need**

The key word is faqīr, the state of dependence and poverty — used in the Qur'an both for material want and for the soul's standing before God, and Moses applies it to himself in the first person. The prayer's structure repays attention: he does not name what he needs. No bread, no shelter, no protection, no destination — need of whatever good You send down, addressed to a God who knows the inventory better than the beggar does. The commentators heard in the open clause the full condition of the creature: the man is not reporting a shortage; he is declaring a relationship — dependent, on watch, dependent on the Sender for the definition of "good" as much as for its delivery. The prayer is therefore the exact opposite of Egypt's theology, where Pharaoh proclaimed himself the source of his people's goods.

Ibn Kathīr records where the prayer was made and who heard it. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī said that the *shade* was a tree: he sat beneath it.
