And ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib said that when Moses spoke the words of the prayer, the women heard him. That second report changes how the next verse reads. The invitation that arrives walking bashfully is not only a father's reward for the watering; it follows a prayer that had been overheard by the people best placed to answer it. The man asked God for whatever good He might send, in the hearing of no one he could see, and the answer walked back from the house he had just helped.

**The Shepherd's Curriculum**

The Prophet said: Allah did not send any prophet but that he herded sheep — and when his companions asked whether it applied to him too, he answered that he had tended the sheep of the people of Makkah for a few qīrāṭs, a small wage (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2262). Moses is the hadith's standing illustration: the man who will shepherd a nation out of an empire learns the trade on an old man's flock in Madyan, for wages of room and bread. The curriculum is not accidental in this Book. Shepherding trains precisely the muscles a prophet needs — patience with the slow, protection of the weak from predators, endurance of solitude, and authority exercised without wealth or force.
verses.25:
> Then one of the two women came to him, walking bashfully. She said, “My father is inviting you so he may reward you for watering ˹our animals˺ for us.” When Moses came to him and told him his whole story, the old man said, “Have no fear! You are ˹now˺ safe from the wrongdoing people.”

**An Invitation That Arrives Walking Bashfully**

The verse follows the messenger before it delivers the message: one of the two women came to him, walking bashfully. The adverb is doing real work — it describes a gait that keeps its distance from every impropriety, and the tradition read it as the walk of a free woman managing a public approach to a strange man with modesty intact. The wording joins a hadith the Prophet himself spoke about this very scene: he described Moses as an extremely shy man who covered himself completely. Told how God once cleared him of slander when a stone ran off with his clothes and he chased it unclad before his people (reported in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Abū Hurayrah). The Prophet's Moses is the same man this verse shows — shyness as a constitution, not a mood — and the daughter who approaches him carries the matching quality. The invitation is issued by the shy to the shy, at arm's length, in daylight, for a stated and lawful purpose: wages owed for work done.

The reading of *bashfully* rests on ʿUmar. Ibn Kathīr records that the Commander of the Faithful described her as covering herself from the men with the folds of her garment, and he carries a second report through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from ʿAmr ibn Maymūn, in which ʿUmar said: *"She came walking shyly, putting her garment over her face. She was not one of those audacious women who come and go as they please."* Ibn Kathīr grades that chain ṣaḥīḥ. He reads her words with the same care. She did not invite him in her own name, which might have raised a doubt in his mind about her, but in her father's: my father is inviting you to reward you for the watering. And he reads the old man's reassurance as a statement of jurisdiction — calm yourself, you have left their kingdom and they have no authority in our land — which is why the fear that had driven Moses since the city gate ends in this verse and not before.

**The Story the Verse Sits Inside**

The invitation arrives after two acts we are told about a few verses earlier. Moses had reached the well of Madyan and found a crowd watering their herds and two women holding their animals back; he stepped in and watered for them (28:23 — *“Apart from them, he noticed two women holding back ˹their herd˺.”*). When they returned home, the father asked how they had managed, and the answer came from one of the daughters: *hire him for us; the best you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy* (28:26 — *“One of the two daughters suggested, “O my dear father! Hire him. The best man for employment is definitely the strong and trustworthy ˹one˺.”*). So the messenger who comes walking bashfully in this verse has already been examined — for strength in the work and trustworthiness with the animals and with the two women at the well. Her recommendation is a hiring, and her father's invitation is the offer.

**What Was Offered and What Was Asked**

The father's proposal has Moses' service as its payment: eight years, with the tenth optional, in a reading the commentators give as the marriage portion (28:27 — *“The old man proposed, “I wish to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you, provided that you stay in my service for eight years.”*). Later Islamic law would put the bride-price elsewhere, and the commentators noted the difference, because the story is a report of a custom rather than a legal precedent for the community of the Prophet. What matters for the reader is what Moses did with a decade of exile: he took the terms, worked them out, and walked away from Madyan a married man with a covenant kept — the fugitive from the killing in Egypt who had gone out with nothing.
verses.26:
> One of the two daughters suggested, “O my dear father! Hire him. The best man for employment is definitely the strong and trustworthy ˹one˺.”

**The Daughter Who Makes the Case**

For the second time in the scene, one of the two women takes the initiative — and this time the initiative is a hiring recommendation made to her own father. The verse records no embarrassment in the structure: the household's employment decision is argued, out loud, by a daughter, and the father proceeds to act on her analysis. In the sūrah's ledger of who acts and who is acted upon, the pattern is now unmistakable: the women of this story move its plot — the mother who released her son to the river, the sister who tracked him and spoke up in the palace, the queen who stayed the first decree. Now the daughter who turns a guest into an employee. The men, by contrast, are mostly institutions — a court, a council, a decree. The Qur'an's casting here was countercultural enough to stay startling, and it is framed not as exception but as competence: her argument is simply better than anyone else's in the scene.

**The Evidence Behind Her Verdict**

The father tested the recommendation, and Ibn Kathīr preserves the exchange from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Shurayḥ the judge, Abū Mālik, Qatādah, Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq and others. When she called Moses strong and trustworthy, her father asked her what she knew of that. She answered with two observations. He had lifted a rock that only ten men could lift, and that was his strength. And when she came back with him she had walked in front, and he told her to walk behind him and, if he lost the way, to throw a pebble so that he would know which way to turn; that was his trustworthiness. The daughter's verdict was not intuition. It was a report of two things she had watched him do, and the father hired on the evidence.

**Three Readers of Character**

Ibn Masʿūd placed her among the three most discerning people. The people with the truest insight, he said, were three: Abū Bakr in his judgment of ʿUmar; the man of Egypt who bought Joseph and told his wife (12:21 — *“Take good care of him, perhaps he may be useful to us or we may adopt him as a son”*); and the companion of Moses, when she said, *O my father, hire him.* The company is instructive. Each of the three saw, in a man who had nothing yet, exactly what he would turn out to be, and each acted on it at once. The words of Joseph's buyer are the very words this sūrah has already put in the mouth of Pharaoh's wife over a basket (28:9 — *“Perhaps he may be useful to us or we may adopt him as a son.”*); the daughter at the well is the second woman in the chapter to be right about Moses before anyone else was.
verses.27:
> The old man proposed, “I wish to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you, provided that you stay in my service for eight years. If you complete ten, it will be ˹a favour˺ from you, but I do not wish to make it difficult for you. Allah willing, you will find me an agreeable man.”

**A Dowry Paid in Years**

The old man moves from hiring to marriage in a single speech. The contract's architecture is one of the Qur'an's most instructive legal sketches: a daughter's hand offered against eight years of service, extendable to ten at the groom's own free choice, with the extra two expressly labeled a favor rather than an obligation. The structure answers a practical problem — Moses owns nothing with which to pay a dower — and solves it in the currency he does own: labor. The father converts his own wages claim into a marriage gift, taking what Moses owes him as an employee and gifting its worth to his daughter as her settlement. Islamic law would later name such arrangements precisely, and the Prophet himself ratified the principle in a reported case when a penniless man asked to marry: he asked what Qur'an the man knew, and married the couple for the sake of what he had memorised (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5087) — the dower measured in what the groom truly has. Moses has strength and trustworthiness; the old man prices the first and banks the second.

Ibn Kathīr's paraphrase of the offer keeps its generosity in view: eight years of tending the flock, and if Moses wished to give two more that was his to give, but if not, eight was enough; and the old man's last sentence means that he did not intend to press him, inconvenience him or argue with him. Ibn Kathīr then adds the one prophetic report he has for the scene. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that ʿAlī ibn Rabāḥ al-Lakhmī heard ʿUtbah ibn al-Nadar al-Sulamī, a Companion, narrate that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Moses, peace be upon him, hired himself out for the purpose of keeping chaste and to feed himself."* The report names the two goods the contract secured for a penniless man: a lawful marriage and bread. It is the Prophet's ﷺ own summary of why a future messenger spent a decade as a hired shepherd, and it leaves no room for reading the years as wasted.

**What the Contract Shows About the Law**

Two points in the arrangement stayed with the jurists and the commentators. The first is that the dower was paid in service, and Islamic law later recognized services as a valid dower: the Prophet married a man to a woman for what he knew of the Qur'an, (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5087), which fixes the principle that a dower need not be money. The second is the conditionality built into the terms by Moses rather than by the old man — *whichever of the two terms I complete, let there be no blame against me* — which the jurists read as the right of the one who owes a duty to choose among the alternatives offered, and as grounds for keeping a contract's written words as its measure. The verse before this one gives the father's words: eight years, and if you complete ten, that is from you. Moses chooses without being forced into the longer term, and the old man gains a son-in-law who will not be held to more than he agreed.

**What the Marriage Meant for the Story**

Moses' years in Madyan are the part of his life the Qur'an describes with the fewest words, and this verse is the hinge of them. He had left Egypt with a death sentence over him, and he came out of those years with a household, a trade, and a father-in-law who had measured him at a well and offered him a place. The next scene in the sūrah finds him travelling with his family at night, and the fire he sees on the mountain road is what ends the exile (28:29 — *“He said to his family, “Stay here, ˹for˺ I have spotted a fire.”*). The contract at the well is where the fugitive becomes the man who can be sent back.
verses.28:
> Moses responded, “˹Then˺ it is ˹settled˺ between you and I. Whichever term I fulfill, there will be no ˹further˺ obligation on me. And Allah is a Witness to what we say.”

**A Fugitive Who Negotiates**

The answer is a contract clause, and its first lesson is the man delivering it: the refugee with nothing negotiates anyway. Moses accepts the offer — but he adds a term of his own, and the term is the whole speech: whichever of the two terms I complete, let there be no blame and no injustice toward me. The commentators noted the key word's range — ʿudwān names both aggression and injustice — so the clause protects him from either party's overreach: no guilt for taking the shorter term, no penalty for declining the longer. The man who has lived under a system where the strong rewrite terms at will builds the protection into his own contract's text. Slavery in Egypt was, at bottom, the impossibility of saying no to a term; Moses' first act of freedom is to say, in the plainest words available: the contract binds only as written. The fugitive who learned law in Pharaoh's courts writes his liberation's grammar in one sentence at a well in Madyan.

Ibn Kathīr explains the clause as Moses' own restatement of the terms. The matter is as you say: you have hired me for eight years, and if I complete ten that is my choice, but if I do the lesser I will still have kept the covenant and met the condition. The fuller term is allowed and remains something extra. He compares it to the pilgrim's choice at Minā (2:203 — *“Whoever departs swiftly on the second day is not sinful, neither are those who stay behind”*), and to the Prophet's ﷺ answer to Ḥamzah ibn ʿAmr al-Aslamī, a man who fasted a great deal and asked about fasting on a journey: *"If you wish, then fast, and if you wish, do not fast"* — even though, Ibn Kathīr adds, fasting was the better of the two on the evidence of other reports. The pattern is the same in all three cases. Two terms are offered; the shorter carries no blame; the longer carries more reward; and the choice belongs to the one who owes the duty.

**God as Witness to the Bargain**

The verse's last clause is the one the scene needed: *wa-Allāhu ʿalā mā naqūlu wakīl* — and God is a witness and a trustee over what we say. The old man had offered the marriage; Moses had added a condition; and the sentence puts the whole agreement under an authority neither party can escape. *Wakīl* carries the sense of one entrusted with a matter, and the use of it here means that the contract does not depend on the honour of either signatory or on the memory of what was said at a well. It is written where the terms cannot be edited, which is exactly what the man who had lived under Pharaoh's courts needed.

**Which Term Was Kept**

The next verse reports the outcome: when Moses had completed the term and was travelling with his family, he saw the fire at the mountain (28:29 — *“When Moses had completed the term and was travelling with his family, he spotted a fire on the side of Mount Ṭûr.”*). The commentators read the report as Moses' having fulfilled the longer of the two terms — the ten years — since the age of full strength and prophethood came to him once the service was done, and since the tie between the two men was finished honourably. The man who had asked for protection instead of payment walked away from Madyan with a family, a father-in-law's blessing, and a covenant that both sides had kept — and the next thing in his story is the summons at the burning bush.

The reading that he served the full ten rests on a report Ibn Kathīr takes from al-Bukhārī. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that a Jew from the people of al-Ḥīrah asked him which of the two terms Moses had fulfilled. He answered that he did not know until he had gone to the scholar of the Arabs and asked him, and he went to Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn ʿAbbās said: *"He fulfilled the longer and better of them, for when a Messenger of Allah said he would do a thing, he did it."* The answer settles the question by character rather than by arithmetic. A messenger who had spoken of ten years as a favour he might give would not, in Ibn ʿAbbās's judgment, have left it ungiven, and the next verse's *completed the term* is read in that light.
verses.29:
> When Moses had completed the term and was travelling with his family, he spotted a fire on the side of Mount Ṭûr. He said to his family, “Stay here, ˹for˺ I have spotted a fire. Perhaps from there I can bring you some directions or a torch from the fire so you may warm yourselves.”

**The Term Completed**

The contract runs its course in half a sentence: when Moses had completed the term. The commentators differed on which term — some held he served the eight and chose to complete the full ten; others counted ten and then additional years; the sūrah itself records only completion, and its silence lets the point stand: the man who insisted on bounded terms served them out whole. What the decade produced is visible in the clause that follows — he was travelling with his family: a wife from the household of a prophet, children, flocks, and the settled identity of a householder. The stateless fugitive of verse 22 owns a family now, and the road he travels is the road back toward Egypt, which he left in fear and approaches without yet knowing why. The sūrah's method of compression — three decades in half a verse, a decade in a clause — teaches its reader to measure formation, not duration: the term's worth is in what it built, and the building is done.

Ibn Kathīr, who takes the term to be the longer one on the strength of Ibn ʿAbbās's answer given under the previous verse, then relays what the narrators said about the journey. Moses missed his country and his family and resolved to visit them in secret, without Pharaoh and his people knowing; so he gathered his household and the flock his father-in-law had given him and set out. The night was cold, dark and rainy. They stopped to camp, and whenever he tried to light a fire he failed, and while he was puzzling over that he saw a fire burning far off in the direction of the mountain. Ibn Kathīr explains the two hopes in his speech from that setting: *some directions*, because they had lost their way, and *a torch*, so that they could warm themselves against the cold. The verse's family scene is therefore a scene of small failures — a route lost, a fire that would not catch — and the sūrah lets the greatest night of Moses' life open as a domestic errand that was going badly.

**The Two Terms Already on Record**

The sūrah has already recorded the two terms of the agreement with Moses' father-in-law — eight years, and ten if he wished to complete the term — which is why the verse says he completed the term without specifying its length (28:27–28 — *“If you complete ten, it will be ˹a favour˺ from you, but I do not wish to make it difficult for you.”*). The Book records the years of service in the same story in the sūrah of Ṭā Hā, where the mother is told that God has arranged the matter (20:37–40 — *“And surely We had shown You favour before”*), and the fire on the mountain then opens the call to prophethood (28:30 — *“But when he came to it, he was called from the bush in the sacred ground to the right side of the valley: “O Moses! It is truly I. I am Allah—the Lord of all worlds”*). The chapter's method is to pass over the ten years in half a sentence and to dwell on the night of the fire, since the account's purpose is the mission rather than the biography.

**What the Term Was and Why It Matters**

The verse says that when Moses had completed the term and was travelling with his family, he saw a fire on the side of the mountain and told his people to wait while he went to it. The commentators differed over the term: some read it as the longer period of the two the father had offered, which the reports give as ten years, and some as the shorter one of eight. The Book leaves the number open and states only that the term was completed, which the sūrah uses to mark the end of the years in Midian and the beginning of the mission.

**What the Fire Began**

The verses that follow give the call at the valley of Ṭuwā, the signs of the staff and the hand, and the command to go to Pharaoh (28:30-32 — *“But when he came to it, he was called from the bush in the sacred ground to the right side of the valley: “O Moses! It is truly I. I am Allah—the Lord of all worlds”*). The Book's account of the years in Midian is given in a few sentences, and the sūrah moves from the sheep to the burning bush without a break. The Sūrah of Ṭā Hā tells the same moment with more of the dialogue, and the two accounts together give the community the whole scene.

**What the Passage Teaches**

The sūrah has already said that God was preparing the man during the years nobody was watching, and the verse in front of us gives the end of that preparation without comment. The Book does not say what Moses had learned in the ten years, and it does not need to: the reader has watched a fugitive become a man with a family, a trade and a route home. The Sūrah of the Story tells the account to the Prophet in Makkah, and the arrangement of the passage is part of what it is saying to him.
verses.30:
> But when he came to it, he was called from the bush in the sacred ground to the right side of the valley: “O Moses! It is truly I. I am Allah—the Lord of all worlds

**Called From the Tree**

The fire he climbed toward answers him by name: he was called from the bush — the tree of the blessed spot, at the valley's right side. The geography is recorded with the care of an eyewitness: a specific slope, a specific side, a specific tree, and a voice issuing from it. The commentators held fast to the plain reading — God addressed His servant from the tree, as the verse says — and the earliest tradition wrapped the site in the vocabulary of sanctuary: the ground is holy because the address happened there, not the address because the ground was special. A bush burning without being consumed is the scene as later scripture frames it; the Qur'an's own frame is the call itself, and its first word is a man's name.

Ibn Kathīr fixes the geography by reading this verse with a later one. The call came from the side of the valley that lay on Moses' right, the side adjoining the mountain to the west, which is how he understands the sūrah's own later phrase (28:44 — *“on the western side of the mountain”*). It follows, he writes, that when Moses set out toward the fire he was walking in the direction of the qiblah with the western mountain on his right. He found the fire burning in a green bush on the mountain's side by the valley and stood amazed at what he saw, and then his Lord called him. The gloss on the words of the call is the theology of the whole scene: the One addressing you is the Lord of all that exists, who does what He wills, beside whom there is no god or lord, exalted above any likeness to His creation in His nature, attributes, words and deeds.

**God Spoke to Moses Directly**

The Qur'an states elsewhere, in one unadorned clause, what this verse stages: to Moses, Allah spoke directly (4:164 — *“There are messengers whose stories We have told you already and others We have not. And to Moses Allah spoke directly”*). The directness is the event's uniqueness — among all the messengers, Moses is singled out for speech without intermediary, and the later tradition enshrined him as the one God addressed face to face. The theologians of Islam would fight for centuries over the nature of that speech — whether God's word is created or uncreated, an argument that flared two centuries after the Prophet over the Qur'an's own status — and this verse stood near the center of the storm: if the words from the tree are God's speech, what exactly did Moses' ears receive?
verses.31:
> Now, throw down your staff!” But when he saw it slithering like a snake, he ran away without looking back. ˹Allah reassured him,˺ “O Moses! Draw near, and have no fear. You are perfectly secure

**The Staff's Career Ahead**

What Moses sees as terror, the sūrah's later verses will display as instrument. The same staff, cast at the same command in Pharaoh's court, will devour the sorcerers' illusions (7:117 — *“Then We inspired Moses, “Throw down your staff,” and—behold!—it devoured the objects of their illusion”*), and God's instruction in that hour tells the whole design: cast what is in your right hand, and it will swallow what they have fabricated (20:69 — *“Cast what is in your right hand, and it will swallow up what they have made, for what they have made is no more than a magic trick.”*). The trembling serpent on the mountain is therefore the audition of the court scene — Moses must first be mastered by the instrument he will master, because a messenger who has not feared his own sign cannot wield it before the mighty. The staff's biography in this Book runs from a shepherd's prop, to a serpent on holy ground, to the wonder that breaks Egypt's magicians, to the rod that splits the sea; and it begins here, in the gap between a man's running heels and his Lord's recall. The verse teaches what every subsequent sign will confirm: in God's hand, the ordinary is a deposited weapon, waiting for the command that arms it.

Ibn Kathīr connects the command to the exchange recorded in Sūrah Ṭā Hā, where Moses is asked what is in his right hand and answers (20:18 — *“It is my staff! I lean on it, and with it I beat down ˹branches˺ for my sheep, and have other uses for it.”*). The point of the question, he writes, is that the stick was the one Moses knew so well — the most familiar object he owned. His description of what it became is the description of a thing to be fled from: it moved fast for all its size, its mouth was huge and its jaws snapped, and it swallowed every rock it passed with a sound like a stone falling into a valley. Moses turned and did not look back, and Ibn Kathīr defends him in one clause: it is human nature to flee from such a thing. What steadied him was not courage but the command to draw near and the assurance of safety, and on hearing it he returned to where he had stood. The verse teaches the order in which fear is dealt with: the assurance comes first, and the return follows it.

**The Shepherd Meets the Shepherd**

Beneath the drama, the scene completes an identification that the sūrah has been assembling for two verses: the Lord who calls Himself the Lord of the worlds is addressing a man whose decade has been spent keeping sheep — and the first exercise of the call is handling a stray, of sorts, that will not stay put. The Prophet's words about the prophets' common trade — every one of them herded sheep (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2262) — find their deepest illustration here: the skills of the shepherd are exactly the skills the mission will demand, patience with the stubborn, protection of the scattered. The habit of putting the flock's life above one's own comfort. The serpent that spooked him and the recall that steadied him are the first lesson in that second shepherding: from this night forward, the flock will be a nation, the wolves will be Pharaoh's soldiers, and the staff will be everything it turned out to be. The scene's arithmetic of fear deserves the closing word: the object that terrified him and the object he will carry into court are the same length of wood. What changed was neither the staff nor the shepherd; it was the command's author. A thing in Moses' hand is a stick; a thing thrown at God's word is a sign — and the whole distance between superstition and revelation is measured in whose order set the thing moving.
verses.32:
> Now put your hand through ˹the opening of˺ your collar, it will come out ˹shining˺ white, unblemished. And cross your arms tightly to calm your fears. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. They have truly been a rebellious people.”

**The Hand in the Bosom**

The second sign is administered to Moses' own body: put your hand inside your collar and draw it out white, without blemish. The commentators identified the garment's opening — the jayb, the collar slit of the shirt — and noted the parallel account in chapter 20, where the hand is drawn toward the side; the two wordings describe the same gesture, the hand entering at the chest's opening and emerging transformed. The sign's design is exact: not a wound healed, not a limb restored, but purity produced where no defect was visible — skin shining white without the blight that whiteness usually means in affliction. The sign spoke the language of Egypt's own obsessions: a court that read omens in bodies was handed a body that showed the Giver's command over its substance. And it was given first to Moses in private — the messenger sees the proof on his own arm before the audience sees it on the mountain of their pride, because signs are entrusted before they are displayed.

Ibn Kathīr's glosses give each clause its measure. The hand would come out shining white, as if it were a piece of the moon or a flash of lightning, and *unblemished* means without any trace of the whiteness of disease. For the gesture he cites two early readings that agree: Mujāhid said it was to be free of terror, and Qatādah said to be free of fear. Moses was commanded, whenever he felt afraid, to draw his hand to his side, and the fear would leave him. Ibn Kathīr then adds a note of his own, offered as a possibility and not a ruling: perhaps if a person does the same, following the example of Moses, and places his hand over his heart, his fear will go or grow less, if God wills — and he closes the thought with the words *in Allah we place our trust*. The two proofs he identifies as the staff turned serpent and the hand drawn out white, clear evidence both of the power of the One who does as He chooses and of the truth of the man through whom they appeared; and the rebellion charged against Pharaoh's court he reads as disobedience toward God and defiance of His commands and His religion.

**The Two Signs Across the Book**

The two signs given to Moses are the staff and the hand, and the sūrah of Ṭā Hā lists them together when Moses is asked what is in his right hand and is answered with the command to throw it down (20:17–21 — *“˹Allah added,˺ “And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?”*). The same signs are worked before Pharaoh in the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf, where the staff becomes a serpent and the hand turns white (7:107–108 — *“Then he drew his hand ˹out of his collar˺ and it was ˹shining˺ white for all to see”*), and the verse here adds the instruction to press the arm to the body — the commentators explain the gesture as the way a startled man holds his arm to himself, since the whiteness of the hand could be mistaken for a disease. The signs given to one prophet belong to the same purpose as the sign asked of Muhammad in this sūrah's opening: the proof is granted by God alone.
verses.33:
> Moses appealed, “My Lord! I have indeed killed a man from them, so I fear they may kill me

**The Old Ledger, Opened at the Summit**

Moses stands at the summit of favor — addressed directly by the Lord of the worlds, equipped with two signs — and the first thing he places before his Lord is the street in Egypt: I killed a man among them. The confession he made once in private (28:16 — *“He pleaded, “My Lord! I have definitely wronged my soul, so forgive me.” So He forgave him, ˹for˺ He is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful”*) is now restated at the moment of commission, unprompted, as the objection that seems to him to disqualify the mission. The parallel account in chapter 26 records the same disclosure in the same position — they have a charge against me. I fear they will kill me — which shows how the Qur'an consistently frames the event: not as a sin re-hidden but as a fact re-declared whenever the mission approaches its danger. The commentators read the candor as the mark of the prophets' scrupulousness: a man who could have let the signs speak and stayed silent chooses instead to put his worst file on the table before the mission starts. The servant who confesses without being asked is the servant whose record needs no investigation.

**The Fear, Stated in Its Exact Weight**

The fear he names is specific: they will kill me. This is not anxiety about failure or stage fright before the court — it is the plain arithmetic of a wanted man walking into his victim's nation. Egypt's machinery has a decade-old killing of one of its own on file, with the perpetrator identified in public speech as a tyrant with ambitions (28:19 — *“You only want to be a tyrant in the land.”*); the mission requires him to stand in front of that machinery and announce the overthrow of its god. The Qur'an's honesty about this fear is part of its proof: a manufactured hero would arrive at Pharaoh's court already fearless, but the Book's chosen messenger arrives with his danger priced in his own words. The commentators noted the sequence in the prayer — the fact first, then the fear — as the anatomy of honest speech to God: state what you did, state what you dread, and let the two sit in the same sentence without excuses. Moses does not ask to be excused from the mission; he simply refuses to pretend the danger away.
verses.34:
> And my brother Aaron is more eloquent than I, so send him with me as a helper to support what I say, for I truly fear they may reject me.”

**The Strength Admitted**

Moses' second objection turns from his record to his tongue: my brother Aaron is more eloquent than I. The admission is precise — not that he cannot speak, but that his brother's speech is stronger where the mission needs it most, before the most formidable orator-class of the age. The parallel in chapter 20 shows the same confession in fuller anatomy: uplift my heart for me, ease my task for me, untie the knot from my tongue so they may understand my words (20:25–28 — *“so people may understand my speech”*). Moses speaks of a physical impediment in that account — a knot to be loosened — and the commentators treated the stammer as the plain sense of his request. The courage of the admission should be marked: before the Lord who equips him, the messenger does not perform confidence; he itemizes limits. The man who will carry God's word to Pharaoh begins by telling God exactly what the word will pass through — a heart needing strengthening and a tongue needing help.

Ibn Kathīr gives the reason for the impediment as the tradition gave it to him, without a chain: as a child, offered the choice between a date and a pearl, Moses picked up a live coal by mistake and put it on his tongue, and speech was difficult for him from then on. That is the knot he asks to have loosened in the prayer quoted above. Two further glosses sharpen the request. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq read *to support what I say* as *to explain to them what I say*, since Aaron could understand him where they might not. And Ibn Kathīr states the general rule behind the request in one line: the word of two carries more weight in people's minds than the word of one. The prophet is not asking for a better speaker in his place. He is asking for a second voice to the same testimony, and the reason he gives is the fear of being called a liar.

**Send Him With Me as a Helper**

The request is carefully framed: not send him instead of me — send him with me, as a support who confirms me. The commentators caught the distinction and its theology: prophethood is not transferable, and Moses is not negotiating his office away; he is asking for reinforcement inside it. The word for helper — one who buttresses from behind, in the root's own picture — names the role Aaron will hold for the whole mission: the elder brother, the first believer, the voice that strengthens the arm when the arm shakes. The structure also teaches what delegations are for in this Book: not the dilution of responsibility but the completion of it — one messenger carries the call, the second shores the carry. Moses' specific request — that Aaron support what I say — keeps the order of the mission intact: the speech remains Moses', the confirmation is Aaron's. God will answer by strengthening Moses' arm through his brother (28:35 — *“Allah responded, “We will assist you with your brother and grant you both authority, so they cannot harm you. With Our signs, you and those who follow you will ˹certainly˺ prevail.”*) — the reinforcement lands on the original messenger.

**The Fear of Being Rejected**

The stated ground of the request is the last clause: I fear they will deny me. The distinction matters because it shows what Moses thought eloquence was for: not persuasion by performance, but clarity enough to remove every excuse. A people whose rebellion is habitual (28:32 — *“Now put your hand through ˹the opening of˺ your collar, it will come out ˹shining˺ white, unblemished. And cross your arms tightly to calm your fears. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. They have truly been a rebellious people.”*) will deny a weak voice and deny a strong one; the strong one at least denies them their plea of never hearing it clearly.
verses.35:
> Allah responded, “We will assist you with your brother and grant you both authority, so they cannot harm you. With Our signs, you and those who follow you will ˹certainly˺ prevail.”

**Authority They Cannot Reach**

The second grant names the protection: an authority given to both, so that they will not be reached. The key word, sulṭān, is the Qur'an's term for binding authority — proof, warrant, dominion — and the same root describes Satan's admitted limit in his last-day confession: I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you answered me (14:22 — *“I only called you, and you responded to me.”*). Authority, in this Book, is always borrowed and always bounded — the question is whose warrant a power carries. The grant to the brothers is the counter-warrant to Egypt's: the state's whole apparatus of compulsion is bounded by the reach of the court's writ, and the verse sets God's given authority against it with a promise of non-reachability. The promise's fulfillment will be literal — Pharaoh's armies pursue to the sea and touch neither brother — and the commentators folded its meaning wider: no harm reaches the one under God's warrant except what He appoints, and what He appoints is never loss. The mission's protection is not the absence of danger; it is the ceiling on danger's reach.

Ibn Kathīr reads the answer as the granting of everything asked, and he ties it to the two verses that record the grant: the answer given in Sūrah Ṭā Hā (20:36 — *“All that you requested has been granted, O Moses”*), and the statement of Aaron's appointment (19:53 — *“And We appointed for him—out of Our grace—his brother, Aaron, as a prophet”*). He preserves a saying of one of the early generations on that appointment: no one ever did a greater favour for his brother than Moses did for Aaron, for he interceded for him until God made him a prophet and a messenger with him to Pharaoh and his chiefs. The *authority* he glosses as overwhelming evidence, and the promise that they would not be reached he explains by their role: they would be conveying the signs of God, and God protects the one who conveys His message. The last clause he sets beside the decree that governs every mission (58:21 — *“I and My messengers will certainly prevail”*). The victory promised to two men in a valley was not a special arrangement; it was the standing law of prophethood applied to them.

**Two Men Against a State**

The asymmetry deserves its arithmetic. Egypt in this sūrah is the complete power: a ruler styling himself god, a machine of administration (Hāmān), standing armies, and a demography of the knife. Against it, the verse deploys two brothers and a bundle of signs — and declares the outcome in advance. The world has never mistaken which side of that ledger counts its soldiers, and the Qur'an wants the ledger read precisely so: the verse's promises are not confidence-building rhetoric but the announcement of a different arithmetic, in which the Lord of the worlds' warrant outweighs conscription. The commentators' earlier notes gather here — the authority is sent down (11:96 — *“Indeed, We sent Moses with Our signs and compelling proof”*), the proof is manifest (23:45 — *“Then We sent Moses and his brother Aaron with Our signs and compelling proof”*) — and the pattern holds across the Book: God's victories are consistently staffed by the few and the weak, because the staffing is the argument. When two men prevail over the age's superpower by signs, no reader can credit the arm that won.
verses.36:
> But when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said ˹arrogantly˺, “This is nothing but conjured magic ˹tricks˺. We have never heard of this in ˹the history of˺ our forefathers.”

**The Court's Double Defense**

The reception is delivered in two sentences, and together they are the complete defensive architecture of a court cornered by evidence. The first sentence discredits the signs: nothing but invented sorcery — an explanation that accounts for the phenomena while refusing their source. The second sentence discredits the message: we never heard this from our forefathers — an appeal to inheritance as the measure of truth. The commentators treated the two answers as two registers of one refusal: the court cannot deny that something happened, so it denies the classification — magic, not miracle; novelty, not revelation. The design deserves naming because it has never gone out of use: when evidence cannot be denied, its source is relabeled; when doctrine cannot be answered, its novelty is itself made the charge. Moses' signs were clear — the verse says so — and their clarity is exactly what forced the court into explanations this flimsy.

**"We Never Heard This From Our Forefathers"**

The second defense is the verse's lasting exhibit, and the Qur'an hunts it across the Book: when it is said to them, follow what God has sent down, they answer, we follow only what we found our fathers doing — even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided? (2:170 — *“We ˹only˺ follow what we found our forefathers practicing.”*). One commentator made the verse's function explicit: it is a standing condemnation of blind conformity to ancestral belief, the argument that truth expires at the horizon of inherited memory. The reasoning's flaw is arithmetic: every doctrine now old was new at its beginning; every forefather honored by this court received his rites from someone who first introduced them. The Qur'an's own word for the load the ancestors carried is burden — the imagery of men carrying their loads on their backs (6:25 area — *“The disbelievers would ˹even˺ come to argue with you, saying, “This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables!”*) — inherited wrong honored precisely because it was inherited. Against it the verse sets Moses' claim: guidance is judged by its source and its proof, not by its age in a family's memory. The court's forefathers-argument measures truth with a clock; the verse's answer is that clocks do not think.

Ibn Kathīr is exact about what the court claimed never to have heard. It was not the signs, which were in front of them, but the call to worship God alone with no partner: we have never seen anyone among our forefathers following this religion, they said; we have only ever seen people who associate other gods with God. That identification matters. The novelty they objected to was monotheism itself, and the antiquity they appealed to was the antiquity of idolatry. Ibn Kathīr also notes what preceded the two sentences: the court saw the miracles with its own eyes and knew they were from God, and it fell back on stubbornness and false argument out of disbelief and pride, hoping to defeat Moses with tricks, position and power. None of it worked, but the verse records the attempt because the attempt is the permanent shape of an establishment refusing evidence.

**The Same Court in Every Age**

The verse's two defenses became the Qur'an's permanent inventory of rejection, and the sūrah's own audience had heard both recently in Makkah: the recitation called sorcery, and its message dismissed as what the ancients said or did not say. The commentators noted the pattern's reach — Abraham's people claiming they found their fathers doing so (21:53 — *“They replied, “We found our forefathers worshipping them.”*), the general verdict that none believes a warning unless he follows the way of the ancients.
verses.37:
> Moses responded, “My Lord knows best who has come with ˹true˺ guidance from Him and will fare best in the end. Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.”

**The Case Handed Up**

Moses' answer to the court's double defense is not a debate but a referral: my Lord knows best. The refusal to argue on the court's terms is the sentence's doctrine. The court has offered two classifications — sorcery and novelty — and Moses answers by relocating the question to the only bench with jurisdiction: who came with guidance from Him, and whose is the outcome of the Home. The commentators noted what the reply refuses: no entanglement in the court's categories, no defense of the signs' mechanics, no genealogical counter-argument about whose forefathers said what. The referral is not evasion; it is precision — the question the court is actually deciding is whose claim is true, and that question has exactly one competent Judge. A messenger's authority is never strengthened by accepting the opposition's framing; Moses answers the frame by dissolving it.

**Whose Is the End of the Home**

The second half of the referral moves the timeline: the true outcome is not the court's verdict today but the end of the Home — and the end, the commentators explained, carries both meanings the Arabic holds: the final outcome of the matter and the final abode, the Hereafter in its beatitude. The phrase relocates victory and loss to a horizon the court's power cannot touch: Pharaoh can rule the outcome of an afternoon; he cannot rule outcomes. The same standard appears on Moses' own lips to his people in chapter 7 — seek help through patience and prayer. The earth is God's, He leaves it to whom He wills, and the outcome belongs to the reverent (7:128 — *“The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous.”*) — and the sūrah itself will reserve the eternal Home for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth (28:83 — *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth.”*). The referral's timeline is so the mission's deepest comfort: the court's verdicts are provisional by definition, and the only verdict that stands is scheduled.
verses.38:
> Pharaoh declared, “O chiefs! I know of no other god for you but myself. So bake bricks out of clay for me, O Hamân, and build a high tower so I may look at the God of Moses, although I am sure he is a liar.”

**Bricks, Fire, and a Tower**

The practical command follows the creed: bake bricks for me, O Hāmān, and build a tower. The order lands where the sūrah's readers expect it — with the officer named at the persecution's beginning (28:6 — *“and to establish them in the land; and through them show Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers ˹the fulfilment of˺ what they feared”*) and again at the basket's landing (28:8 — *“And ˹it so happened that˺ Pharaoh’s people picked him up, only to become their enemy and source of grief. Surely Pharaoh, Hamân, and their soldiers were sinful”*), the permanent second man of the regime, here commissioning construction. The detail of the bricks carries its own history: fired clay and mortar belong to the building tradition of Egypt's Nile valley — where wood is scarce and kiln-baked brick is the old technique — and the Qur'an's choice of material fits the setting with the precision its critics spent a century denying. The tower's stated purpose is the creed's architecture: a stairway to the skies, to reach the God of Moses — or in this verse's wording, to look at Him. The commentators noted whether the structure was ever begun; the credible readings treat the command as theater — a demonstration for the chiefs, staging the state's answer to heaven's evidence. The bricks are the regime's reply to the signs: proof answered with public works.

**"So I May Look at the God of Moses"**

The tower's declared aim is an account of knowledge: Pharaoh will climb until he sees Moses' God, and sight will settle the dispute. The commentators heard the irony the story was built to deliver: the God of Moses is not located upward in creation's attic, to be observed from a taller building — He is the Lord of the worlds, nearer than the climber's own jugular. The tower is theology's category error built in baked clay. The Qur'an's account of Moses himself makes the point from the believer's side: even Moses, God's spoken-to prophet, could not bear the theophany when he asked for it, and the mountain crashed to dust (7:143 — *“When his Lord appeared to the mountain, He levelled it to dust and Moses collapsed unconscious.”*). Pharaoh's project so answers the wrong question with the wrong instrument: God is not found by ascending, but received by submission — and the tower, even finished, could only deliver its builder to a longer fall.

Ibn Kathīr's reading of the declaration begins with how it was received (43:54 — *“And so he fooled his people, and they obeyed him”*): Pharaoh called his people to acknowledge his divinity, and they answered him out of weak and foolish minds. On the tower itself he goes further than the readings given above. In his account the structure was built, and it was the tallest ever seen on earth, raised so that Pharaoh could show his people that Moses was lying about a god other than himself. He also records Ibn Jarīr's judgment about what Pharaoh's denial covered. The question for Pharaoh was never whether God had sent Moses, because he did not acknowledge the Creator's existence at all; that is why he had asked (26:23 — *“And what is ‘the Lord of all worlds’?”*), why he had threatened (26:29 — *“If you take any other god besides me, I will certainly have you imprisoned.”*), and why he tells the chiefs here that he knows of no god for them but himself. On either reading the tower was not a search. It was a piece of theatre built by a man who had already decided there was nothing to find, and the sūrah records the boast so that the sea can answer it.

**The Council That Cannot Say No**

The scene's staging completes its meaning: the declaration is addressed to the chiefs, the commission to Hāmān — the regime's whole machinery mobilized around one man's self-deification. No voice in the council registers the absurdity, because the system that produces the absurdity is the council: verse 4's factions, the notables class the Qur'an convicts across its pages, the administrators of the sons' murder. The commentators' political reading is exact: tyranny's final stage is not the tyrant's madness but the court's silence — the point at which no instrument of the state can cost the creed anything. The sūrah has already produced its contrast in the believing man of Pharaoh's house who will argue alone in this same council (40:28 — *“A believing man from Pharaoh’s people, who was hiding his faith, argued, “Will you kill a man ˹only˺ for saying: ‘My Lord is Allah,’ while he has in fact come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?”*), and his loneliness is the measure of the court's capture. Pharaoh says there is no god for you but me, and the silence that answers is the kingdom's true confession: it has one god, and he is speaking.

The claim is not new in his mouth — the sūrah's parallel accounts record him proclaiming to Egypt, I am your lord, the most high (79:24 — *“saying, “I am your lord, the most high!”*). Claiming not to know any lord besides himself — but here it is spoken in council, as state doctrine, with the chiefs convened to hear it.
verses.39:
> And so he and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land with no right, thinking they would never be returned to Us

**Arrogance in the Land, Without Right**

The verse reads like a coroner's summary: he and his hosts exalted in the land without right. The word for their self-exaltation is the same root the sūrah used of Pharaoh at his introduction — he exalted himself in the land (28:4 — *“Indeed, Pharaoh ˹arrogantly˺ elevated himself in the land and divided its people into ˹subservient˺ groups, one of which he persecuted, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women.”*) — and the verse's placement closes the biography with the same verb it opened: the man's whole career was one long rising in his own estimate. The phrase without right carries the legal weight: arrogance is not attitude but trespass — authority exercised where none was granted. The Qur'an's accounting of Pharaoh is consistent on this point from beginning to end: his crime is not strength but the claim that his strength owes nothing, the usurpation of a lordship that belongs, as his victim-nation's prayer will put it, to God alone. The soldiers are included in the verdict because they are the trespass's instruments: every hierarchy of violence that marched behind the claim shares its ledger.

Ibn Kathīr reads the two clauses as cause and belief. They were arrogant oppressors who spread corruption in the land, and they believed there would be no Resurrection; the second is why the first went unchecked. He sets beside the verse the two lines of Sūrah al-Fajr on men of the same kind: the scourge of punishment poured out on them, and the reason it could not be escaped (89:14 — *“your Lord is truly vigilant”*). The word for vigilance there is the image of one lying in wait on the road. Pharaoh's creed of no return assumed an empty road ahead; the verse that answers it says the road was watched the whole time.

**The Creed Measured Against the Verse**

The verse's two clauses are one syllogism in the sūrah's argument: arrogance in the land is enabled by the assumption of no return. The pairing recurs across the Qur'an — those who exult in the land and scheme against the blessing of God, and God's answer: My plan is flawless while they are give respite (7:183 area — *“I ˹only˺ delay their end for a while, but My planning is flawless”*); the ones who thought they would not return, and the opening of the gates of heaven's punishment. The commentators' refrain fits here: the certainty of the return is the load-bearing wall of all public morality. Remove it, and the strong do exactly what this verse records — exalt, and trespass, and price the weak at nothing. The sūrah's own closing verses will hang the moral directly: that Home of the Hereafter is given to those who seek no exaltation in the earth and no corruption, and the outcome belongs to the reverent (28:83 — *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth.”*). Pharaoh's biography and the believers' hope are set on the same scale: one creed of no return, one creed of the Home — and the sea will grade the exam.
verses.40:
> So We seized him and his soldiers, casting them into the sea. See then what was the end of the wrongdoers

**The Sea That Opened Both Ways**

The instrument deserves its own reading, because the sea is the story's oldest character. It carried the condemned infant to the palace in verse 8; it carries the condemners to the bottom in verse 40. The same water that served the decree's authors at their height executes the decree's judgment at their fall, and the symmetry is the sūrah's signature of providence: the plans of the powerful are written in a medium that belongs to Someone else. The Qur'an's fuller accounts add the detail the symmetry needs: the sea opened for Israel and closed over Egypt — the identical water serving as corridor and coffin within one night, selection exercised not by the tide but by the Judge. The drowning is recorded across the Book in seven separate chapters, and the repetition is doctrine: the event functions as the standing exhibit of how the return Pharaoh denied actually operates — suddenly, terminally, and by the very nature he ruled.

Ibn Kathīr's gloss on the seizure is one clause long, and it fixes the pace: We drowned them in the sea in a single morning, and not one of them was left. The whole apparatus the sūrah has taken forty verses to describe — the classes, the register of births, the knives, the council, the kilns — was closed in the time it takes a tide to turn. The verse's *So* is doing the work of a verdict: the arrogance of verse 39 and the seizure of verse 40 are one sentence in the grammar and one event in the record.

**The Believer's Water, the Tyrant's**

The Qur'an preserves one scene from inside the drowning that this sūrah's brevity omits: as the water closed, Pharaoh cried that he believed in what the Children of Israel believed (10:90 — *“But as Pharaoh was drowning, he cried out, “I believe that there is no god except that in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am ˹now˺ one of those who submit.”*) — and the answer he received fixed the scene's lesson for every reader: faith at the moment of the seizure is not the return, it is the return's arrival. The body of the man who claimed godhood was displayed as a sign for those after him, preserved where his army was not, a monument not of honor but of evidence.

**"Behold How the Wrongdoers Ended"**

The closing command — behold how the wrongdoers fared in the end — converts the event into an assignment. The refrain is one of the Qur'an's standing instruments: travel through the land and see how the deniers ended, addressed to every generation with roads and ruins (12:109 — *“Have the deniers not travelled through the land to see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before them?”*, 40:21 — *“Have they not travelled throughout the land to see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before them?”*). The seeing commanded is not tourism; it is induction — the reader is told to treat history as evidence, to walk the earth's wrecked empires and read the pattern the sea just displayed. The commentators heard in the refrain the verse's whole argument: God's judgments on the arrogant are not hidden events but public records, open to any walker with eyes. The command's plural address includes the sūrah's own audience — the persecuted Makkans, whose city's chiefs held the same creed as Pharaoh's — and its logic was meant to be acted on: caravans passed the dead towns of ʿĀd and Thamūd on every northbound journey, and the Qur'an kept asking what they saw there.
verses.41:
> We made them leaders inviting ˹others˺ to the Fire. And on the Day of Judgment they will not be helped

**Leadership Turned Inside Out**

The verse hands Pharaoh and his party the sūrah's oldest title — and reverses it. Verse 5 promised the oppressed they would be made models of faith; verse 41 announces the opposite appointment: We made them leaders inviting to the Fire. The same divine governance that raises the crushed to imamate raises the corrupt to infamy, and the parallel is the argument: leadership in this Book is always functional — a position from which others are led somewhere. Pharaoh led Egypt's institutions, its soldiers, its cult; the road he pointed down ended at the Fire, and the verse says so in the same grammar verse 5 used for the covenant. No reader can miss the symmetry or its harshness: God does not merely punish tyrants; He converts their rank into the measure of their ruin, because the higher the post, the wider the gate it opens for those who follow.

Ibn Kathīr explains whom they led. They became leaders to the Fire for those who followed them and took their path, rejecting the messengers and denying the Creator; the leadership is of a road, and the road has its own travellers in every age. The refusal of help on the Day of Judgment he reads together with the humiliation of this world: the two are joined and connected, and he cites the Qur'an's own summary of the destroyed nations (47:13 — *“there was none to help them”*). A leader whose followers cannot help him and whose Lord will not is the exact inversion of the promise made to Moses and his party six verses earlier.

**The Anti-Image of Moses' Party**

Set beside the promise to the followers of the signs — you and those who follow you will prevail (28:35 — *“With Our signs, you and those who follow you will ˹certainly˺ prevail.”*) — the verse completes a matched pair of processions. Two leaders, two invitations, two destinations: Moses calls to the Lord of the worlds through evidence; Pharaoh calls to himself through decree; and each party is defined by whose voice it walks toward. The Qur'an builds its whole social vision out of this figure — the word for party itself means a group distinguished by whom it follows — and the verse fixes the fire-bound procession's final state: leadership without help, followers without excuse. The sūrah's readers belong, by choice, to one procession or the other; there is no third road between the two imams.
verses.42:
> We caused a curse to follow them in this world. And on the Day of Judgment they will be among the outcasts

**A Curse With a Calendar**

The curse of this verse was not left as abstraction — the commentators identified its schedule: the plagues that struck Egypt in succession, the humiliations that stripped the regime's prestige decade by decade, and the final doom at the sea. Pharaoh's Egypt experienced its sentence in installments, each one public, each one aimed at the pretension named in verse 38: water turned to blood, the river that raised their foundling turned hostile, the sky and the granary alternately weaponized. A curse that follows is a curse with dates attached, and the dates teach as much as the blows: between the first sign and the last, the court was given every interval a heart could need to turn. The verse so records not a thunderbolt but a pursuit — measured, patient, and inescapable at its own pace.

Ibn Kathīr reads the curse differently from the plague-schedule given above, and the two readings are not rivals. On his account, God decreed that Pharaoh and his people would be cursed by the believers among His servants who follow His messengers, just as in their own time they were cursed by the prophets and their followers; the curse that *follows* them is the standing verdict of every believing generation. For the outcasting on the Day of Judgment he gives Qatādah's parallel, the sentence passed on the same Pharaoh in Sūrah Hūd (11:99 — *“They were followed by a curse in this ˹life˺ and ˹will receive another˺ on the Day of Judgment. What an evil gift to receive”*). The plagues were the curse in the body of Egypt; the curse in the mouths of believers has outlasted Egypt by three thousand years, and it is renewed every time this verse is recited.

**The Ledger Closes on Both Sides of Death**

Read whole, the verse divides the account cleanly: the curse belongs to this world, the outcasting to the next — and neither cancels the other. The commentators' larger point stands in the structure: worldly punishment is not the full sentence, and worldly success is not acquittal. Egypt's plagues were real; so was the Fire's invitation. The pairing corrects two errors at once — the believer who thinks the wicked always prosper until the last day, and the cynic who thinks the plagues settled the account. The sūrah's audience, watching the mighty of Makkah dine at leisure on confiscated reputations, needed the pairing exact: some sentences run in history, some run after it, and the Qur'an's God issues both against the same files.
verses.43:
> Indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture—after destroying earlier nations—as an insight for the people, a guide, and mercy so perhaps they would be mindful

**Scripture After the Wreckage**

The verse dates the giving of the Book with unusual care: after We had destroyed the former generations. The commentators named them — the people of Noah, of Lot, of Ṣāliḥ — the civilizations whose ruins studded the caravan routes of Arabia. The timing is doctrine, not chronology: the Torah entered history trailing the evidence of what refusal costs. Israel received its Book knowing that the world's earlier experiments in denial had test results — drowned, overturned, swallowed. Scripture's first readers were, in this sense, survivors' children, and the Book opened with an argument their eyes could still check: the tell-tale ruins. The Qur'an's own audience, hearing this verse in Makkah, stood in the same seat — their trade caravans passed ʿĀd and Thamūd's empty houses on every northern journey — and the verse's placement here, just after Pharaoh's drowning, hands the same inheritance forward: revelation always arrives trailing evidence.

Ibn Kathīr draws a line through history at this verse. The Torah was given to Moses after Pharaoh and his chiefs had been destroyed, and after its revelation, he writes, no nation was again punished with an overwhelming calamity of that kind; instead the believers were commanded to fight the enemies of God among the idolaters. The earlier pattern he illustrates from Sūrah al-Ḥāqqah, where Pharaoh, those before him and the overturned cities are listed together (69:10 — *“each disobeying their Lord’s messenger, so He seized them with a crushing grip”*). The gloss on the three gifts follows: *insight* is guidance out of blindness and error, *a guide* is guidance to the truth, and *mercy* is the showing of the way to righteous deeds. The verse thus marks a change in how God deals with rejection. Before the Book, the sea; after the Book, the Book itself, carried by a community charged to establish it.

**The Pattern the Verse Names**

The pairing of Scripture with destroyed generations is the sūrah's own refrain. The Book asks its readers again and again how many generations were cleared away, and how many towns were overturned (17:17 — *“˹Imagine˺ how many peoples We have destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord as All-Aware and All-Seeing of the sins of His servants”*; 19:74 — *“˹Imagine, O Prophet˺ how many peoples We have destroyed before them, who were far better in luxury and splendour”*), and it states the reason in the same breath: unjust people. The verse here adds the reason the Book was given to Israel at that point in their history, and the next verses complete the picture: God was not present with Moses on the mountain, and the revelation came to a people who had not had a warner for a long time, so that they could not say nobody had told them (28:46-47 — *“But ˹you have been sent˺ as a mercy from your Lord to warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, so perhaps they may be mindful”*). Book, gap and warning are one arrangement, and the verse states the timing as carefully as it states the gift.
verses.44:
> You were not there ˹O Prophet˺ on the western side of the mountain when We entrusted the Commandments to Moses, nor were you present ˹in his time˺

**The Prophet Was Not There**

The verse says that the Prophet was not on the western side of the mountain when the matter was settled with Moses, and that he was not among those who witnessed it. The verse is part of the account of Moses in this sūrah, and it states a fact about the man who is telling the story.

Ibn Kathīr places the verse in a family of statements that the Qur'an makes about its own narrator. God told the Prophet ﷺ about Mary in the same form (3:44 — *“You were not with them when they cast lots to decide who would be Mary’s guardian”*), and about Noah and his people (11:49 — *“Neither you nor your people knew it before this”*), and here, after telling the story of Moses from beginning to end, He says it again. The force of the series, in Ibn Kathīr's account, is the man it describes: an unlettered man who could not read books, raised among a people who knew nothing of these matters, speaking of events centuries past as though he had heard and seen them. The *western side* he locates precisely: the side of the mountain where God spoke to Moses from the tree, with the valley between. The sentence claims nothing for the Prophet ﷺ except absence, and it is the absence that makes the knowledge evidence.

**Why the Verse States This**

The people the Prophet was arguing with knew where he had been. He had never travelled to the mountain, he had never studied the books of the earlier communities, and there was no teacher in Makkah who could have given him this account. The verse puts that fact at the front of the story, and it lets the reader work out what it means: the account of a man who died thousands of years earlier, with details of what was said at a mountain and what happened in a valley, is being recited by someone who had no access to the events. The next verse tells the Prophet that he was not present with the people of Midian either, and the verse after that says what he did receive. The Book uses the same argument in other sūrahs when it says that the Prophet was not among the men who made the earlier accounts and that he had no book to read from (29:48 states that he never read a book before it — *“You ˹O Prophet˺ could not read any writing ˹even˺ before this ˹revelation˺, nor could you write at all. Otherwise, the people of falsehood would have been suspicious”*), and the sūrah of Yūsuf calls the stories it tells the best of stories and says that they came by revelation (12:3 states both — *“We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the best of stories through Our revelation of this Quran, though before this you were totally unaware ˹of them˺”*).

**What the Sūrah Has Been Doing With Moses**

The chapter has been reciting the account of Moses from the day he was put in the river to the day he spoke to God at the mountain, and it has been drawing a line between what the Prophet knew and what he was given. The verses before this one describe the promise given to Moses and the men who were asked to wait (28:43 — *“Indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture—after destroying earlier nations—as an insight for the people, a guide, and mercy so perhaps they would be mindful”* and the verses around it set the scene, and the same sūrah describes the early years of Moses at 28:7 — *“We inspired the mother of Moses: “Nurse him, but when you fear for him, put him then into the river, and do not fear or grieve.”* and the journey to Midian after that). The verse in front of the reader interrupts the account to state that the man reciting it was not present, which is how the sūrah turns the story into evidence.

**What the Verse Asks of the Reader**

The verse leaves the reader with the question the community in Makkah had to face: where did this come from? The sūrah will answer in its own words a few verses later when it tells the Prophet that he never expected the Book to be given to him and that it came as a mercy from his Lord (28:86 states it — *“You never expected this Book to be revealed to you, but ˹it came˺ only ˹as˺ a mercy from your Lord. So never side with the disbelievers ˹in their disbelief˺”*). The verse in front of the reader states the absence so that the answer to the question cannot be anything but the One who was present at the mountain. The Book says in the same sūrah that God chose Moses and spoke to him, which is the event the verse is pointing at (28:46 — *“And you were not at the side of Mount Ṭûr when We called out ˹to Moses˺.”* mentions the call from the side of the mountain, and 20:11 — *“But when he approached it, he was called, “O Moses”* through 20:14 — *“‘It is truly I. I am Allah! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me. So worship Me ˹alone˺, and establish prayer for My remembrance”* narrate it in full in the sūrah of Ṭā Hā).
verses.45:
> But We ˹later˺ raised ˹several˺ generations, and the ages took their toll on them. Nor were you living among the people of Midian, rehearsing Our revelations with them. But it is We Who have sent ˹this revelation to you˺

**Ages That Dissolve a Message**

The verse fills the centuries between Moses and Muhammad with one image: generations raised, and ages wearing them down. The commentators read the wearing-down morally — over the long stretch, people came to abandon the remembrance of God — and the image is exact: doctrines do not usually die by refutation. They die by erosion, each generation rubbing a little more off the stone, until what remains of a prophet's teaching is its calendar and its vocabulary. The verse so states, in one clause, the reason the Qur'an exists as a renewal: revelation is not defeated by time, but it is buried by it, and someone must dig. The same clause explains why every prophet's audience thinks its inheritance is original: the ages are long, and memory is short, and the erosion happens below the level at which anyone notices.

**Not in Midian Either**

The second denial completes the audit: you did not dwell among the people of Midian, rehearsing Our revelations with them. The verse closes the other road by which the Prophet could have "collected" the Moses material — the tradition of Shuʿayb's land, the storied well, the shepherd's decade. The commentators noted the completeness of the series: not at the mountain's western side, not in Midian, not in Egypt's story's other stations — the Prophet's biography contains no gap in which the study could have occurred. He was a boy who herded for Makkah's families, then a merchant on the Syrian run, then a husband, then a messenger; no desert decade, no monastery archive. The verse's dryness is its force: the hypothesis of borrowing is not answered by argument but by itinerary.
verses.46:
> And you were not at the side of Mount Ṭûr when We called out ˹to Moses˺. But ˹you have been sent˺ as a mercy from your Lord to warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, so perhaps they may be mindful

**The Mountain Named, the Absence Repeated**

The third denial in the series closes on the most storied location of all: the side of al-Ṭūr, the mountain where We called. The naming is pointed — of all the scenes the Prophet did not witness, this is the one his opponents' arguments leaned on, because the call at the mountain is where revelation as such happened: the direct address, the commission, the beginning of speech between God and man. The verse concedes the Prophet was not there and pivots in the same breath: but you are sent as a mercy. The pivot is the verse's whole logic — the Prophet's mission is not weakened by missing the mountain, because his office and Moses' office share one Sender; the absence of the experience is the presence of the commission. Arabia never heard a warner before him, which makes his arrival the region's first — the one claim no borrowed manuscript could confer.

Qatādah, in the report Ibn Kathīr gives, said that the call at the mountain's side is the call to Moses, and Ibn Kathīr explains why the sūrah returns to the same scene a third time under a new description. Verse 44 named the place and the commission; this verse names the *call*, which is the more specific thing, and the Qur'an speaks of that call elsewhere in the same terms (19:52 — *“We called him from the right side of Mount Ṭûr, and drew him near, speaking ˹with him˺ directly”*; 79:16 — *“His Lord called him in the sacred valley of Ṭuwa”*). The three denials are therefore not repetition. Each takes one layer of the event — where it happened, what was settled, what was said — and states that the man now reciting it was present for none of them.

**Mercy as the Mission's Job Description**

The verse names the Prophet's sending as a mercy from your Lord — the phrase the Qur'an elsewhere magnifies into his whole biography: We have sent you only as a mercy for the whole world (21:107 — *“We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world”*). The wording deserves the weight: the warning he carries is itself classified as mercy, because a warning is the data a soul needs to turn before the turn becomes impossible. The commentators paired the two clauses deliberately — a mercy to warn — so that neither softens into error: the mercy is not indulgence, and the warning is not wrath. For a man being stoned by the very people he was sent to, the verse supplied the identity that outlasted their verdict: his mission's category was fixed in heaven's vocabulary before his first audience, and no rejection on earth could amend it.
verses.47:
> Also so they would not say, if struck by an affliction for what their hands have done: “Our Lord! If only You had sent us a messenger, we would have followed Your revelations and become believers.”

**The Excuse God Retires in Advance**

The verse names the alibi it was sent to destroy: if punishment ever overtakes them for what their hands have done, they will plead that no messenger came. The commentators explained the grammar's elision that carries the logic: were it not that the deniers, when affliction strikes, will plead that no warner reached them, the punishment might have hastened — the Prophet's arrival is, in practice, the reason the sentence is still pending. The teaching is exact and severe: God does not destroy in haste, and the presence of a messenger among a people is the one document every other defense depends on. With the Prophet among them, the plea is pre-empted — no people on earth could say heaven's notice never arrived, because the man reciting in their marketplace was the notice.

Ibn Kathīr reads the verse as the closing of a door. The Prophet ﷺ was sent to them so that the proof would be established against them and no excuse would remain when God's punishment came for their disbelief; the plea that no messenger or warner had reached them was answered in advance. He gathers the verses that state the same principle across the Book: the rule for all the messengers (4:165 — *“so humanity should have no excuse before Allah after ˹the coming of˺ the messengers”*), and the address to the People of the Book about the long gap before this Prophet (5:19 — *“making things clear to you after an interval between the messengers”*). The Makkans had never had a warner; the People of the Book had gone centuries without one. The same sending answered both silences, and the verse says why: not because a messenger was owed, but because an excuse was not to be allowed.

**Lest the Punishment Come Early**

The verse implies a doctrine about the world's patience: the affliction their hands have earned is being withheld for the sake of the excuse's removal — mercy running ahead of justice. The commentators connected the teaching to the standing principle elsewhere in the Book: God does not destroy a people for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware (6:131 — *“This ˹sending of the messengers˺ is because your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware ˹of the truth˺”*), and never punishes until a messenger has warned (17:15 — *“And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺”*). The sequence is legal: hands commit, warning documents, then sentence falls. The verse so reveals how much of the world's apparent stability is forensic — generations standing in the dock's anteroom while the paperwork of their own defense is being delivered to their doors. The Quraysh heard this verse as living defendants: the punishment they mocked was late precisely because the messenger they mocked was present.
verses.48:
> But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, “If only he was given the like of what Moses had been given.” Did they not deny what had been given to Moses earlier? They claimed, “Both ˹Scriptures˺ are works of magic, supporting each other!” Adding, “We truly deny both.”

**Two Sorceries, Backing Each Other**
