The charge that finally surfaces is the conspiracy theory of refusal: two sorceries supporting one another — the Quraysh claiming the Torah and the Qur'an were co-conspirators, each lending the other false credit. The commentators preserved the variant readings: some heard sorcerers — Moses and Muhammad performing a two-man deception across the centuries. The absurdity is structural: to make the charge work, a book revealed across twenty-three years in a city of idolaters must have been coordinated, a millennium in advance, with a scripture preserved by a people the Arabs barely knew. But the charge's absurdity is its function: it explains the Qur'an's evident knowledge of Moses without conceding the source — the same maneuver as verse 36's invented magic, now upgraded to an alliance. Denial's last stage is always the order of the universe: the truth is too well informed to be false, so it must be organized.

Ibn Kathīr's account of the two readings differs in one detail from the one given above, and it should be recorded. Read as *two magics*, the phrase means the Torah and the Qur'an; this was Ibn ʿAbbās's view in the reports of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah and al-ʿAwfī, and Ibn Kathīr grounds it in the next verse, which asks for a book better guided *than these two*. Read as *two magicians*, the phrase means Moses and Aaron, working together and supporting one another; this was the view of Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Abū Razīn, and Ibn Kathīr calls it a good suggestion before adding *and Allah knows best*. He also lists what the objectors were asking for when they demanded the like of what Moses was given: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the parting of the sea, the shading cloud, the manna and the quails — and he points out that none of it moved Pharaoh's court, which answered (10:78 — *“Have you come to turn us away from the faith of our forefathers”*). The demand for Moses' signs was made by people who would have answered them exactly as Pharaoh did.

**The Sourcing They Hid**

The commentators transmitted a detail that completes the verse's indictment: the challenge itself was coached. The Quraysh, consulting the Jewish communities of their region about matters of prophecy, were told to test Muhammad by the Moses standard — the demand in this verse was proposed by people who professed Moses' book. The coaching proves the demand's insincerity twice over: the standard was suggested by outsiders precisely because it sounded unanswerable, and the suggesters themselves had not accepted the standard they recommended. The verse's audience is convicted by their own sources: the community that guaranteed Moses' signs supplied the measure, and the Quraysh wielded it without believing in the measure-maker. Refusal, the verse shows, will borrow from anyone — even the people whose book it intends to reject.

The coaching has a name in Ibn Kathīr's record: Mujāhid ibn Jabr said that the Jews told Quraysh to say this to Muḥammad ﷺ, and that the verse's reply followed. Ibn Kathīr then shows how often the Qur'an itself pairs the two books the objectors were rejecting together. The jinn who heard the recitation described it as (46:30 — *“a scripture revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it”*), and Waraqah ibn Nawfal, told of the first revelation, said that this was the Nāmūs who had come down to Moses. The pairing the Quraysh meant as an accusation was, in the mouths of the first believers, the recognition that made belief possible. Ibn Kathīr closes with his own ranking: of all the books sent down, none is more perfect, more eloquent or more noble than the Qur'an, and next to it stands the book given to Moses son of ʿImrān (5:44 — *“Indeed, We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light”*).

**The Demand and the Answer It Received**

The next verse meets the demand head on: say, then bring a book from God that is a better guide than these two, and I will follow it, if you are truthful (28:49 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Bring then a scripture from Allah which is a better guide than these two so I may follow it, if your claim is true.”*) — the Torah and the Qur'an being the two the verse has just named. The Book uses the same move wherever a proof is demanded of the messenger: the sign is turned back on the people asking for it, and if they cannot produce what they demand of him, the following verse draws the conclusion, that they are following nothing but their own desires (28:50 — *“Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people”*). The Book also answers the demand more fully in the sūrah of the Spider, where the men who insisted that signs come down on the Prophet are asked whether it is not enough that the Book has been sent down and recited to them, and the verse calls it a mercy and a reminder for a people who believe (29:50-51 — *“Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, ˹which is˺ recited to them. Surely in this ˹Quran˺ is a mercy and reminder for people who believe”*). The signs of Moses, the staff and the shining hand, are named in the Book itself (27:12 — *“˹These are two˺ of nine signs for Pharaoh and his people.”*; 20:22 — *“And put your hand under your armpit, it will come out ˹shining˺ white, unblemished, as another sign”*), and the point of the passage is not that the Prophet had no signs. It is that the men asking for a sign had already refused the greatest of them.
verses.49:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Bring then a scripture from Allah which is a better guide than these two so I may follow it, if your claim is true.”

**The Challenge Turned Around**

The command is a reversal: the men who demanded a Moses-standard from Muhammad are handed a standard of their own — produce a scripture from God that guides better than these two, and the Prophet will follow it. The commentators placed the verse in the Qur'an's family of standing challenges: produce a sūrah like it, calling your witnesses besides God, if you are truthful (2:23 — *“And if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it and call your helpers other than Allah, if what you say is true”*). Bring ten forged sūrahs (11:13 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Produce ten fabricated sûrahs like it and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”*); bring a single sūrah (10:38 — *“Or do they claim, “He made it up!”? Tell them ˹O Prophet˺, “Produce one sûrah like it then, and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”*); and the widest form — if all humans and jinn banded together to match this Qur'an, they could not, no matter how they supported each other (17:88 — *“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If ˹all˺ humans and jinn were to come together to produce the equivalent of this Quran, they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported each other.”*). Each challenge shares the anatomy: the burden shifts to the accuser, the criterion is public, and the stakes are total — the accuser's own claim requires the production. Verse 49's version is the family's most strategic member: it does not ask for eloquence but for guidance, the one quality the objectors had spent three verses conceding by accident.

**"Better Guided Than These Two"**

The criterion deserves its precision: a book from God that is better guided — more leading, more directing of human life toward truth — than the Torah and the Qur'an together. The commentators noted what the framing concedes and what it forecloses: it concedes that guidance is the proper test of scripture — not antiquity, not formatting, not miracles on demand — and it forecloses every answer except production. A critic cannot win by arguing that the Qur'an is beautiful, or ancient, or influential; the challenge asks only for a book that guides better, and the field of candidates is empty. The criterion also quietly restates the Qur'an's self-description from verse 43: the Book's function is insight, guidance, mercy — and the challenger is invited to beat the function, not the packaging.

Ibn Kathīr grounds the phrase *these two* in the Qur'an's habit of naming the two books together, and he gathers the places where it does so: the Book brought by Moses as a light and a guidance, followed at once by (6:92 — *“This is a blessed Book which We have revealed—confirming what came before it”*); and at the end of the same sūrah, the Torah given (6:154 — *“completing the favour upon those who do good, detailing everything, and as a guide and a mercy”*), followed by (6:155 — *“This is a blessed Book We have revealed. So follow it and be mindful ˹of Allah˺”*). The challenge in this verse assumes that pairing. The objectors had called the two books partners in a fraud; the Qur'an agrees that they are partners, states in what, and asks for a third that guides better. Ibn Kathīr glosses the closing condition, *if your claim is true*, as a reference to their whole effort to refute the truth with false arguments — an effort the demand for a better book exposes, since no such book was ever produced.
verses.50:
> So if they fail to respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who could be more astray than those who follow their desires with no guidance from Allah? Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

**Desire as a Competing God**

The Qur'an's word for the engine is desire in the plural — the caprices, the inclinations of the self — and its most famous usage makes the religious stakes plain: have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god? (25:43 — *“Have you seen ˹O Prophet˺ the one who has taken their own desires as their god? Will you then be a keeper over them”*). The phrase is exact: desire-worship is not metaphor but substitution — a will other than God's holds final authority in the person's decisions. The commentators traced the theme across the Book: prophets warned not to bend to the people's whims, rulers commanded to judge by what God sent down and not to follow their appetite. In this verse the plural matters: no single lust rules the deniers — a whole economy of preferences does, each negotiation between pride, habit, profit, and fear producing the day's refusal. Worship of desire is so polytheism of the moods, and the Quraysh's marketplace of idols had its exact double inside their chests.

**Guidance Withdrawn From the Wrongdoing**

The closing sentence states the settled rule: God does not guide the wrongdoing people. The commentators paired it with the verse of the sealed faculties — those who take desire as their god are left by God to stray knowingly, their hearing and hearts sealed, a cover on their sight (45:23 — *“˹And so˺ Allah left them to stray knowingly, sealed their hearing and hearts, and placed a cover on their sight.”*). The pairing defines the withdrawal precisely: it is not the removal of the Book — the Word has been steadily delivered (28:51 — *“Indeed, We have steadily delivered the Word ˹of Allah˺ to the people so they may be mindful”*) — but the removal of the Book's effect, guidance as inner traction. A person can hold a lamp and walk into walls; the sentence describes the second half of that process, the walking, which is the self's own doing. The rule's severity is the rule's mercy in the long run: a will that could be overridden would not be a will, and a guidance that compelled would produce the obedience of furniture. God's refusal to force the desire-enslaved is the price of having made them free.
verses.51:
> Indeed, We have steadily delivered the Word ˹of Allah˺ to the people so they may be mindful

**The Word, Delivered to Completion**

The verb is the verse's substance: We have steadily delivered the Word — carried it through, connected it piece to piece, brought it to its destination. The commentators gave the two classical readings: We elaborated the Word for them, and We completed the Word for them — both circling the same fact: revelation here is presented as a finished conveyance, not a fragmentary rumor. Them, the commentators noted, may mean the Quraysh, the Jews, or both — the Word's delivery is wide enough to name every party in the dispute the sūrah has been conducting.

**Stage by Stage, on Purpose**

The verse's adverb — steadily — carries the teaching about gradual revelation. The Qur'an defends the method elsewhere in its own words: the disbelievers asked why the Qur'an was not sent down all at once, and the answer was that staged delivery steadies the Prophet's heart and lets each portion land on its living moment (25:32 — *“˹We have sent it˺ as such ˹in stages˺ so We may reassure your heart with it.”*). The commentators read the method's wisdom across the twenty-three years of the mission: a law about orphans arrived when orphans were being wronged; a verse about treaties arrived when treaties were being tested. The Word, in other words, was not delivered to the abstract but to the actual — and the steadiness was its style: no century of silence between Moses and the Qur'an's own arrival, no lost interval for the ages to erode. The delivery the verse announces is the shortest, best-audited chain the message has ever had.

The three glosses the early readers gave the verb are preserved in Ibn Kathīr's record. Mujāhid read *we have conveyed the Word* as *we have explained the Word to them*, and al-Suddī said something similar. Qatādah's gloss is the one the sūrah's own shape confirms: He has told them what He did in the past and what He will do in the future. The past is the story the sūrah has just told — the river, the palace, the street, the sea. The future is the promise to the oppressed, sounded in verse 5 and paid at the water's edge. One delivered Word holds both, and that is what *steadily* means: the telling runs end to end, from what God did to the generations to what He will do for the ones made to wait.
verses.52:
> ˹As for˺ those ˹faithful˺ to whom We had given the Scripture before this ˹Quran˺, they do believe in it

**Believers Already Found in the Earlier Books**

Against the people who refused the message in the verses before, this verse sets a group the argument had forgotten: people who held a scripture before the Qur'an and believe in it when it arrives. The commentators named them. Among them was the rabbi ʿAbdallāh ibn Salām, whose first question on hearing of the Prophet's arrival was whether his prophethood could be true, and who declared his belief as soon as he was sure. Among them was Salmān al-Fārsī, who travelled through one faith after another before finding the last. Among them were Christian monks in Syria and Abyssinia, and Waraqa ibn Nawfal, who recognised the revelation at its very beginning.

The verse's work in the sūrah's argument is to supply evidence. The people best placed to test a new scripture, the custodians of the scriptures it claims to continue, were among the first to accept it, while the men who had no scripture at all demanded that it surpass two books they themselves rejected.

Ibn Kathīr sets the verse beside the family of verses that speaks of the same people, and his readings come from them. They are the ones given the Book who recite it as it should be recited (2:121 — *“Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed. It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it”*), and the ones who believe in God and in both revelations, humbling themselves before Him and never trading His revelations for a fleeting gain (3:199 — *“Indeed, there are some among the People of the Book who truly believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you ˹believers˺ and what was revealed to them. They humble themselves before Allah—never trading Allah’s revelations for a fleeting gain”*). The image he keeps from the family is the one from the story of the pen: when the Word is recited to those who were given knowledge before it, they fall upon their faces in prostration (17:107 — *“they fall upon their faces in prostration”*). The delegation the next section names is this family in the sūrah's present tense: the recitation reaches ears that had kept the sound, and the bodies answer before the mouths argue.

**Recognition, Not Just Conversion**

The wording is exact: they believe in it, and the "it" is this Qur'an. The commentators noticed how the recognition worked. People who knew what revelation feels like, its weight and its mark on the conscience, needed no committee to certify the Qur'an. They heard their own books speaking inside it. The sūrah has already quoted their testimony, that they find the coming Prophet described in their Torah and Gospel (7:157 mentions the description — *“˹They are˺ the ones who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whose description they find in their Torah and the Gospel.”*).

So the verse builds a chain of witnesses running through the objectors' own authorities. The people of Makkah rejected the Qur'an while citing Moses, and the people of Moses accepted the Qur'an while citing Moses. One of the two groups is misreading its own evidence, and the verse's place, immediately after the refusers' own words, lets the reader decide which group kept the experts.

**"Before It": The Priority That Prepared Them**

The phrase before it carries the verse's quiet teaching about preparation. Their earlier scripture was not old stock that had been superseded. It was training. This answers a worry running through the sūrah: the passage of ages had worn down the message between prophets (28:45 mentions the gap — *“But We ˹later˺ raised ˹several˺ generations, and the ages took their toll on them. Nor were you living among the people of Midian, rehearsing Our revelations with them. But it is We Who have sent ˹this revelation to you˺”*). But the wear was not the same everywhere. Here and there a person had kept the sound of the original in his ear, and those ears were the first to ring true when the Qur'an was recited.

**The Delegation That Heard It First**

Ibn Kathir records who these hearers were. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said this was revealed concerning seventy priests sent by an-Najāshī, the ruler of Ethiopia. When they came to the Prophet ﷺ he recited Sūrah Yā Sīn to them from its opening until he finished the sūrah; they wept and embraced Islam, and these verses along with others were revealed about them.

He attaches a second report that settles a practical question the verses raise. Imām Aḥmad records from Abū Umāmah that on the day of the Conquest of Makkah he was walking beside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as he rode, and the Prophet ﷺ said, among other beautiful words, *"Whoever among the people of the two Books becomes Muslim will have his reward twice, and he has the same rights and duties as we do. Whoever among the idolators becomes Muslim will have one reward, and he has the same rights and duties as we do."*

Those two reports answer different halves of the passage. The first explains the scene the verses describe — a delegation that recognised the recitation on hearing it, which is exactly what the verse says happens to those who were given knowledge before it. The second settles what followed for them: not a second-class membership but the same rights and duties, with the reward doubled rather than discounted. That detail matters, because a reader might suppose that arriving late to a revelation carries a penalty. The report says the opposite, and it was given at the Conquest, when the question of what newcomers were owed was not theoretical.
verses.53:
> When it is recited to them, they declare, “We believe in it. This is definitely the truth from our Lord. We had already submitted ˹even˺ before this.”

**"This Is the Truth From Our Lord"**

The declaration's middle beat is forensic: this is the truth from our Lord — the hearers identify the recitation's source by its family resemblance to what their Lord had already sent them. The commentators' note deserves its weight: these were the people whose lives had been shaped by Torah and Gospel — their prayer, their law, their stories — and their verdict is that the Qur'an is from the same Sender, not the same compiler. The identification is the precise refutation of verse 48's conspiracy charge: the two books cannot be co-conspirators, because one of them certifies the other as its colleague's genuine issue. The experts of the older document examined the newer and signed it — and the verse records the signature inside the newer document itself, a testimony that could not be forged without forging the whole.

The last clause of the confession carries a word the tradition defines. When they say *we had already submitted (even) before this*, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, in the report Ibn Kathīr carries, reads the submission as belief in the One God and sincere response to His commands, held before the Qur'an came. The claim is not that they held a copy of this Book. It is that they had kept the orientation this Book requires — one God, answered — and the recognition of the verse is that orientation meeting its own object. Their preparation was not information. It was a direction the new revelation arrived already pointing along.

**The Priority of Hearing**

That the verse builds recognition on recitation deserves its own reflection: the Qur'an's self-presentation as heard truth — in their own tongue, clear — is not a concession to an illiterate marketplace but a religious claim about how revelation travels: by voice, from lungs to ear to conscience, the oldest channel there is. The commentators paired the verse with the standing pattern of the faithful in every age — the Book heard, the heart answering before the committee convenes. The scene's economy is instructive against the Quraysh's procedures: they demanded delegations, standards, likenesses; the believing hearers of the Book performed the recognition in a sentence. What was missing in Makkah was never evidence; it was the ear that its evidence requires.
verses.54:
> These ˹believers˺ will be given a double reward for their perseverance, responding to evil with good, and for donating from what We have provided for them

The verse's first quality is the ground of the double reward, and it is patience — holding the truth when two Books agree on one sender is not easy for people, Ibn Kathīr notes, and the wage is paid for exactly that difficulty. The Ṣaḥīḥ report he sets beside the verse names the three who receive their reward twice, in the words the Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke, carried by Abū Burda from Abū Mūsa al-Ashʿarī: a man among the People of the Book who believed in his Prophet and then believed in me; a slave who discharged his duty to God and to his masters; and a man who had a slave woman and taught her well, then freed her and married her. The first of the three is the people of this verse, and the other two show the rule's reach: the double wage is paid wherever one faith stands on the back of an earlier faith kept honestly.

**Answering Bad with Good**

The second quality named in the verse is a policy rather than a mood. These people push back evil with something better. The Qur'an explains how that works elsewhere: good and evil are not the same. Answer evil with what is best, and the one between whom and you there is enmity may become a close friend (41:34 states the promise — *“Good and evil cannot be equal. Respond ˹to evil˺ with what is best, then the one you are in a feud with will be like a close friend”*). The commentators gathered the places where the Book repeats this virtue. It belongs to the servants of the Most Merciful, and it belonged to the household of Abraham. They also noticed what it produces: an attack that is answered well can turn the attacker.

For the people the verse describes, who had just accepted the faith, this was practical day-to-day guidance. Anyone who joined the Muslim community in those years often did so against the anger of his own family and town, and he would spend his first years as a believer answering exactly that anger with the better response. The verse is not asking for weakness. It hands over a weapon, because an answer that rises above the attack beats it.

**Spending Out of What Was Given**

The third quality completes the picture: they give out of what God has provided them. The wording matters. It says what We provided, which puts every possession back to its Source before any instruction to share it is given. The point the commentators draw is that giving is not a person handing over what is his own. It is passing along a trust that was placed with him.

For the community described here, the command was structural. It was made up of Makkan traders, Madinan farmers and refugees from both, and what held it together was this transfer. Families in Madinah sheltered the emigrants out of their own supplies. Placed beside patience and beside answering evil well, spending shows the balance of the portrait. These believers are not only patient and forgiving; they are the people who pay for others. Enduring, answering and giving: a whole community in three actions.
verses.55:
> When they hear slanderous talk, they turn away from it, saying, “We are accountable for our deeds and you for yours. Peace ˹is our only response˺ to you! We want nothing to do with those who act ignorantly.”

**The Ear's Discipline**

The verse opens on the battlefield of the ear: when they hear idle talk — the frivolity, the slander, the noise a hostile city produces daily — they turn away from it. The commentators read the turning as trained conduct, not temperament: the servants of the Most Compassionate are described elsewhere in exactly this posture — when the foolish address them, they answer with peace (25:63 — *“The ˹true˺ servants of the Most Compassionate are those who walk on the earth humbly, and when the foolish address them ˹improperly˺, they only respond with peace”*). The discipline matters because the ear is where most wars start: an insult is an invitation, and most of history's quarrels are two invitations accepted. These believers decline the venue: the talk passes their hearing and dies there. The verse's realism should be noted — it does not say they never hear; it says what they do once they have. Turning away is a skill, and the verse presents it as part of the double-rewarded character the previous verse began.

Ibn Kathīr reads the turning away as more than silence; it is separation. They do not mix with the people who indulge in the vain talk, and the Qur'an describes the same posture elsewhere in its portrait of the disciplined (25:72 — *“and when they come across falsehood, they pass ˹it˺ by with dignity”*). His gloss on the reply's last clause fixes what they refuse: if a foolish person speaks to them in a foolish manner and says something to which it does not befit them to respond, they turn away and never answer in kind with ugly speech — they say nothing but good words. The peace they offer is not the absence of a reply. It is the only reply the situation deserves, given once, and the conversation is not continued.

**Peace as a Complete Reply**

The reply they give is one word of surrender that is not surrender: peace be upon you. The commentators preserved the incident the tradition attached to the verse: certain People of the Book, entering Islam before Abū Jahl, were followed from the gathering by his abuse — and answered only with peace. The reply's lineage runs deep in the Qur'an: Abraham says it to his idolatrous father — peace be upon you. I will pray to my Lord for your forgiveness (19:47 — *“Abraham responded, “Peace be upon you! I will pray to my Lord for your forgiveness. He has truly been Most Gracious to me”*) — and its final form is the parting of ways spoken to deniers: you have your way, and I have my way (109:6 — *“You have your way, and I have my Way.”*). Peace, in this lineage, is not appeasement; it is the refusal to accept the quarrel's premise — that worth is contested in conversation. The word hands the speaker's dignity back to its Owner and closes the exchange without a casualty.

**Forbearance Without Surrender**

The verse completes the portrait that verse 54 began — patience, beautiful response, spending — and its placement is the lesson: the slander-response follows the double wage because forbearance is the wage's hardest installment. The commentators' summary deserves the close: these believers have truth without needing the last word, which is the test of possession. The quarrelsome are still bargaining; the secure have left the market. And the sūrah's own history sharpens the point: the same chapter that recorded Moses' restrained referral before Pharaoh's court (28:37 — *“Moses responded, “My Lord knows best who has come with ˹true˺ guidance from Him and will fare best in the end. Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.”*) now records the converts' restrained peace before Abū Jahl's abuse — the two scenes are one discipline at two scales. The Qur'an pays both with the same currency: the Hereafter's weights, where the last word is worth nothing and the kept soul is worth everything.
verses.56:
> You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best who are ˹fit to be˺ guided

**The Verse of the Beloved Uncle**

The tradition attached this verse to the hardest scene of the Prophet's life: the deathbed of Abū Ṭālib, the uncle who had raised him, shielded him through the boycott and the years of mockery, and refused the faith to the end. The Prophet urged him toward the word by which he could plead for him before God — and the old man's answer, recorded in the soundest collections, was that he would not say it lest the Quraysh mock that he said it only in fear of death (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1360). The verse descended on that grief: you do not guide whom you love. No verse in the Qur'an carries more consolation per word for the earnest, because it addresses the exact wound of every guide — that love is not a passport into hearts, and the best-beloved may die outside the door the guide stood knocking on for forty years.

The fuller report, in the Two Ṣaīḥs through az-Zuhrī, gives the scene its shape, and Ibn Kathīr preserves it in full. When Abū Ṭālib was dying, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and found Abū Jahl and ʿAbdullāh ibn Abī Umayya at his side. He said to his uncle: *"O my uncle, say: there is no god but Allah — a word by which I may defend you before Allah"* — and the two kept answering for him: *will you leave the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib?* He kept urging the word; they kept pressing the dynasty; and at the end he died on the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib. The Prophet ﷺ said then: *"By Allah, I will keep seeking forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden"* — and the forbidding came (9:113 — *“It is not ˹proper˺ for the Prophet and the believers to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives”*). The verse fell on that exact sequence: the love that could not carry the word, the word that would not be said, and the forgiveness that was prayed and then closed by revelation.

**Love Is Not a Lever**

The verse's teaching generalizes through the Qur'an's own gallery: Adam's son murdered his brother though their father was the first prophet; Noah's son refused the ark and drowned in sight of his father's call; Abraham pleaded for his idolatrous father until revelation closed the file — Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing (9:114 — *“Abraham was truly tender-hearted, forbearing”*). The commentators gathered the cases into the verse's doctrine: guidance is not a fluid that flows along affection, and prophethood itself confers no jurisdiction over the will. The teaching's mercy is its severity: it forbids the guide to measure his effort by its yield, since the yield was never his to command. The Prophet, who could persuade an empire's worth of strangers, could not move the man whose shoulder he had slept against — and the verse tells him, and every guide after him, that this asymmetry is the design, not the failure.
verses.57:
> They say ˹to the Prophet˺, “If we were to follow ˹true˺ guidance with you, we would certainly be snatched away from our land.” Have We not established for them a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺ to which fruits of all kinds are brought as a provision from Us? But most of them do not know ˹this favour˺

**The Fear They Confessed**

The verse quotes the Quraysh's true reason in their own words: if we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land. The commentators read the admission with care: the speaker concedes the guidance is real — the objection is not truth but consequence; they feared being ostracized by the surrounding Arabs, whose idols their sanctuary's economy served. The confession is the verse's exhibit: disbelief, in Makkah, was an economic position. The men who demanded miracles in verse 48 are revealed here as men who believed enough to calculate the price of believing — and calculated against it. The Qur'an's honesty about its opponents is again its mark: they are not quoted as fools but as men with interests, which is the more damning file.

**A Sanctuary With a Supply Chain**

The verse describes the haven with a provisioner's precision: to which the fruits of everything are brought — a safe harbor whose supplies arrive from every horizon. The commentators located the geography: Makkah, barren ground that grows almost nothing, fed by the caravans its sanctuary attracted — the Quraysh's own winter and summer journeys, the trading runs to Yemen and Syria, secured by the House's peace. The sūrah of the Quraysh names the same economy in its four verses: their security in the journeys and the feeding against hunger and the security against fear — all of it from the Lord of the House (106:4 — *“Who has fed them against hunger and made them secure against fear”*). The verse's point is the ledger's first line: the land they feared to lose was never their achievement; it was provision from His presence, delivered through the very sanctity they were trading away.

Ibn Kathīr's answer to the excuse turns it against itself. The sanctuary had been safe since it was built — safe through every season of idolatry its commerce ran under — and the question the verse poses is the one the Quraysh could not answer: how could the sanctuary be safe for them while they were in disbelief and shirk, and how could it not be safe for them the day they became Muslims and followed the truth? The fruits he traces come from the surrounding regions, from Ṭāʾif and elsewhere, with the trade goods of the caravans. The fear in their own sentence — *snatched from our land* — names a loss that could not happen the way they imagined, because the safety they feared to lose had never come from the thing they were being asked to give up.

**"But Most of Them Do Not Know"**

The closing clause returns the sūrah's oldest refrain — most people do not know — now aimed at the benefactors themselves: most of them know not that it is God who established them and kept them safe. The commentators' reading is exact: the ignorance is not of facts but of authorship. The Quraysh knew their market days and their alliance networks; what they did not know — or refused to file — was whose gift the arrangement was. The verse so completes the chapter's account of knowledge in miniature: the palace never knew its nurse was the mother (28:13 — *“But most people do not know”*), and the sanctuary never knew its Keeper was the Giver (28:57 — *“Have We not established for them a safe haven ˹in Mecca˺ to which fruits of all kinds are brought as a provision from Us?”*). The same blindness, at two scales — and the cure is the same: a messenger, reciting, until the gift is traced to its Giver.
verses.58:
> ˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly. And We ˹alone˺ were the Successor

**The Question With a Catalogue Behind It**

The verse opens with the Qur'an's standing rhetorical survey: how many a town have We destroyed — a question the Book asks in a dozen registers, each one pointing at ruins its audience could visit. The commentators listed the companion verses: the towns destroyed for their wrongdoing in chapter 7, the overturned in chapter 21, the mightier towns of chapter 47 — how many societies We destroyed that were far superior in might (47:13 — *“˹Imagine, O Prophet,˺ how many societies We destroyed that were far superior in might than your society—which drove you out—and there was none to help them”*). The question's force is experiential: Arabia's caravans camped in these dead cities; the ruined wells and fallen towers were the landscape's own museums. The verse is not speculation — it is a guided tour with an itinerary the listeners had walked, and the guide's question has one purpose: make them count what comfort bought the previous tenants.

**"Exulting in Their Ease"**

The destroyed are identified by their signature: they exulted in their life of ease — the word the commentators glossed as prosperity without gratitude, plenty enjoyed as if self-made. The term links the verse directly to Pharaoh's biography, which is the sūrah's own illustration: his hosts exulted in the land without right (28:39 — *“And so he and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land with no right, thinking they would never be returned to Us”*), and the verse's placement shows the same file being read across history — every ruined town was a smaller Pharaoh's Egypt. The commentators' note is precise: the ease was not the crime; the crime was the ease's interpretation — wealth read as endorsement, comfort read as permanence. The Qur'an's doctrine of prosperity, established in its earliest pages, runs through here: ease is a test's furniture, and the spoiled are those who thought the furniture was the house.

The exulters Ibn Kathīr identifies are the ones who denied the blessing of the ample provision — prosperous, and ungrateful for the very prosperity. The Qur'an's own parable stands in the sūrah of the Cattle, and he sets it beside the verse: a society that dwelt secure and well-content, its provision coming to it in abundance from every place, met its Lord's favours with ingratitude, and was made to taste hunger and fear (16:112 — *“And Allah sets forth the example of a society which was safe and at ease, receiving its provision in abundance from all directions. But its people met Allah’s favours with ingratitude, so Allah made them taste the clutches of hunger and fear for their misdeeds”*). The parable is the catalogue the question opens: the same town, before and after — comfortable from every direction, then taken while it was still wrongdoers.

**Dwellings That Outlive Their Owners**

The verse records the ruins' afterlife with a traveler's eye: there are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little — and the commentators corrected the obvious misreading: it is not that a few people survived. It is that the structures survived, sheltering caravans, herders, and the occasional passerby while the nations that built them were gone. The image is the verse's coldest statistic: a civilization's total output, reduced to windbreaks. The commentators connected the motif to the Qur'an's funeral verse for the drowned of Pharaoh's party: neither heaven nor earth wept over them, nor were they reprieved (44:29 — *“Neither heaven nor earth wept over them, nor was their fate delayed”*) — extinction without eulogy. The dwellings standing over the absence are the verse's own epitaph: the world kept the buildings and lost the builders, because the buildings were never the civilization.
verses.59:
> Your Lord would never destroy a society until He had sent to its capital a messenger, reciting Our revelations to them. Nor would We ever destroy a society unless its people persisted in wrongdoing

**The City That Is Named First**

The verse says that God does not destroy a town until He has sent a messenger to its central city. Commentators identified that city as Makkah, whose old name meant the mother of towns. Others read the phrase more widely: the main city of a people, the place whose fall brings the whole region down with it. In either reading, the point is where the warning is delivered. Notice is served at the centre rather than at the edges, so the countryside cannot say it never heard and the capital cannot say it did not know.

**A Rule of Fair Judgment**

This is one of the Book's standing rules about how nations are judged: no destruction without a messenger. The same rule appears in the sūrah of the Night Journey, where God says He never punishes a people until He has sent a messenger (17:15 states it — *“And We would never punish ˹a people˺ until We have sent a messenger ˹to warn them˺”*), and again in the Cattle sūrah, where no community is destroyed while its people are unaware (6:131 states it — *“This ˹sending of the messengers˺ is because your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware ˹of the truth˺”*). Taken together, these verses say that punishment without warning is not part of God's government.

The rule is strict and it is complete. No city falls on an average score, and no generation is punished for the record of its ancestors. Before a town is destroyed, a man stands in it, reciting the signs in its own language, at its own centre. The verse's place in the sūrah fixes where Makkah stands in this history. Just before it, the Prophet ﷺ is described as a warner sent to a people who had received no warner before (28:46 states it — *“But ˹you have been sent˺ as a mercy from your Lord to warn a people to whom no warner has come before you, so perhaps they may be mindful”*). Notice, in other words, has been served.

Ibn Kathīr reads the *mother town* as Makkah, and the verse as the reason for the mission's width. The unlettered Prophet ﷺ was sent from the Mother of Cities as a messenger to all cities and towns, Arab and non-Arab alike — and the Two Ṣaḥīḥs carry his own summary of that reach: *"I have been sent to the red and the black."* The clause is the sūrah's quiet claim about Makkah's place: it is not the edge of the message's territory but its source, the town the warning radiates out of. When any other town is destroyed, on this reading, its notice has already been served at this one.
verses.60:
> Whatever ˹pleasure˺ you have been given is no more than ˹a fleeting˺ enjoyment and adornment of this worldly life. But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting. Will you not then understand

**"Better and More Lasting"**

The comparison's two adjectives do the verse's work: what is with God is better and more lasting — and the commentators carried the tradition's arithmetic: this world against the Hereafter is a speck against the sea. The Hereafter's goods are lasting because they do not end, while everything here has an end by its very nature. The Qur'an's short sūrah at the Book's end states the comparison in its compressed form: the Hereafter is better and more lasting (87:17 — *“even though the Hereafter is far better and more lasting”*) — the same two adjectives, the same verdict. The word better matters as much as lasting: the next life is not only longer; it is superior in kind — the appetite that the world's pleasures fatigue is met there without fatigue. The verse's economy should be noted: it does not say the world is worthless; it says the world is the lesser asset, and the believer is being directed to the greater one while holding the lesser.

The arithmetic the previous section calls *a speck against the sea* is the Prophet's ﷺ own words, and Ibn Kathīr carries them: *"By Allah, the life of this world in comparison with the Hereafter is as if one of you were to dip his finger in the sea — let him see what comes back to him."* The image does the verse's comparison with no abstraction. Whatever the finger brings up against the water it holds is the whole world's claim on a person's time, and the verse's *will you not then understand* is a question the image has already answered. Better and more lasting is not a judgment about quality; it is a report about quantity that happens to be infinite.

**Adornment: The Word's Own Precision**

Why adornment? The commentators connected the term to its sibling verse — the world's goods named as an ornament (33:28 — *“O Prophet! Say to your wives, “If you desire the life of this world and its luxury, then come, I will give you a ˹suitable˺ compensation ˹for divorce˺ and let you go graciously”*) — and the choice of word carries the teaching: adornment is for display, and display is for others. Much of what wealth purchases is not use but appearance — the watched house, the heard reputation, the envied ease — and the verse files all of it under decoration: beautiful, temporal, and inert. The word also explains the world's seduction mechanism: adornment works on the eye from a distance and loses detail on approach — which is why the Qur'an insists the Hereafter's goods are better, not merely later: seen up close, the world's shine is thinner than its invoice. The verse so trains a habit of appraisal: ask of every possession whether it is being enjoyed or merely displayed, and note that neither verb survives the grave.
verses.61:
> Can those to whom We have made a fine promise—which they will see fulfilled—be like those who We have allowed to enjoy the pleasures of this worldly life, but on the Day of Judgment will be brought ˹for punishment˺

**The Verse That Prices Two Lives**

The question sets two men side by side and asks whether they can be the same. The first is the one given a fine promise — the Garden, pledged in revelation — and who will see the pledge paid. The second is the one handed the world's enjoyment and nothing else, summoned on the Day of Resurrection among the arraigned. The commentators explained the comparison's target: the poor and afflicted believers of Makkah were being told, against every visible measure, that they outranked the comfortable deniers — and the verse's own tradition named the two archetypes, the Prophet and Abū Jahl, standing at the two ends of the same city. The comparison's power is its refusal of appearances: by every observable index — food, security, followers — the denier lived better. The verse removes the visible index from the scales and weighs what remains: a promise with a Guarantor against an enjoyment with a foreclosure date.

**The Two People Side by Side**

The verse sets two lives beside each other and lets the reader do the comparison. One was promised a good promise and will meet it. The other was given the enjoyment of this life and will be brought forward on the Day among the condemned. The verse before it states the terms plainly: whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of this life and its glitter, and what is with God is better and longer lasting (28:60 — *“But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting.”*). The sūrah of the Heights and the sūrah of the Most High use the same pair of words about the world and the reward, and the Book keeps returning to the comparison because the visible world is so persuasive to the person standing in it.

**What "Meeting the Promise" Means**

The promise is *lāqīhi*, a thing a person meets, like a road he arrives at rather than a prize he collects. The Book uses the same word for meeting God and for meeting the record, and the choice says that the promise is as real as anything in front of a person's eyes. The sūrah then shows what happens on the day the two groups are separated, when the call goes out asking where the partners are that they used to claim (28:62-64 — *“˹Watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”*). Nothing in the verse says the man of the world had no gifts. He had them, and they ran out.

Ibn Kathīr preserves the readings the tradition gives the verse's target. Mujāhid and Qatādah read the arraigned as those who are punished — the enjoyment's owner stands among them on the Day. Some said the verse was revealed concerning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abū Jahl, and some said concerning Ḥamza and ʿAlī against Abū Jahl; both views were narrated from Mujāhid, and he keeps the apparent meaning above them: the comparison is wider than any pair, a figure of all who were promised and all who were only given. The sūrah's own audience had both types in one city, and the verse's question works on any city that contains both.
verses.62:
> ˹Watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”

**The Question That Ends All Questions**

The verse stages the Day's opening interrogation as a single question: where are those you claimed were My associate-gods? The call is addressed to the misleaders — the commentators tied the pronoun to the leaders whose disavowal fills the next verse — and the question's genius is its smallness. Not a lecture on theophysics, not a recital of their sins: one question about location. Where are they? The objects of a lifetime's worship are summoned to appear, and their absence is the whole verdict. The commentators listed the claimed partners' kinds — idols, jinn, angels, the righteous dead — and the question works identically on each: worship's premise is presence with power to respond, and on that Day the premise is tested by a single roll call.

**The Roll Call's Echo Through the Sūrah**

The question is a refrain: verse 74 will ask it again, word for word, before the sūrah's final testimony scene — the repetition drumming the scenario into the listener's reflexes. The commentators connected the doubling to the Qur'an's oral pedagogy: a scene of such consequence is shown twice so that no reciter's audience can claim it was mentioned once. The scene also closes a circle the sūrah opened: Pharaoh's court legislated worship of the king (28:38 — *“Pharaoh declared, “O chiefs! I know of no other god for you but myself. So bake bricks out of clay for me, O Hamân, and build a high tower so I may look at the God of Moses, although I am sure he is a liar.”*) — the claim itself — and here is the claim's day in court, with the king and his theology both absent. The tyrant who demanded to be the nation's god will stand in a crowd of claimants, all equally discoverable by the same question, none of them locatable.

Ibn Kathīr reads the call as rebuke in the form of a question, and he sets beside it the verse that records the roll call's outcome in full. The claimants come back to God all alone as they were created the first time, having left behind everything they had been given; the intercessors they counted on are not seen with them, the ties between them are cut, and the claims they made have vanished (6:94 — *“you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time—leaving behind everything We have provided you with. We do not see your intercessors with you—those you claimed were Allah’s partners ˹in worship˺. All your ties have been broken and all your claims have let you down”*). The question of this verse and the report of that one are the same scene: the roll call is the question, and the absence is the answer.
verses.63:
> Those ˹misleaders˺ against whom the decree ˹of torment˺ is justified will cry, “Our Lord! These ˹followers˺ are the ones we caused to deviate. We led them into deviance, for we ourselves were deviant. We disassociate ourselves ˹from them˺ before You. It was not us that they used to worship.”

**The Confession's Anatomy**

The speech proceeds in four moves, and the commentators anatomized each: they led these people astray; they themselves were astray first; they disavow their followers before God; and — the stunning close — it was not us they worshipped. The first two clauses establish the chain of corruption: deviation propagates like infection, and the carrier was infected before he infected — which is why verse 42's curse was earned. The third clause is the severance: disavowal, the same scene the Qur'an stages in chapter 2 — those who were followed will disown those who followed, when they see the punishment, and the bonds between them will be cut. The fourth clause is the scene's coldest fact: the followers did not, in the end, worship their leaders; they worshipped their own attachments, using the leaders as furniture.

The speakers of the confession Ibn Kathīr names: those about whom the Word has been fulfilled are the Shayatīn and the evil jinn, together with those among the people who used to advocate disbelief — the misleaders whose roll call verse 62 staged. They will testify against their followers first — *these are the ones we led astray* — and then disavow the worship they were given, which is the same two-move severance the Qur'an stages for the taken gods themselves: they will deny their worship and turn against them (19:82 — *“But no! Those ˹gods˺ will deny their worship and turn against them”*). The confession is thus not only the leaders' sentence. It is the record of how the chain of misguidance breaks, link by link, at the point where each link had thought the next one would hold it.

**The Followers Left Holding Nothing**

The scene's asymmetry completes its warning: the misleaders keep their confession, and the misled keep the bill. The Qur'an returns to this severance repeatedly — the followers will wish they had a means of return when they see the punishment — and the commentators read the pattern as the standing fate of secondhand religion: whoever lets another carry his accountability has handed his deed to a man with his own sentence to serve. The bond that united them, chapter 2 says, will be cut; chapter 23 adds that no kinship will remain between them on that Day. The misleaders' speech is so the last thing their followers ever receive from them — a public disavowal — and the Qur'an shows it to the living precisely so that no one buys dependence twice: once with attention now, and once with damnation then.

**The Severance Across the Book**

The confession is one of a family of scenes the Book gives at the reckoning, and the followers' complaint is recorded in the sūrah of the Combined Forces: "We only followed you; will you relieve us of any of the punishment?" (33:67–68). The sūrah of the Bee gives the answer of the leaders, who repudiate the responsibility and say they were led astray as their followers were (16:86 — *“And when the polytheists see their associate-gods, they will say, “Our Lord! These are our associate-gods that we used to invoke besides You.” Their gods will throw a rebuttal at them, ˹saying,˺ “You are definitely liars.”*), and the sūrah of Abraham records the weaker ones asking why they did not help them when they had followed them (14:21 — *“They will all appear before Allah, and the lowly ˹followers˺ will appeal to the arrogant ˹leaders˺, “We were your ˹dedicated˺ followers, so will you ˹then˺ protect us from Allah’s torment in any way?”*). The verse's own account adds the leaders' admission that they were themselves astray first, which is the fact the rest of the scene turns on.
verses.64:
> It will be said ˹to the disbelievers˺, “Call upon your associate-gods ˹for help˺.” So they will call them, but will receive no response. And they will face the punishment, wishing they had been ˹rightly˺ guided

**The Crowd That Will Watch the Call Fail**

The verse's scene has spectators, and the commentators' wider reading of the Qur'an's Hereafter crowd-scapes includes them: the audience of the failed call is every soul whose worship was directed correctly. The design is instructional — the destruction of the fabrication is displayed, not merely recorded, because its end is part of the lesson for those who never built one. The scene's geometry completes the sūrah's doctrine of testimony: the fabricated gods fail in public so that the Truth's monopoly is public too; the verse 75 witness stands in the same courtroom where this silence is performed. For the living, the scene assigns a vantage: the believer is being seated, in advance, in the section of the court where answered prayer is the norm — and the seating is earned in the present tense, one directed call at a time.

**The Same Call, Staged a Second Time**

The Book stages the same call a second time later in the sūrah, where the disbelievers are told on that Day to call on the partners they claimed, and they call and are not answered, and the punishment comes into view between them (28:74 — *“And ˹watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”*). The scene closes with the confession recorded in the next verse, where the disbelievers are asked what answer they gave the messengers and they are left with nothing to say (28:65–66 — *“And ˹watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, asking, “What response did you give to the messengers?”*). The point stands in the sūrah's own frame: the gods that were partners in this world turn out to have no part in the next, and the call is recorded so that the abandonment is heard.

Ibn Kathīr reads the last clause as the crowd's own verdict, arriving where the call fails. They will call, they will receive no answer, and they will see the torment — and when they see the punishment with their own eyes, they will wish that they had been guided in this world. The wish is the verse's point: guidance was available in the only place it can be, and the Day shows them the difference between the two options at the one moment the difference is fully visible. The Qur'an stages the same scene with its barrier between the callers and the called (18:52 — *“So they will call them, but will receive no response. And We will make them ˹all˺ share in the same doom”*).
verses.65:
> And ˹watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, asking, “What response did you give to the messengers?”

**The Response That Was Given**

The question's phrasing carries its own reminder: a response was given — every audience answered, in practice if never in words. The commentators noted the Qur'an's realism here: disbelief is itself a reply, and so is delay, so is selective obedience, so is the applause that changes nothing. The audit does not ask whether you answered — it asks what your answer was. The scene's doctrine is the completion of verse 59's rule: a messenger was sent to every mother-city that was judged, reciting the signs; therefore the file for every people contains both the recitation and the response, matched and dated. On the Day, the reading of the file is a formality — which is why the verse's question sounds less like inquiry than like sentencing's preamble.

Ibn Kathīr sets the Day's question beside the questions of the grave, which run on the same file. In the grave the one asked: who is your Lord, who is your Prophet, what is your religion — and the believer answers with the testimony while the disbeliever's answer is the silence that has no content. The one who was blind to the signs in this world, Ibn Kathīr writes, will be blind in the Hereafter and further astray, and the question of this verse is the same one at the scale of a people: what did you do with the messengers — an answer that is not collected on the Day, because it was collected in life.

**Mercy's Mirror in the Audit**

The verse's hard procedure sits inside a mercy that the sūrah has documented for eighty verses: the audit exists because the deliveries existed. No community is questioned about a message it never received — the rule verse 59 legislated — and no question is asked here except the one whose answer the hearers already have, having lived it. The Day's questions, in the Qur'an's portraits, never solicit new information; they transfer the file from the hidden register to the public one. The mercy is in the timing: the same question — what did you do with the message? — can be asked by the reader's own conscience tonight, at no cost, with the full means of changing the answer still on the table. The verse's scene is so a preview sold at the price of attention: the cheapest audit ever offered, and the only one whose failure can still be cured.
verses.66:
> They will be too dumbstruck on that Day to ask one another ˹for answers˺

**The Silence After the Questions**

The verse records the crowd's condition rather than any answer: the tidings will be obscured for them on that Day, and they will not question one another. The commentators gave the two classical readings — the arguments they might have raised are blotted out, or the news of one another is blotted out — and both converge on the same portrait: a humanity reduced to its own file, with no collateral left to consult. The scene follows the audit question of verse 65: asked what they answered to the messengers, the assembled have nothing to offer — no plea to trade, no neighbor to poll, no precedent to cite. Speech itself is the faculty being sentenced, in a day where speech was the currency of every refusal they ever made.

Ibn Kathīr records Mujāhid's gloss for the obscuring, and it names the last collateral the crowd tries to cash: the proof is blotted out from them so that they will not be able to ask one another for help by virtue of their blood ties. Kinship is the final currency of the excuse economy — the one that outlasts every argument, every precedent and every ally — and the verse reports it expired. The silence of the Day is not the silence of the unprepared. It is the silence of a market where every instrument of support, including the oldest, has stopped clearing.

**The End of the Excuse Economy**

The first reading carries the verse's legal weight: the tidings — the pleas, the arguments — are obscured, meaning no valid argument remains available. The commentators' summary is precise: the Hereafter is the one venue where advocacy runs out, because its cases were all adjudicable in life and every extension has expired. The Qur'an has documented the excuse economy across this sūrah — no messenger came (retired by statute in verse 59), the message was sorcery (refuted by its own craftsmen's surrender), the standard was Moses (answered by his people's own converts) — and verse 66 shows the economy's final closure: not one surviving plea, not even the mutual reassurance that wrong is normal. The silence is not imposed from outside; it is the natural condition of a market whose goods have all expired.
verses.67:
> As for those who repent, believe, and do good ˹in this world˺, it is right to hope that they will be among the successful

**The Door the Verse Restores**

After four verses of arraignment, silence, and unanswered calls, the verse swings open a door: but as for one who repents — the particle of exception doing the work of a whole gospel. The commentators placed the verse's mercy precisely: it stands between the scenes of the condemned, so that no listener leaves the recitation trapped in the courtroom. The sequence is the Qur'an's standard mercy-map: show the end of refusal in full — the roll call, the disavowal, the unanswered prayer — and then, while the fear is still warm, name the exit: repentance, faith, righteous work. The door's placement is its eloquence: it is announced at the exact moment the listener can feel what it is worth.

**"It Is Right to Hope"**

The promise's phrasing is among the gentlest in the Book: perhaps he will be among the successful — and the commentators delivered the classical rule about such particles: when God speaks a perhaps, it is not uncertainty but mercy of address — a promise made to sound like hope so that the striving it commands feels like pursuit rather than compliance. The rule's consequence is exact: the verse is a guarantee dressed as a possibility, and the dress is for the wearer's dignity — success that arrives as pure decree would produce no love. The commentators also heard the word's echo of verse 61's fine promise: the same receiver of the pledge, now described by his verbs. The hope is so the currency of the relationship: God speaks in hope's grammar so that the servant may live in hope's energy.

The three verbs of the door carry the sūrah's own schedule. The repentance, the belief and the righteous deeds are done in this world, Ibn Kathīr notes; the success is counted on the Day of Resurrection. The door therefore opens now and closes where the chapter's whole accounting stands: the verse does not promise that the Day will be gentle to anyone, only that the man who turns, believes and works while the turning is still possible is to be counted among the successful — and the *perhaps* that dresses the guarantee is the mercy the previous section described.
verses.68:
> Your Lord creates and chooses whatever He wills—the choice is not theirs. Glorified and Exalted is Allah above what they associate ˹with Him˺

**Creation and Choice as One Act**

The verse pairs the two verbs — creates and chooses — and the pairing is its theology: the same hand that makes the material selects the instrument. The commentators transmitted al-Ṭabarī's preferred reading — Your Lord creates what He wills and chooses the choicest of what they have — God selecting the best available from among the very people objecting to the selection. The reading turns the objection inside out: the objectors are, in the same breath, the inventory being drawn from — the choice ran through their own households and passed over their own criteria. The doctrine lands on every generation's merited discomfort: God's choices are made from among us, which means our exclusion from any office is never scarcity of candidates but the election's freedom — and freedom is the Sender's, as the verse says twice.

The clause *no choice have they* the commentators read as a negation: it was not for them to have a choice in what is appointed — and the Qur'an states the same rule in the verse of the decree (33:36 — *“It is not for a believing man or woman—when Allah and His Messenger decree a matter—to have any other choice in that matter”*). The objectors' case, in that reading, is not that God chose badly; it is that He chose at all, without consulting them. The verse answers the complaint at its root: the inventory is His, the choice is His, and the objection was never a candidate.

**Submission as the Trained Outcome**

The commentators transmitted, from the Sufi master al-Shādhilī, the verse's inward fruit: forsake the directing of things, and if you must direct, direct yourself not to direct — the art of aligning one's will with the Will that chooses. The teaching is not passivity: the creature's sphere of choice — effort, repentance, work — is real and commanded; what is surrendered is the directorship of outcomes and offices. The verse so heals the believer's two chronic inflammations: envy of others' appointments (the choice was not yours to give) and anxiety over one's own (the choice was not yours to secure). Between those two releases lives the actual spiritual life: work assigned, results owned by the Chooser, and the heart's constant refrain matching the verse's close — glory to Him above what we would have arranged instead.
verses.69:
> And your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal

**Hidden and Shown: The Whole Range**

The verse uses two verbs that bracket everything inside a person: what is concealed and what is displayed. The commentators noted how wide this is. God's knowledge is not limited to the secrets people manage to keep. It covers the whole range, including the things worn openly and the concealments that failed. The pairing corrects two opposite mistakes. The person who performs in public believes that the self he shows is the whole self. The person who conspires believes that the self he hides is safe. Neither register is unknown to the One who reads.

For a believer, the verse turns hypocrisy into something technically impossible. The gap between what is in the chest and what is on the tongue is recorded as a gap rather than discovered by accident. The only strategy left standing is to close the gap, and to become through repentance and practice what one appears to be.

The same register the Qur'an states elsewhere in its own words: it is the same with Him whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he hides by night or goes about freely in the day (13:10 — *“It is the same ˹to Him˺ whether any of you speaks secretly or openly, whether one hides in the darkness of night or goes about in broad daylight”*). The verse's two verbs — conceal and reveal — are that statement narrowed to one people: the audience's split self is not a discovery the Day will make. It is already on record, in both registers, from the moment the splitting began.

**Why the Verse Sits Here**

Its placement, right after the words about the Lord who creates and chooses, is precise. The resistance to the Prophet was conducted, like most resistance, in two registers at once: public mockery over private fear, and loud scorn over secret conviction. The commentators supply the texture. Some of the Prophet's fiercest opponents were known to move their lips along with the recitation when nobody was watching, and some of his quietest listeners were the ones whose chests concealed the most.

The verse tells the Messenger, and tells every teacher who comes after him, that what he can observe is incomplete information. The contempt he sees from where he stands is seen from above as well, and so is the crack in it. That rules out two mistakes for anyone who calls people to God: despair at open rejection, and confidence in open acceptance. The record being written is written in a room he cannot see.
verses.70:
> He is Allah. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. All praise belongs to Him in this life and the next. All authority is His. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**The Creed Stated Plain**

The verse sets down the whole creed in four clauses, without argument: He is Allah — there is no god but He; His is the praise, in the first and the last; His is the judgment; and to Him you will be returned. The commentators read the placement as the sūrah's religious seal: after eighty verses of narrative — baskets, courts, plagues, seas, treasures, trials — the chapter's argument arrives at the identity of its Narrator, stated in the naked formula of worship. The position is deliberate: the creed lands with the stories' weight behind it, because the listener has just watched this Allah act — choose, deliver, drown, provide, forgive, choose again. The verse does not ask for the formula's acceptance; it presents the formula as the summary of everything the listener has already been shown.

**His Is the Judgment — and Then the Return**

The third clause names the running sovereignty: His is the judgment — the word carrying decision, rule, and wisdom together. The commentators paired its two registers: in this world, all creaturely authority functions only within God's delegated judgment; in the next, He judges directly between His creatures with no intermediary left standing. The clause's placement after the praise clause is doctrine: the One praised is the One ruling — worship and governance are not separate departments. And the fourth clause closes the verse on return: to Him you will be brought back — the verb of permanent arrival, the same return Pharaoh denied (28:39 — *“And so he and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land with no right, thinking they would never be returned to Us”*) and the verse's whole argument has now showed at scale. The sequence — praise, judgment, return — is the believer's whole orientation compressed into a single breath: live praised, governed, and homeward.

Ibn Kathīr's glosses give the four clauses their weight. The praise is His in all that He does, for His justice and His wisdom; the decision is one that none can put back, held by might and power and wisdom and mercy together; and the return is the Day on which everyone is rewarded or punished according to his deeds, with nothing of the deeds concealed. The creed the verse states plain is thus not a formula to be accepted but an audit to be faced: praise for the doer, decision above appeal, return with the file complete.
verses.71:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if Allah were to make the night perpetual for you until the Day of Judgment, which god other than Allah could bring you sunlight? Will you not then listen?”

**"Will You Not Then Listen"**

The verse closes on an odd verb for an argument about light: will you not hear? The commentators caught the pairing's design: the ear is the night's organ — in darkness, hearing is the sense that carries a person — so the question of the perpetual night is addressed to the faculty that the night proves. The correspondence is exact: verse 72's day-question ends with will you not see?, the day's organ. The two questions are so tailored to their hemispheres, and the tailoring teaches the verse's deeper method: God's signs are audited by whichever sense each sign serves — and each of the reader's own faculties is being recruited as its own witness. The listener who will not hear a question about hearing has exhausted the verse's remedies; the question's repetition in the next verse shows the Reader willing to try the other sense.

**The Mercy Inside the Hypothesis**

The perpetual night is hypothetical — and the hypothesis's non-fulfillment is the daily evidence. Every morning in the audience's lifetime had arrived on schedule: the sun that Pharaoh claimed lordship over, the light the Quraysh traded under, the dawn Moses' mother rose to — the same event, relaunched without a single failure across the species' whole memory. The commentators' reading of the verse as an invitation to gratitude follows: the counterfactual's horror is the gratitude's ledger — the switching of night and day is not a natural right but a standing mercy, withheld from no generation by the One who could withhold it by a single command. The verse so converts an astronomical routine into a religious audit: what would you pay, in that locked night, for one hour of this morning you walked through untouched?
verses.72:
> Ask ˹them also˺, “Imagine if Allah were to make the day perpetual for you until the Day of Judgment, which god other than Allah could bring you night to rest in? Will you not then see?”

**The Mirror Challenge: The Locked Day**

The counterfactual flips: if God made the day permanent until the Day of Resurrection — which god besides Allah could bring you night to rest in? The pairing with verse 71 is deliberate architecture: the two hypotheses together cover the whole cycle, proving that whichever half is withdrawn, the other half's restoration is beyond every associate-god's reach. The commentators explained the day's gift that the hypothesis removes: rest — the night as the creature's appointed shelter from exposure and labor. A perpetual day is not a blessing multiplied; it is a blessing weaponized: work without end, sight without mercy, heat without shadow. The verse's insight is psychological as much as astronomical: the human being does not only need light — he needs the ending of light, and no power he worships can supply an ending.

**"Will You Not Then See"**

The closing question switches organs: will you not see? — the day's faculty, as the commentators noted, matching verse 71's ear. The design completes the two-verse apparatus: each hemisphere's question is addressed to the sense that hemisphere serves. That the reader's own body convicts him — the eyes that enjoy the day's light cannot fail to see the day's Argument, and the ears that carry him through the night cannot fail to hear the night's. The rhetoric leaves no neutral faculty: every sense is deputized. The commentators' wider point follows: denial is not an information failure — the evidence is piped through the deny-er's own senses, daily, at full brightness; refusal is the only word left for it, and the verse's question makes the refusal conscious by asking it to look at what it is refusing.
verses.73:
> It is out of His mercy that He has made for you the day and night so that you may rest ˹in the latter˺ and seek His bounty ˹in the former˺, and perhaps you will be grateful

**"Made for You"**

The verse's middle phrase carries its warmth: He made for you — the design addressed to its beneficiaries. The commentators heard in the construction the personal register of all provision: the cycle's scale is planetary, but its addressee is singular — you. The teaching dignifies the ordinary: the reader's last night's sleep was a designed delivery, and this morning's light is addressed mail. The phrase also grounds the verse's argument from mercy: provision that is for you implies a Giver who knows you — and the knowledge theme of verse 69 stands behind this one: the One who reads the chest designed the schedule the chest rests by. The believer's gratitude, in this light, is not a mood but an accurate reading of the arrangement's address label.

**The Seeker's License in the Day's Design**

The verse's clause about the day — that you may seek of His bounty — deserves its own hearing as permission. Labor, in the verse's design, is not the curse of a fallen world but the assigned channel of provision: the day is made for the seeking, and the seeking is directed at His bounty — which makes every honest occupation a form of prayer conducted with the hands. The commentators' reading dignifies the whole spectrum of work: the farmer's field, the merchant's caravan, the craftman's bench are all doors of the same bounty, and the verse removes the false ranking between "spiritual" and "worldly" effort — both are the day's business, and both are addressed to the Giver. The clause also carries the seeking's ethics in miniature: bounty sought of Him is bounty sought lawfully, because the address defines the channel.

Ibn Kathīr's practical gloss on the alternation is a mercy of opportunity: whoever misses something of worship during the night can make it up during the day, and whoever misses something during the day can make it up at night. The two halves of the cycle cover each other's failures, which is one more sense in which the arrangement is made *for you* — the schedule is forgiving by design. The Qur'an names the pair's office elsewhere in the same breath of remembrance and gratitude: He is the One who has put the night and the day in succession for such as desires to remember or desires to show His gratitude (25:62 — *“And He is the One Who causes the day and the night to alternate, ˹as a sign˺ for whoever desires to be mindful or to be grateful”*).
verses.74:
> And ˹watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”

**The Question Asked a Second Time**

The verse returns to the question the sūrah has already put once: on that day God will call them and ask where the beings are that they claimed were His partners. The same question was asked earlier in the sūrah (28:62 records the first time — *“˹Watch for˺ the Day He will call to them, “Where are those you claimed were My associate-gods?”*), and its return is deliberate.

**Why the Question Comes Back**

The Book repeats things so that people cannot say they never heard them. The first asking comes before the account of the reckoning, and the second comes after it. Between the two the reader has been shown what happens when the account is opened: the men who led others astray deny the ones who followed them, the callers get no answer, and the crowd is silenced.
