The question that returns is therefore not new information; it is the same question with the evidence now in front of the reader.

**What the Verse Says to the People of Makkah**

The men of Makkah were not in the habit of saying that their idols made the sky and the earth. They thanked the idols for other things: for the safety of the town, for the trade that came and went, for the rain when it came. The Book had already answered that claim and said that the provision came from God alone. The question in front of the reader takes the whole list and asks the men to produce the gods they thanked. The sūrah has just described the mercy of the night and the day, which both arrive whether or not anybody thanks anyone for them (28:73 — *“It is out of His mercy that He has made for you the day and night so that you may rest ˹in the latter˺ and seek His bounty ˹in the former˺, and perhaps you will be grateful”* names the night for rest and the day for seeking provision). The question follows that reminder.

**What the Second Asking Adds**

The second asking is narrower than the first. The first covers the claim that these beings were partners in God's rule; the second presses on the claim that they gave what only God gives. The reader who has followed the sūrah knows that the idols were thanked for the harvest and for the safety of the sanctuary, and that the Book has already said the sanctuary was made safe by God and the provision came from Him. The verse leaves the men of that time with nothing to say and leaves the reader with a question about his own thankfulness.

**What the Verse Leaves With the Reader**

The verse asks the reader to name the things he credits for what he has. A person can thank God aloud and still live as though his money, his contacts or his luck were the real cause of his safety. The sūrah's habit is to name the gift and the giver together, and the question in front of the reader is the point where the two are separated and weighed.
verses.75:
> And We will bring forth a witness from every faith-community and ask ˹the polytheists˺, “Show ˹Us˺ your proof.” Then they will ˹come to˺ know that the truth is with Allah ˹alone˺. And whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them

**They Will Know the Truth Is Allah's**

The verse records the discovery rather than the sentence: then they will know that the truth belongs to God — knowledge arriving as the case closes. The commentators noted the tense's precision: they will know — the verb of the unveiled, the same knowledge-by-necessity verse 62 described, arriving after the window in which knowing could have been chosen. The scene so completes the Qur'an's standing pattern: faith's value lies in its voluntariness before evidence becomes unavoidable; the Day supplies certainty to everyone and credit to no one. The phrase's content matters equally: the truth is God's — He held it throughout the dispute; the communities' versions were borrowings against it, and the borrowing is now called due. Every argument the deniers ever filed was, in the end, a try to relocate the truth's ownership — and the verse announces the repossession.

**Their Fabrications Forsake Them**

The verse's closing clause ends the partnership: what they used to fabricate will fail them — and the commentators listed the fabricated: idols invented, lies told, the whole constructed religion of convenience. The word fails them — the phrase of an ally deserting the field — completes the sūrah's longest arc: the associates who could not be found (62), could not answer (64), and now formally defect. The abandonment is the fabrication's own nature coming due: things that were made hold only as long as their makers hold, and the maker's death dissolves the make. The scene's teaching for the living is inventory doctrine: audit what you lean on, and ask what it is made of — everything fabricated holds in this world's weather and fails in the next world's. Only what was never fabricated — the Truth, which is God's — survives the transfer of venue.

**The Challenge the Book Files Elsewhere**

The demand for proof is the same challenge the Book puts to the claimants of special standing: bring your proof if you are truthful (2:111 — *“The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”*; 27:64 — *“Or ˹ask them,˺ “Who originates the creation then resurrects it, and gives you provisions from the heavens and the earth? Is it another god besides Allah?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof, if what you say is true.”*), and the closing discovery — that the truth belongs to God — is the counterpart of the confession of the misleaders. The witness from every community is the prophet of that community, as the sūrah of the Women states (4:41 — *“So how will it be when We bring a witness from every faith-community and bring you ˹O Prophet˺ as a witness against yours”*), and the sūrah of the Bee describes the same proceeding (16:84 — *“˹Consider, O Prophet,˺ the Day We will call ˹a prophet as˺ a witness from every faith-community.”*). The verse's phrase about the destruction of their claims is the fitting end of the dispute: the case is not lost for want of argument but for want of the thing argued about.

Ibn Kathīr records Mujāhid's gloss on the witness — it is a Messenger — and he marks what the demand is aimed at: the proof of the claim itself, that Allah had any partners. The claimants are asked for the evidence of their own premise, and the silence that follows is the evidence's absence in the record.
verses.76:
> Indeed, Korah was from the people of Moses, but he behaved arrogantly towards them. We had granted him such treasures that even their keys would burden a group of strong men. ˹Some of˺ his people advised him, “Do not be prideful! Surely Allah does not like the prideful

**The Wealthiest Man in the Story**

The sūrah now introduces its second great figure. Korah, of the people of Moses, owned so much that a group of strong men was needed just to carry the keys to his storerooms. The commentators placed him in the older record as the Israelite who rebelled against Moses, and the Qur'an's portrait adds the detail the story needs: he was one of the oppressed nation's own sons, raised from among slaves into wealth that embarrassed empires.

His role in the sūrah is set by what precedes him. The chapter has already given its judgement on the world's goods, calling them the enjoyment and adornment of this life while what lasts with God is better (28:60 states it — *“But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting.”*). Korah is what maximum acquisition looks like when that judgement is refused. Pharaoh held power and Korah held gold, and the sūrah files both under the same verdict by its end.

Ibn Kathīr gives the identification the older record kept. Ibn ʿAbbās said Qārūn was the son of Mūsā's paternal uncle — the view also of Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfāl, Sammak ibn Ḥarb, Qatādah, Mālik ibn Dīnār and Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Jurayj named him: Qārūn ibn Yashār ibn Qāḥiṭh, and Mūsā the son of ʿImrān ibn Qāḥiṭh — the prophet's own cousin, of the same house of ʿImrān that produced the man who would lead his people out of Egypt. The sūrah's *of the people of Moses* is thus literal to the degree the tradition makes it so: the richest man in the story is the prophet's own kin, which is what makes the arrogance of the clause an affront inside the family.

The keys carry a report of their own, and it prices the fortune in its own terms. Al-ʿAmaʿsh narrated from Khayṭāmah that the keys of Qārūn's treasure were made of leather, each one like a finger, and each was for a separate storeroom; when he set out anywhere, the keys were carried on sixty mules, white-blazed on the foreheads and white at the feet. The detail the verse needed was never the gold; it was the carrying-cost of the gold — a body of strong men strained by the keys, and a mule-train following the man. The fortune is measured by the machinery it required, and the machinery is what verse 81 will show failing in a single motion.

**What His Own People Told Him**

The verse reports that his people told him not to exult, because God does not love those who exult. That advice is the sūrah's own teaching put into the mouth of his community. It is not an instruction to be poor. The chapter that follows it tells him to seek the home of the Hereafter while not forgetting his share of this world, to do good as God has done good to him, and not to seek corruption in the land (28:77 gives all three — *“Rather, seek the ˹reward˺ of the Hereafter by means of what Allah has granted you, without forgetting your share of this world.”*).

So the community's counsel was balanced from the start. What they objected to was not his wealth but the way he carried it.

**God Does Not Love the Exultant**

The closing clause is the verse's teaching: God does not love those who exult. The commentators tied it to the chapter's running theme. It names those who exult in the land without right (28:39 describes them — *“And so he and his soldiers behaved arrogantly in the land with no right, thinking they would never be returned to Us”*) and the towns that exulted in their ease before they were taken (28:58 describes them — *“˹Imagine˺ how many societies We have destroyed that had been spoiled by their ˹comfortable˺ living! Those are their residences, never inhabited after them except passingly. And We ˹alone˺ were the Successor”*). Exulting is the signature fault of every prosperous refusal in the Book.

The precision matters. The crime is not wealth, since wealth is a gift, and the Book is full of wealthy people it honours. The crime is the self-worship that wealth can produce: the quiet conversion of a gift into a merit, and of possessions into an identity. Korah is introduced by the very clause that will finish him, and every line between, the advice of his people, the parade of his finery and the command that opens the earth, works out a sentence the reader has already read.
verses.77:
> Rather, seek the ˹reward˺ of the Hereafter by means of what Allah has granted you, without forgetting your share of this world. And be good ˹to others˺ as Allah has been good to you. Do not seek to spread corruption in the land, for Allah certainly does not like the corruptors.”

**Seeking the Best of Both Worlds**

The verse is the advice given to Korah by his people, and it tells him to use what God has given him to seek the home of the last life without forgetting his share of this one, to do good as God has done good to him, and not to seek corruption in the land because God does not love the men who spread it. The verse holds two duties together and refuses the idea that they pull against each other.

**What the Advice Was Answering**

The verses before this one describe Korah and his situation: he was one of the people of Moses, he became arrogant toward them, and he was given treasures so heavy that a group of strong men could not carry the keys (28:76 gives that picture — *“Indeed, Korah was from the people of Moses, but he behaved arrogantly towards them.”*). His people gave him the advice in front of the reader, and the sūrah records his answer in the verse that follows, where he says that his wealth came to him from his own knowledge (28:78 records it — *“Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed some from the generations before him who were far superior to him in power and greater in accumulating ˹wealth˺?”*). The advice is therefore the community's answer to a man who thought his wealth was proof of his worth. The Book tells the same story of arrogance and its ending in the sūrah of the Cave, where a man with a garden says that he cannot see it ending, and the Book says that he wronged his own soul by it (18:35 — *“And he entered his property, while wronging his soul, saying, “I do not think this will ever perish”* describes his words, and 18:42 — *“And so all his produce was ˹totally˺ ruined, so he started to wring his hands for all he had spent on it, while it had collapsed on its trellises. He cried, “Alas! I wish I had never associated anyone with my Lord ˹in worship˺!”* tells what happened to the garden).

**The Balance in the Middle Clause**

The clause about not forgetting one's share of this world is the sentence most often quoted from the verse, and its meaning is that a person may enjoy what God has made lawful. The teachers of the community read it as a refusal of two extremes: the man who spends his life only on the world and the man who denies himself what God has permitted and calls that religion. The tradition carries the saying attributed to Ibn ʿUmar, which the commentators recorded, that a person should work for this world as though he would live forever and for the next life as though he would die tomorrow. The Book states the same balance elsewhere when it tells the believers to eat of the good things God has given and to be grateful (2:172 — *“O believers! Eat from the good things We have provided for you. And give thanks to Allah if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺”* gives that instruction to the believers, and 7:32 — *“Ask, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has forbidden the adornments and lawful provisions Allah has brought forth for His servants?”* asks who has forbidden the good things God brought out for His servants).

Ibn Kathīr's gloss on *your portion* is a bill of rights, and it is the clause's whole meaning. The Lord has rights over you, your self has rights over you, your family has rights over you, and your guests have rights over you — and the clause is the command to give each of them their due. The verse does not tell the rich man to forgo the world. It tells him that the world's claims on him are real and itemized, and that forgetting them — not having them — is the sin the advice exists to prevent.

**Doing Good as God Has Done Good**

The verse's next clause asks the man who has been given much to pass on what he received. The Book keeps tying wealth to generosity in the same way: it tells the believers to spend from what God has given them (2:254 — *“O believers! Donate from what We have provided for you before the arrival of a Day when there will be no bargaining, friendship, or intercession.”* gives the instruction before a day arrives when no trade will help), and it describes the men who give in the day and the night, in secret and in public, and says that their reward is with their Lord (2:274 gives the promise — *“Those who spend their wealth in charity day and night, secretly and openly—their reward is with their Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve”*). The verse in front of the reader says that the way to seek the home of the last life is to use the gift to do good, which means the wealth is not condemned; the use of it is what decides.

**The Warning About Corruption**

The verse ends by forbidding the spreading of corruption in the land, which the Book refuses as a habit rather than a single act. The sūrah has just told the story of Pharaoh, who spread corruption and enslaved a people, and it has already given the rule that the home of the last life belongs to the men who do not seek to be unjust or to spread corruption (28:83 states the rule — *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth.”*). The Book names the same wrong in the sūrah of the Cow, where it says that God does not love corruption (2:205 describes the man who spreads it — *“And when they leave ˹you˺, they strive throughout the land to spread mischief in it and destroy crops and cattle. Allah does not like mischief”*), and it tells the community that whatever harm comes from corruption returns to the people who made it. The verse in front of the reader gives the rich man the rule that governs wealth, and it gives the community a standard it can use to judge any fortune: what was it used for, and what did it leave behind? The sūrah of the Consultation gives the two sides of the promise in one sentence when it says that whoever seeks the harvest of the next life will have it increased and whoever seeks the harvest of this life will be given a share of it (42:20 states both — *“And whoever desires ˹only˺ the harvest of this world, We will give them some of it, but they will have no share in the Hereafter”*).
verses.78:
> He replied, “I have been granted all this because of some knowledge I have.” Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed some from the generations before him who were far superior to him in power and greater in accumulating ˹wealth˺? There will be no need for the wicked to be asked about their sins

**The Self-Made Man's Creed**

Korah's reply is the creed of the self-made in one clause: this came to me on account of a knowledge I have. The commentators parsed the claim's layers: some took the knowledge as commercial skill — the crafts and competencies of a fortune; some transmitted the reports that he was an alchemist, reports the tradition itself dismissed; others read the phrase as opinion — in my view, I earned this. Every reading converges on the doctrine beneath: the attribution of provision to the self. The claim is the mirror-image of verse 57's error: the Quraysh knew not that God established them; Korah actively asserted the opposite credit. Between passive ignorance and active self-crediting, the Qur'an files both under the same verse — most of them know not — because the knowledge owed is the same: that what the hands gather was handed.

Ibn Kathīr carries a reading that pins the phrase to self-worth, and he gives it in one man's sentence. The wealth came to him, on this reading, because God knows he deserves it and is pleased with him; and Imām ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam explained the verse: *"Were it not for the fact that Allah is pleased with me and knows my virtue, He would not have given me this wealth."* He sets the same creed beside the man whose pattern the sūrah files it under: touched by hardship he calls on God, and when the blessing returns he says the words of this verse (39:49 — *“When one is touched with hardship, they cry out to Us ˹alone˺. Then when We shower Our blessings upon them, they say, “I have been granted all this only because of ˹my˺ knowledge.” Not at all! It is ˹no more than˺ a test”*). And he names the creed's sociologists: it is what those with little knowledge say whenever they see a man God has given much and cannot explain it otherwise.

**The Question That Answers Him**

The verse answers the creed with a question: did he not know that God destroyed generations before him, stronger in might and greater in gathering? The commentators listed the parallel challenges — have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, more established in the land, with rivers flowing at their feet? (6:6 — *“We had made them more established in the land than you.”*) — the standing argument from history's actuarial tables. The question's logic is exact: if wealth followed from knowledge and power, the greater accumulators would still be standing; the ruins of the greater are the falsification of the merit-creed — and the falsification was standing in plain view of any man with Korah's education. The question's opening — did he not know — indicts by prior access: the information that refutes his creed was not hidden; it was unexamined, because the creed was doing too much work for its owner to audit it.

**No Interrogation Needed**

The verse closes on the sentence's procedure: the guilty will not be questioned about their sins. The reason is in the clause: their sins — the deeds are already known, itemized by the Knower of what breasts conceal (28:69 — *“And your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal”*); the Day's questions exist for the record's completion, not for the Judge's information.
verses.79:
> Then he came out before his people in all his glamour. Those who desired the life of this world wished, “If only we could have something like what Korah has been given. He is truly a man of great fortune!”

**Power as a Public Argument**

The scene teaches the political function of display: the parade is an argument in the language of things, and it works on exactly the audience it targets. The commentators' realism holds across ages: no tyrant's court and no magnate's lobby ever relied on reason alone; the procession, the palace, the launched product are arguments addressed to the eyes — because sight is the belief-channel of the undisciplined. The Qur'an's counter is the next verse's knowing cohort, but this verse's honesty comes first: the display works. A treasury paraded through a public square recruits more believers than a sermon, and the recruits' creed is stated in their wish — fortune belongs to the displayed. The verse's gift to the reader is the parade's secret, told in advance: what converts the crowd is the lexis of things, and things are the world's own adornment (28:60 — *“Whatever ˹pleasure˺ you have been given is no more than ˹a fleeting˺ enjoyment and adornment of this worldly life. But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting. Will you not then understand”*) — rented, and priced to fail.

**Adornment as the Display's Whole Truth**

The verse's chosen word for what Korah wore is adornment — the same word verse 60 used to price the world — and the choice is the display's sentence before the earthquake: he came out in his decoration. The commentators' eye catches what the word concedes and denies at once: the display was genuinely beautiful — the silks shone, the procession gleamed — and it was genuinely surface, the world's own category, priced as enjoyment and ornament. The parade so shows verse 60 in motion: maximum adornment, zero duration. The verse's diagnostic for the reader is wearable too: every presentation a life makes — the clothes, the credentials, the curated feed — falls under the same file label. Decoration is lawful, even lovely; the error is the crowd's: reading the decoration as a verdict about the man.
verses.80:
> But those gifted with knowledge said, “Shame on you! Allah’s reward is far better for those who believe and do good. But none will attain this except the steadfast.”

**The Answer Given in Public**

This verse completes a scene the sūrah has been building. The counsel was given first (28:77 records it — *“Rather, seek the ˹reward˺ of the Hereafter by means of what Allah has granted you, without forgetting your share of this world. And be good ˹to others˺ as Allah has been good to you. Do not seek to spread corruption in the land, for Allah certainly does not like the corruptors.”*). Then the man refused the belief behind it (28:78 records that — *“He replied, “I have been granted all this because of some knowledge I have.” Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed some from the generations before him who were far superior to him in power and greater in accumulating ˹wealth˺? There will be no need for the wicked to be asked about their sins”*). Then he came out in his finery for everyone to see (28:79 records the parade — *“Then he came out before his people in all his glamour. Those who desired the life of this world wished, “If only we could have something like what Korah has been given. He is truly a man of great fortune!”*). Now the answer comes, in the square, in front of the display, on the record.

The commentators notice the design. This is the last time Korah hears the truth spoken freely. The wisdom he had silenced in private now answers him in public, and the command that destroys him arrives one verse later, in front of the same crowd (28:81 tells it — *“Then We caused the earth to swallow him up, along with his home. There was no one to help him against Allah, nor could he even help himself”*). The verse leaves the reader standing in that square, with the parade passing and the crowd murmuring about what it wishes it had. The question it presses on every generation is which group a person stands in. Not which procession he happens to watch, but whose side he is on when the next one passes: the side that wishes, or the side that knows, whose correction time always proves right.

**"Woe to You": Correction as a Duty**

The men who knew open their answer with a word the comfortable skip: woe to you. It is a public rebuke, aimed at the crowd, in the space where the parade is happening. The commentators are careful about when such a rebuke is allowed. These men spoke because the error was about belief itself and because they were qualified to speak. That makes it correction rather than insult.

The content of the rebuke is the verse's real gift: God's reward is better, and patience is the gate to it. The scene also teaches the community a second kind of protection. When private counsel fails, as it failed with the wealthy man in the verse before, the people who know must correct the audience his display is recruiting. A parade like that does real damage, because it manufactures wishes, and wishes are corrected in public or not at all.

The promise the correction rests on carries a prophetic report of its own, and Ibn Kathīr carries it: Allah has prepared for His righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and the heart of a human cannot comprehend — and the verse he tells the reader to read if he wishes (32:17 — *“No soul can imagine what delights are kept in store for them as a reward for what they used to do”*). The patience that gates the reward he reads with two early voices: as-Suddī said none shall reach Paradise except the patient, and Ibn Jarīr specified the patience — the forgoing of the love of this world for the sake of the Hereafter — and noted that the clause, though it fell from the people of knowledge's mouths, stands in the verse as God's own words.
verses.81:
> Then We caused the earth to swallow him up, along with his home. There was no one to help him against Allah, nor could he even help himself

**The Earth Answers**

The verse carries out the sentence the counsel verses delayed: We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. The instrument is the point — no invading army, no rival fortune, no plague; the ground itself, the most stable thing a treasure-owner knows, receives the command. The commentators related the reports that Moses was granted the power to call upon the earth for this — the prophet's staff, his hand, and now the ground beneath the fortune all conscripted as evidence. The display of verse 79 had been built to say this cannot end; the earth's command said otherwise in one motion, and the verse reports the motion without embellishment, because the fact needed none.

Ibn Kathīr binds the swallowing to the sin of display, with two prophetic reports that make the crime visible. Al-Bukhārī recorded, from Sālim that his father told him the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"While a man was dragging his lower garment, he was swallowed up, and he will remain sinking down into the earth until the Day of Resurrection"*; and Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū Saʿīd that the Prophet ﷺ said a man among the people before you went out in two green garments, walking proudly in them, and God commanded the earth to take him, so that he keeps sinking in it until the Day of Resurrection — a chain Ibn Kathīr grades ḥasan. The reports are not about Qārūn; they are about the crime Qārūn committed, and they price it in the sūrah's own currency. The ground that received the parade is the ground that receives the man, and the display that recruited the crowd of verse 79 is the display that made the swallowing deserved.

**No Party, No Self**

The closing clause prices the fortune's protection at zero twice over: he had no party to help him against God, and he could not help himself. The word for party, the commentators noted, is the Arabic of a battle-support company — the allies a man musters in war. Korah, who could fund any company, discovered the one battlefield where money conscripts nothing: against God's command, no retinue marches. The second failure is starker: the man of verse 78's self-credit — all this by my knowledge — could not devise one application of that knowledge to save his own body. The verse's arithmetic is the chapter's verdict on the self-made creed: the knowledge that could not gather what God withheld could not retain what God recalled. Wealth's two promised protections — patronage and competence — are shown failing in the same breath, on the record, before the same audience the parade had recruited.
verses.82:
> And those who had craved his position the previous day began to say, “Ah! It is certainly Allah Who gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills of His servants. Had it not been for the grace of Allah, He could have surely caused the earth to swallow us up! Oh, indeed! The disbelievers will never succeed.”

**The Overnight Conversion of the Wishing Crowd**

The verse returns to the parade's audience, and the scene's irony is complete: those who wished for his position yesterday — the desire-cohort of verse 79 — are standing at the crater today, reciting theology. The commentators noted the shift's completeness: the same crowd that read the display as fortune now reads the disappearance as doctrine — it is certainly Allah who outspreads and straitens provision for whom He wills of His servants. The conversion's speed is the lesson, not a comedy: the crowd was never far from the truth; it was near-sighted, not blind. One event re-calibrated the whole faculty. The Qur'an's realism about audiences includes this encouraging fact — the parade's recruits are recoverable, sometimes overnight, because what recruited them was evidence, and evidence moves.

**The Creed They Recite**

The confession they produce is the Qur'an's own doctrine of provision: God outspreads and straitens for whom He wills — the formula repeated across the Book, in the thirteenth chapter: Allah gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills (13:26 — *“Allah gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills.”*). The seventeenth: Surely your Lord gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills (17:30 — *“Surely your Lord gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills. He is certainly All-Aware, All-Seeing of His servants”*). The commentators gave the particles their due: the alas at the sentence's head is read as emphasis or as a cry against the audience's own yesterday — know that God outspreads — so the recitation is both creed and self-reproach. The doctrine's content repairs exactly the error the parade had planted: provision is not earned by the displayed, nor denied to the hidden; it is administered, by will, across a population the watcher cannot audit. The crowd learned in one morning what Korah refused across a fortune's lifetime.

**What the Verse Records**

The verse finishes the story of Qārūn by naming the reaction of the people who had envied him the day before. They looked at the ground collapsing under him and said that God gives abundantly and sparingly, and that if God had not been gracious to them they would have been swallowed too, and that the disbelievers do not succeed. The Book gives their change of heart in their own words, and it does not present the crowd as having learnt anything that would change what they did the next day.

**The Law Behind the Verse**

The Book names the sentence the righteous gave Qārūn's people before the disaster: the men of knowledge said that the reward of God is better for the one who believes and persists (28:80 — *“But those gifted with knowledge said, “Shame on you! Allah’s reward is far better for those who believe and do good. But none will attain this except the steadfast.”*). The passage is told in the sūrah beside the story of Moses and his years in Midian and the account of Pharaoh, and it belongs to the sūrah's long argument about wealth as a test rather than a verdict. The Sūrah of the Cave gives the same argument in the parable of the two gardens, and the Sūrah of the Bee states the rule in a command about not being impressed by the goods of the deniers.

**The Word for the Wishing**

The verse says the men who had wished for his position the day before were the ones saying this on the following day. The Book uses the same verb for their wish as the verse before it, so the change is marked by the turning of a single word. The Prophet's own teaching on the subject, in the report that God expands the provision of the servant He loves and restricts it, sits over the passage, and the sūrah's purpose is not to make a doctrine about poverty. It is to state that a person cannot read the favour of God from the size of his house.

The hadith Ibn Kathīr sets over the passage is Ibn Masʿūd's, and its full text sharpens the crowd's confession: *"Allah has alloted character among you just as He has alloted your provision. Allah gives wealth to those whom He loves and those whom He does not love, but He gives faith only to those whom He loves."* The crowd that wished for the fortune the day before is reciting, without knowing it, the doctrine the hadith states: the outspreading of provision is not a verdict on the man who receives it. Their *had it not been that Allah was gracious to us* is the same sentence from the other side — the Hand that gave Qārūn could have given it to them, and the Hand that spared them had been holding them all along.
verses.83:
> That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth. The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous

**Who Inherits the Final Home**

The verse says that God reserves the home of the last life for the men who do not seek to be unjust on the earth or to spread corruption, and it closes by saying that the outcome belongs to the men who are mindful of God. The verse comes after the story of Korah and says what the story means.

The reports on the phrase *seek neither tyranny* fix its lower boundary. ʿIkrimah read it as haughtiness and arrogance; Ibn Jurayj as arrogance and tyranny on the first clause, the committing of sins on the second. And al-Ṭabarī recorded from ʿAlī the gauge the community has used ever since: if a man wants the straps of his sandals to be better than the straps of his companion's sandals, then he is one of those the verse names. The gauge has its boundary in the same record. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked whether a man's liking for a fine garment and fine shoes was a kind of arrogance, and he answered: *"No — for Allah is beautiful and He loves beauty."* The condemned is not the looking good; it is the looking better, and the verse's Home is reserved for the men who never let a garment become a rank.

**The Standing Rule in the Verse**

The Book states the same rule in other places, and the sūrah of the Heights puts it in the mouth of Moses when he told his people that the outcome belongs to the men who are mindful of God (7:128 — *“The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous.”* records his words, and the same rule closes the stories of several sūrahs). The word the verse uses for the outcome covers both the end of the matter and the home at the end of it, and the two meanings work together here: the story of Korah ended in the collapse of everything he had, and the story of the men who did right ended in a home that stays. The verse gives the reader the rule the whole chapter has been proving by example.

**What the Stories in the Sūrah Have Shown**

The sūrah has told three stories that stand as the proof of the verse. Pharaoh enslaved a people and claimed a godhead, and he ended in the sea (28:40 describes what happened to him and his army — *“So We seized him and his soldiers, casting them into the sea. See then what was the end of the wrongdoers”*). Korah was given treasures no group of men could carry, and he ended in the ground with his house (28:81 tells how the earth swallowed him — *“Then We caused the earth to swallow him up, along with his home. There was no one to help him against Allah, nor could he even help himself”*). The mother of Moses placed her baby in the river on a promise, and she was given her son back and made a prophet (28:7 — *“We inspired the mother of Moses: “Nurse him, but when you fear for him, put him then into the river, and do not fear or grieve.”* narrates the first part and 28:13 — *“This is how We returned him to his mother so that her heart would be put at ease, and not grieve, and that she would know that Allah’s promise is ˹always˺ true. But most people do not know”* tells how he was returned to her). The verse in front of the reader takes those three endings and states the law that produced them.

**Who the Verse Is Aiming At**

The men the verse describes are the men who think their power or their wealth excuses them from justice. The sūrah's own story has just shown such a man being asked to be humble and answering that his wealth came from his own knowledge (28:78 reports his words — *“Did he not know that Allah had already destroyed some from the generations before him who were far superior to him in power and greater in accumulating ˹wealth˺?”*). The Book names the same type in other sūrahs: the men who said that their wealth and their children would never end and that they would be given more if God intended good for them (34:35 records the claim and the answer that follows — *“Adding, “We are far superior ˹to the believers˺ in wealth and children, and we will never be punished.”*). The verse in front of the reader states the rule for the men who claim privilege on the earth, and it names the two things they are told to stop: the abuse of power and the spreading of corruption.

**What the Verse Gives the Reader Who Has Little**

The verse gives the community a reason not to envy the rich man's house, and the sūrah makes that point with the words of the men who had been in his position. After Korah was swallowed, the men who had wished for the same wealth the day before said that God had given to what He pleased and held back from what He pleased (28:82 reports their change of mind — *“And those who had craved his position the previous day began to say, “Ah!”*). The Book says in the same sūrah that whoever does good will be given better than it, and that whoever does wrong will be repaid only for what he did (28:84 — *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded with what is better.”* states the two rules, and the sūrah of the Cave says that the best home is with God at 18:46 — *“Wealth and children are the adornment of this worldly life, but the everlasting good deeds are far better with your Lord in reward and in hope”*). The verse in front of the reader tells the poor man that the final home is not bought with wealth but with conduct, and it tells the rich man that his fortune is not proof of anything.
verses.84:
> Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded with what is better. And whoever comes with an evil deed, then the evildoers will only be rewarded for what they used to do

**The Verse of the Two Handings-Over**

The Day's transaction is stated as an exchange: whoever comes with a good deed receives better than it; whoever comes with an evil deed is repaid only for what he earned. The verb is the same in both clauses — coming, bringing, the posture of a worker presenting his output — and the symmetry is the doctrine: everyone arrives with something; the difference is the exchange rate applied at the counter. The commentators paired the verse with the multiplication verse of the sixth chapter: Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold (6:160 — *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. But whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one. None will be wronged”*) — the better-than-it being quantified elsewhere, while here it is left vast on purpose. The evil deed's rate is stated with equal care: only for what they used to do — the word only doing the work of justice's ceiling: no compounding, no interest on wrong, repayment capped at the principal. The verse's two rates are the Qur'an's mercy and justice in a single ledger: good is under-paid forever, wrong is never over-charged.

**What the Verse States**

The verse gives the rule of the exchange: whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and whoever comes with an evil deed will not be repaid except with the like of it. The Book states the same principle in the Sūrah of the Cattle, where ten times the like of a good deed is promised and the punishment is measured by the deed itself (6:160 — *“Whoever comes with a good deed will be rewarded tenfold. But whoever comes with a bad deed will be punished for only one. None will be wronged”*), and it gives the contrast in the Sūrah of the Family of ʿImrān in the same form (3:182 — *“This is ˹the reward˺ for what your hands have done. And Allah is never unjust to ˹His˺ creation.”*). The sentence is one of the Book's summaries of the terms of the Day.

Ibn Kathīr reads the two clauses as the counter's two postures, and he names them: the better-than-it is the position of generosity, because the reward God pays is better than the deed by which it is bought — how can it not be, when He has multiplied it many times over; the measure for measure is the position of justice, because the wrong is repaid at its own size and not an atom more. He sets the second beside the verse that states it in its harshest form (27:90 — *“And whoever comes with an evil deed will be hurled face-first into the Fire. Are you rewarded except for what you used to do”*). The ledger the verse states is mercy on one side of the counter and exactness on the other — and neither side is a bargain.

**What the Sūrah Is Doing With It**

The passage that the verse closes is about the men who were turning the Prophet's message into a matter of signs and of what they were owed, and the verse states what people actually receive, which is not a matter of negotiation. The Sūrah of the Story has told the account of Moses and the palace and the account of Qārūn, and it ends with the declaration that the home of the Hereafter is given to those who do not seek to exalt themselves on the earth (28:83 — *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth.”*). The verse in front of us is the arithmetic of that arrangement, and it is placed in the middle of the sūrah's closing argument.

**The Community's Use of It**

The scholars used this verse and the verse of the Sūrah of the Cattle together to state the rule that the reward of a good deed is multiplied while the punishment of a bad one is not, and the reports on the multiplication of the reward are read with both. The Prophet's own word that the deed is written as one and then increased, in the collection of Bukhārī, is the community's explanation of the verse, and the sūrah's sentence in front of us states the frame in which the multiplication happens.
verses.85:
> Most certainly, the One Who has ordained the Quran for you will ˹ultimately˺ bring you back home ˹to Mecca˺. Say, “My Lord knows best who has come with ˹true˺ guidance and who is clearly astray.”

**The Promise of Return**

The verse addresses a grieving exile with a guarantee: the One who ordained the Qur'an for you will bring you back to the place of return. The commentators transmitted the tradition's setting: the verse, some sources say, was revealed at Juḥfah — the waypoint between Makkah and Madinah — as the Prophet made the hijrah, sorrowing to leave the city of his birth, and the verse informed him that he would return to it. The promise's structure is the sūrah's whole theology compressed into one clause: the same Hand that assigned the Book guarantees the homecoming — revelation and return issued by one Ordainer. The verse has been read on three levels: return to Makkah in victory, return to God at death, return at the Resurrection — and the layers do not compete; they nest, because every homecoming in a believer's biography is the small case of the last one.

The three levels the previous section lists carry their names in Ibn Kathīr's record. In the Tafsīr he appended to his Ṣaḥīḥ, al-Bukhārī recorded Ibn ʿAbbās's comment on the clause: *to Makkah* — a reading also preserved by an-Nasāʾī in his Sunan and by Ibn Jarīr. Al-ʿAwfī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, gives it in two directions at once: he will be brought back to Makkah as He brought him out of it. Mujāhid, in the report Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq carries, says back to your place of birth in Makkah. The other levels the tradition allows — the return at death, and the return at the Resurrection, where the One who ordained the Qur'an will question the man who carried it — sit beside these without competing, because the return that comes first is the one that guarantees the rest.

**Say: My Lord Knows Best**

The command attached to the promise is Moses' answer from verse 37, assigned again: say — My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error. The commentators noted the commission's role: the Prophet, consoled with return, is not handed a verdict against his persecutors — he is handed the referral. The reply's restraint is the mission's discipline to the end: the promise guarantees the road, not the sentencing; the case's judgment stays with the Lord who knows the breasts (28:69 — *“And your Lord knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal”*). The pairing of promise and referral teaches the shape of all waiting: the believer may hold certainty about God's outcome and silence about men's verdicts in the same breath, because the first is the Sustainer's field and the second is not ours to farm. The Prophet's enemies were not named, cursed, or priced in the verse — only the return was pledged, and the knowing was delegated.
verses.86:
> You never expected this Book to be revealed to you, but ˹it came˺ only ˹as˺ a mercy from your Lord. So never side with the disbelievers ˹in their disbelief˺

**A Mercy, Not an Expectation**

The verse tells the Prophet that he never expected the Book to be sent down to him, and that it came as a mercy from his Lord, and it tells him not to side with the men who reject the message. The verse names what the Book is before it names what the Book asks.

**What the Verse Says About the Prophet**

The Book describes the messenger as a man who had no expectation of standing where he stood. The sūrah of the Cave tells him the same thing in its own way when it says that he might destroy himself with grief over the men who did not believe (18:6 pictures his distress — *“Now, perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ will grieve yourself to death over their denial, if they ˹continue to˺ disbelieve in this message”*), and the sūrah of the Spider says that he never read a book before this one and never wrote one with his hand, which is the reason the doubters would have had if he had (29:48 states it — *“You ˹O Prophet˺ could not read any writing ˹even˺ before this ˹revelation˺, nor could you write at all. Otherwise, the people of falsehood would have been suspicious”*). The verse in front of the reader places the mission in the category of a gift rather than a plan the Prophet made for himself, and the sūrah has just told the story of Moses, who was also called to a task he had not expected (28:46 — *“And you were not at the side of Mount Ṭûr when We called out ˹to Moses˺.”* tells how the call came to him on the side of the mountain).

**Why the Book Calls Itself Mercy**

The Book describes itself as mercy in several places, and the description matters because it tells the reader what the message is for. The sūrah of the Bee introduces the Book as guidance and mercy for the believers (16:89 names both — *“We have revealed to you the Book as an explanation of all things, a guide, a mercy, and good news for those who ˹fully˺ submit”*), and the sūrah of the Crowd says that the Book was given as a mercy and a reminder (39:1 — *“The revelation of this Book is from Allah—the Almighty, All-Wise”* states the book's truth and the wider passage names the mercy it brings). The same sūrah in front of the reader says that God gives the Prophet the Book and the wisdom and teaches him what he did not know (4:113 states that gift in the sūrah of the women — *“Allah has revealed to you the Book and wisdom and taught you what you never knew.”*). So the verse's word mercy is not decoration: the commands, the warnings, and the stories are all part of the mercy, which means the reader should read them as help rather than as heavy demands.

**What the Command Not to Side With Them Means**

The verse closes with an instruction to the Prophet not to be a helper to the men who reject the message. This is not an instruction about rudeness or about hatred of people; the Book tells the community elsewhere to deal kindly with people who do not fight them and do not drive them out of their homes (60:8 states the rule — *“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes. Surely Allah loves those who are fair”*), and the sūrah of the Heights tells the Prophet to be patient and not to be like the man who was swallowed by the fish (68:48 gives the comparison with Jonah — *“So be patient with your Lord’s decree, and do not be like ˹Jonah,˺ the Man of the Whale, who cried out ˹to Allah˺, in total distress”*). What the verse forbids is the support that would give the rejection of God's message more weight in the community. The Book makes the same point to the community when it tells them not to lean towards the men who have wronged so that the fire touches them (11:113 gives the warning — *“And do not be inclined to the wrongdoers or you will be touched by the Fire. For then you would have no protectors other than Allah, nor would you be helped”*), and the sūrah in front of the reader has already told the believers to settle their disputes back in God's hands, which is the safe place.

**What the Verse Leaves the Reader With**

The verse leaves the reader with two facts about the message: it was not expected, and it is a mercy. The sūrah has been telling the story of Moses and the destruction of the men who thought they were beyond the law, and it has just stated the rule that the final home belongs to men who do not seek injustice (28:83 gives that rule — *“That ˹eternal˺ Home in the Hereafter We reserve ˹only˺ for those who seek neither tyranny nor corruption on the earth. The ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous”*). The verse in front of the reader tells the Prophet, and through him the community, why the message arrived: not because he asked for it, and not to crush him, but because God intended mercy for the people who would take it. The same sūrah had already described what happens to the men who refuse it in the verse that follows, which tells the Prophet that he cannot guide the men whose hearts are set (28:56 states that — *“You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills, and He knows best who are ˹fit to be˺ guided”*), and it closed its account of Moses with the reminder that the story of the men of the past is a warning and a mercy for the community (28:43 speaks of the mercy that came to them — *“Indeed, We gave Moses the Scripture—after destroying earlier nations—as an insight for the people, a guide, and mercy so perhaps they would be mindful”*).
verses.87:
> Do not let them turn you away from the revelations of Allah after they have been sent down to you. Rather, invite ˹all˺ to ˹the Way of˺ your Lord, and never be one of the polytheists

**Two Audiences for One Command**

The commentators preserved two answers to who this command was first addressed to. Some said it came when Quraysh tried to get the Prophet ﷺ to speak well of their gods, the compromise that would have dissolved the message into their shrine. Others held that the real audience was the believers as a whole.

The widening matters. Whatever the first occasion was, the command outgrew it, because the pressure it names never goes away. Every generation of believers inherits the same three duties: hold on to the signs that have been delivered, keep calling people to them, and keep the belief clean. Every generation has its own group quietly bargaining, its own soft request that the recitation be recited a little less. That the command travels so well is part of how the Qur'an is built. Instructions given to the Prophet ﷺ at the point of greatest pressure become the community's standing work at every pressure afterwards.

**The Verse Before the Closing Statement**

The verse's place in the sūrah's last movement shows what it is doing. The Prophet ﷺ has been given the promise of his return (28:85 gives it — *“Most certainly, the One Who has ordained the Quran for you will ˹ultimately˺ bring you back home ˹to Mecca˺. Say, “My Lord knows best who has come with ˹true˺ guidance and who is clearly astray.”*), the assurance about the Book (28:86 gives it — *“You never expected this Book to be revealed to you, but ˹it came˺ only ˹as˺ a mercy from your Lord. So never side with the disbelievers ˹in their disbelief˺”*), and now the standing orders for the work (28:87 gives them — *“Rather, invite ˹all˺ to ˹the Way of˺ your Lord, and never be one of the polytheists”*), right before the chapter closes on its plainest statement of belief (28:88 gives it — *“And do not invoke any other god with Allah. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. Everything is bound to perish except He Himself. All authority belongs to Him. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned”*).

The sequence is a commissioning in miniature: the return secured, the source of the message made clear, the duty laid down, and then the belief that gives the whole thing its power. The reader who stands at the chapter's edge holds the same sequence as his own commission. His return is promised, his trust is assigned, his call is standing, and the words of belief are about to be said one last time as the sūrah ends.

Ibn Kathīr reads the prohibition as a protection of the reciter's balance, and the reassurance behind it as the sūrah's closing doctrine. Do not let their opposition affect you or put people off from your way, he writes; do not worry about it or pay it any attention — for Allah will make His word supreme, will support His religion, and will make the message with which He has sent you prevail over all the other religions. The command to invite and the promise of supremacy are one sentence: the calling continues while the opposition exists, and the outcome the caller is not asked to carry is the outcome God has already reserved.
verses.88:
> And do not invoke any other god with Allah. There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. Everything is bound to perish except He Himself. All authority belongs to Him. And to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned

**Everything Perishes Except His Face**

The verse's center holds the chapter's heaviest clause: everything perishes except His Face — and the commentators' readings circled its exact sense with care. Some read the Face as God Himself, His Self, the Reality. Others as what is turned toward — every object of aspiration other than God coming to nothing; others as the qualifying exception — all things perish except what is done for His countenance, His religion, the deeds by which He is approached. The commentator tradition cited the Prophet's judgment on the poet Labīd — the truest word spoken by an Arab in poetry: Behold! Apart from Allah everything is vain (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2255a) — the pre-Islamic verse that arrived, unaided, at the Qur'an's doctrine. The commentators also carried al-Rāzī's garment image: the tattered robe is called perished though its fibers remain — creation's perishing is its removal from service, not its annihilation, as the Qur'an states elsewhere: the earth will be changed into a different earth and the heavens as well (14:48 — *“˹Watch for˺ the Day ˹when˺ the earth will be changed into a different earth and the heavens as well, and all will appear before Allah—the One, the Supreme”*). Every reading converges on the clause's practical force: the perishable cannot be worshipped as if it held, because holding is precisely what it does not do.

The reading that the Face is God Himself carries its full weight in Ibn Kathīr's gloss, and the gloss is the doctrine in five words. He is eternal, ever lasting, ever living, self-sustaining — and although His creation dies, He will never die. The word *Face* is His own, used for Himself, so that the sentence means everything except Him; and the judgment that follows — His is the decision, and to Him you will be returned — is the administration of the same fact: what perishes cannot decide, and what returns is returned to the One who did not.

**What the Sentence Is Used For**

The verse closes the sūrah on the declaration that nothing lasts but God, that His is the judgement, and that to Him everything returns. The Book uses the sentence about the face of God in the Sūrah of the Most Merciful, where it says that everything on the earth will pass and the face of the Lord will remain (55:26-27 — *“Every being on earth is bound to perish Only your Lord Himself, full of Majesty and Honour, will remain ˹forever˺”*), and the Sūrah of the Cattle states the same truth about the transience of what people attribute to God. The community's preachers used the verse as a statement of the truth that strips the world of its permanence, and the passage around it is addressed to the men who asked the Prophet to give them a sign and to the men of his own city.

**What the Commentators Did With the Word**

The older commentators discussed what the face of God means here, and their answers run along two lines. One reads it as God Himself, so that the sentence describes the destruction of every created thing and the remaining of its Creator. The other reads the words as a statement of the direction of worship and reliance, that only God is sought. The sūrah itself supplies the answer to the second half, since it says that judgement belongs to Him and that people will be returned to Him, and the verse's own words on either side of the clause put the whole sentence in the language of the end of things.

**Where the Sūrah Ends**

The verse before it tells the Prophet not to call on any god besides God, and it warns that the same destruction applies to everything but Him. The sūrah's last movement is therefore a statement about who is relied on, delivered to a community that had been offered gods and signs for years. The Book ends the account of Moses, the palace and the sea with this sentence, and the placement tells the reader what the whole story was about.
